Title: Ex-councillor Magliocca opposes remote witnesses in fraud trial
Body: Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca is opposed to the Crown calling more than two dozen witnesses 
scattered across the country and beyond via video link on criminal charges.
Defence counsel Aryan Sadat said Monday he only learned this past weekend that Crown prosecutor Aaron Rankin 
intends to call much of his case through remote witness testimony.
But Rankin said the list of witnesses, mostly people allegedly falsely named as recipients of booze or food paid for 
by Magliocca, should not be inconvenienced by having to come to Calgary to give brief evidence.
Rankin told Justice Gord Wong that many of the proposed 27 witnesses are currently serving politicians who don't 
want their schedules interrupted by a trip to Cowtown.
""Mr. Sadat advised me his client would not consent to remote testimony for any witness,"" Rankin told the Calgary 
Court of Justice judge.
Among the proposed witnesses are current Halifax Mayor Mike Savage, former Quebec City council member and 
current Quebec provincial cabinet minister Jonatan Julien, and former Peterborough, Ont. council member 
Stephen Wright, who now resides in Australia.
The remainder of the 27 proposed witnesses reside across Canada.
Magliocca, 59, faces charges of breach of trust by a public officer and fraud over allegations he was reimbursed 
for expenses at outof-
town functions that weren't actually incurred.
Rankin said the witnesses aren't expected to give lengthy testimony when they do give evidence during the trial, 
which is set to run over 11 days until Sept. 26.
""These people attended municipal government conferences not located in Calgary,"" he said.
But Sadat argued there was no evidence any of the witnesses were reluctant to travel to Calgary and suggested the 
prosecutor should have filed affidavits supporting that contention.
Page 2 of 2
Ex-councillor Magliocca opposes remote witnesses in fraud trial
Instead, Rankin called lead investigator, RCMP Const. David Mitchell, who went over several short transcripts of 
interviews with the proposed witnesses showing their statements were brief.
Mitchell said several of the proposed witnesses, such as current Ontario Liberal party Leader Bonnie Crombie, 
brought up the issue of interrupting their busy schedules.
Wong will hear further submissions from Sadat on whether to allow the remote testimony on Day 2 of the trial this 
Friday.

Title: Farewell to the Islamophobia and antisemitism czars; Comment Is the committee replacing them up to the job?
Body: The era of Islamophobia and antisemitism czars is over in Ottawa. Henceforth, the federal government announced 
Wednesday, a new Advisory Council on Rights, Equality and Inclusion will seize itself with such issues in a broader 
fashion, outside of the existing ""silos."" It's a defensible move. But it's worth remembering what a disaster the 
Islamophobia position, in particular, was from the get-go.
At the beginning of February 2023, controversy was raging among Quebec's chattering classes over the 
appointment of Amira Elghawaby as Canada's first Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia. Every 
party in the province's legislature voted to condemn her appointment except the far-left Québec Solidaire, which 
abstained, but days later announced she wasn't ""the right person"" for the job.
Elghawaby's crime, essentially, was to suggest there was Islamophobia in Quebec, which there certainly is. (Tune 
into talk radio in Quebec City and you will likely hear totally unabashed, indeed proud fear of Islam!) Her toe-curling 
apologies fell on deaf ears, and rightly so: Not only did she clearly mean say what she said, but she wasn't far 
wrong. ""The majority of Quebecers appear to be swayed not by the rule of law, but by anti-Muslim sentiment,"" 
Elghawaby wrote in the Ottawa Citizen in 2019, with co-author Bernie Farber, opposing Bill 21 - Quebec's law pr -o 
hibiting certain civil servants from wearing religious symbols on the job.
Worse, La Presse discovered, Elghawaby had questioned Quebecois victimhood. After University of Toronto 
professor Joseph Heath argued French Canadians were ""the largest group of people in this country who were 
victimized by British colonialism,"" she remarked on social media, ""I'm going to puke.""
In addition, an open letter signed by 200-odd Quebec professors, authors and secularists, complained about an 
article Elghawaby wrote in 2020 ""in which she equated the cartoons published by Charlie Hebdo with racism."" 
Charlie Hebdo is the provocatively secular satirical French magazine that dared to publish insolent caricatures of 
Muhammad; Islamist terrorists attacked the publication's office and killed 12 people in 2015.
""Does Canada want to promote a woman and a position that so blatantly conflate legitimate freedom of expression 
with racist remarks?"" the letter asked.
It was a hall-of-fame ""two solitudes"" moment: One can imagine people in then prime minister Justin Trudeau's 
office - which had an 18-wheeler's blind spot with respect to Quebec - blinking uncomprehendingly at the backlash. 
In places where the Liberals are used to vacuuming up votes in English Canada, Elghawaby's appointment was 
widely praised in mainstream media.
Page 2 of 3
Farewell to the Islamophobia and antisemitism czars; Comment Is the committee replacing them up to the job?
Pablo Rodriguez, then Canadian heritage minister and Trudeau's Quebec lieutenant (later and briefly leader of 
the Quebec Liberal Party, before flaming out in a corruption scandal) understood which side of the bread was 
buttered. He declared himself ""hurt and upset"" by Elghawaby's views. Montreal MP Marc Miller, however, who was 
at the time minister of Crown-Indigenous relations, stood by Elghawaby.
""What started with a level of concern about some unfortunate statements (by Elghawaby) is starting to look like a 
pile on, and we're very aware of where that's coming from,"" he said. ""So I think we have to be careful as a nation, 
as people instrumentalize fear of the other, particularly those who have not been represented in the public space, 
like Muslims.""
Miller ""refused to elaborate on where such sentiment was originating,"" The Canadian Press observed. But he didn't 
need to elaborate: He was calling Elghawaby's Quebec critics Islamophobic ... even as he criticized her for saying 
that in so many words.
Today, Miller is heritage minister (now called ""Canadian identity and culture""), and thus nominally in charge of 
defending the elimination of the Islamophobia and antisemitism secretariats. And doesn't he sound a bit different!
""As the world becomes more dangerous and divided, we must hold on to the truth that far more unites us than 
divides us,"" he burbled on X on Wednesday. ""That's why we're creating a new Advisory Council to support our 
efforts to combat hatred and racism, one grounded in our shared values and communities.""
An advisory council ... on ""hatred and racism"" ... that focuses on what ""unites us"" rather than ""divides us""? That 
sounds like a neat trick. One wonders if it'll be worth the hassle.
Look, if you accept that any czar, envoy or advisory committee can make a difference on files like these, then the 
concept makes some sense. One of the problems with appointing specific envoys for specific prejudices is that it 
can become a sort of contest over who's most oppressed - witness the ""I'm going to puke"" remark.
Deborah Lyons, Canada's second official antisemitism envoy (after Irwin Cotler), made the following trenchant 
observation upon resigning in July three months before the end of her term (she was never replaced): ""Support to 
one community should never mean, or be interpreted as, minimizing another community. Our value of inclusivity 
has at its core our ability to hold the concerns of multiple communities in our hearts and minds.""
This new committee will be tasked with doing just that. And of course its success, or even viability, will depend 
entirely on who's appointed to it. And unless they appoint someone willing to massage Quebec's feelings, which 
would defeat the whole stated point of the exercise, they're going to run into the same controversy they did three 
years ago with Elghawaby.
Miller, at least, won't have any problem shifting gears if it all goes wrong.

Title: Final arguments in Law Society case against Alberta 's former justice minister
Body: CALGARY - The lawyer for a former Alberta cabinet minister who is alleged to have broken the legal profession's 
code of conduct says complaints against his client were politically motivated, while counsel for the Law Society of 
Alberta says he was trying to quell legitimate public debate.
The allegations against Tyler Shandro, dating back to his time as provincial health minister early in the COVID-19 
pandemic, involve an interaction with a longtime friend and party colleague about a social media post and two 
family doctors in central Alberta the former minister contacted about their concerns. 
""These are all efforts to make an attack on Shandro's political activities and that should be a factor this panel 
considers in dismissing each of these complaints as not having the appropriate nexus as to the practice of law,"" 
said Grant Stapon, in his final argument to the Law Society of Alberta panel.
""I want you to consider the difference between prosecution and persecution in a case like this.""
The lengthy hearings into the three complaints began in January. Shandro, who was later moved to the justice 
portfolio, was defeated in the May provincial election.
Dr. Mukarram Zaidi, who had posted a photo on social media of Shandro with a caption related to privatizing health 
care, earlier told the hearing the minister and his wife visited his home in March 2020. He said it occurred during 
fractious negotiations between the government and the Alberta Medical Association over fees. 
The photo of Shandro, with a thought bubble caption, said: ""So every Albertan that I can kick off health care is 
another client we can sign up for Vital Partners. We're going to be RICH."" Shandro's wife, Andrea, is the co-founder 
of Vital Partners, a health insurance agency. 
Zaidi said he agreed to take the post down.
In the other cases, two physicians from Red Deer confronted Shandro at an event and one demanded to know why 
he didn't speak to doctors who work in the hospital. 

Page 2 of 3
Final arguments in Law Society case against Alberta 's former justice minister
Shandro found their phone numbers and called both doctors. They talked to him, but said they were upset he had 
obtained their phone numbers and felt intimidated.
Stapon said Shandro was acting as a private citizen in his dealings with Zaidi. In his conversations with the other 
physicians, he was not acting as a lawyer, Stapon said. 
Stapon said this wasn't a case involving misappropriation of funds, breach of trust or fraud.
""None of it involved the practice of law … I'm going to submit he's even innocent of this — it's the equivalent of 
jaywalking.""
But Law Society counsel Ken McEwan wants sanctions against Shandro. He said in a credibility assessment, it's 
the evidence of the witnesses that should be preferred.
""There is a pattern of the respondent … attempting to quell legitimate public debate or criticism by improper 
communications, having the effect and design to intimidate a series of individuals,"" McEwan said. 
""Each involved the respondent engaging in impulsive behaviour, each involves the respondent using inappropriate 
means and methods of communication, each involves the respondent being unable to accept political criticism."" 
A decision on potential sanctions is to be made at a later date. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2023.

Title: Finance head reinstated in Kanesatake
Body: Marie-Claude Bernard, the former finance head for the disbanded Emergency Response Unit (ERU), has been 
reinstated to her position at the Mohawk Council of Kanesatake (MCK) finance department following a labour 
tribunal ruling, the MCK has announced.
A police investigation into the ERU is still ongoing, years after a scandal first broke alleging misappropriation of 
funds intended for COVID-19 pandemic relief, in which members of the ad hoc body were accused of financial 
mismanagement that included large “top-ups,” in which ERU members were paid two salaries.
The report summary also flagged a number of transactions deemed suspicious by the auditor.
Bernard did not respond to multiple requests for comment for this article, but soon after the audit summary was 
released in summer 2022, she told The Eastern Door, “I don’t know how they did the audit, but nobody ever 
contacted me, so I’m sure there’s a lot of wrong things in it, and they need more information.”
She returned to work this week at her previous salary, according to MCK chief Brant Etienne. As Council’s finance 
manager, she was being paid $2,288 biweekly, according to the audit summary. She received an additional $4,720 
biweekly for her role as the ERU’s finance head during the same period, which covers April 2020 to July 2021, for a 
total of $231,122 in that time.
A response from former ERU members after the audit summary was released pointed to overtime compensation as 
a reason for such elevated numbers.
Bernard’s employment was terminated by the MCK near the beginning of this Council term, according to Etienne, 
but Bernard responded with a wrongful dismissal complaint that led to her reinstatement this week.
Other details are yet to be determined, Etienne said.
“She was unjustly dismissed according to the tribunal, she’s been reinstated, and for now we have other things to 
deal with,” he said.
The press release announcing her return indicated that “an evaluation of her case will be conducted” in the new 
year, however this is not a reference to any sanction; rather, it refers to her role in the department, which has been 

Page 2 of 3
Finance head reinstated in Kanesatake
severely understaffed since the recent departure of the subsequent finance manager, Ami-Lee Trentin Hannaburg, 
who accepted a position at the Kanesatake Health Center (KHC).
“Our focus is on making sure the finances of the community are stable, all the bills are being paid, all the employees 
are getting their salaries, that everything is in the black, and it has been for the last four years,” said Etienne.
While Council would be compelled by a ruling to allow Bernard to return, Etienne – who was not in Council at the 
time of the ERU – said he has not seen hard evidence that in his view determines the guilt of any ERU members.
“All of that information that was being fed to people prior to the election and right after, they should rethink if that 
was true or not. If the investigation does find something, then at that time we’ll take action, but so far, where’s the 
body? Where’s the evidence?” he said.
He suggested the ERU investigation has been used as a political wedge by MCK grand chief Victor Bonspille, who 
has railed against the defunct pandemic response unit at public meetings for years.
Bonspille invoked the ERU scandal in comments directly to prime minister Justin Trudeau at the Assembly of First 
Nations (AFN) special chiefs’ assembly earlier this month. There, he said the investigation had been elevated from 
fraud to embezzlement.
Bonspille did not reply to a request for comment for this article.
According to Etienne, the MCK subsequently clarified with police that there was no change in focus.
Contacted by The Eastern Door, Surete du Quebec spokesperson Marc Tessier suggested any determination of 
this nature is premature.
“I can only say that it is an investigation,” Tessier wrote. “It is the result of the investigation which will subsequently 
determine the type of possible accusation. (Example: this involves fraud, embezzlement, breach of trust, etc.)”
The MCK also announced the position of finance clerk was filled this month, easing the burden on the department, 
which still needs to submit the 2023-2024 financial statements that will be made available online and were due in 
July.

Title: FIRST READING: A brief history of politicians calling for Trudeau's resignation
Body: First Reading is a daily newsletter keeping you posted on the travails of Canadian politicos, all curated by the 
National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early version sent directly to your inbox, sign up( 
https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ )here.
TOP STORY
The last week saw two politicians make headlines by calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. 
Former Conservative cabinet minister Joe Oliver did so in the National Post( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/joe-
oliver-for-the-good-of-canada-justin-trudeau-should-go ), which isn't too surprising. More unexpected is the warning 
that came from Liberal-appointed Senator Percy Downe, who said in a new column that the Liberal Party is 
unelectable( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/liberal-heavyweight-calls-for-new-party-leader-predicts-trudeau-
will-decide-soon-whether-to-quit ) so long as Trudeau remains at the helm.
And both Oliver and Downe are in line with current public opinion on this. A recent poll( 
https://angusreid.org/trudeau-step-down-liberal-leadership-poilievre-carney-freeland/ ) by the Angus Reid Institute 
found that 57 per cent of Canadians - including a not-insubstantial number of Liberals - wanted someone new in 
the PMO. That's almost exactly the same finding as an August Abacus Data poll that found 56 per cent of 
Canadians wanting Trudeau's resignation.
It's certainly not unusual for a Canadian prime minister to face public calls for his resignation. So far this year, the 
word ""resign"" or ""resignation"" has been entered into the public record( 
https://openparliament.ca/search/?q=Date%3A%20%221995-11%20to%202023-11%22%20resignation ) more than 
350 times on Parliament Hill - which is about average.
'Omnishambolic foreshadowing': Inside the (indecipherable) thoughts of Mélanie Joly( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/satire-dear-diary-melanie-joly )
Armin Navabi: Queers for Palestine's unholy alliance with Islamic fundamentalists( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/queers-for-palestines-unholy-alliance-with-islamic-fundamentalists )
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: A brief history of politicians calling for Trudeau's resignation
Trudeau has arguably gotten more of these calls than usual. Opposition leaders usually avoid using the ""r word"" 
until they're reasonably sure it's going to yield results. But if there's one thing that's defined Trudeau's premiership, 
it's the ability to plough through scandals that would have ruined any other Commonwealth leader.
Below, a chronological list of all the times that a parliamentarian, past parliamentarian, provincial leader or public 
opinion poll called for Trudeau to resign.
2019: The Tories call for his resignation over SNC-Lavalin
This was the first high-profile call for Trudeau's departure, and the one that sparked international headlines. In the 
midst of revelations that Trudeau had tried to block a bribery prosecution against engineering firm SNC-Lavalin, 
then-Conservative leader Andrew Scheer put out a lengthy statement( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/andrew-scheers-full-statement-calling-for-justin-trudeaus-resignation-over-
snc-lavalin-scandal ) outlining why he thought Trudeau should step down. ""The details are as shocking as they are 
corrupt: multiple veiled threats to her job if she didn't bow to their demands,"" wrote Scheer about Trudeau's 
treatment of his attorney general Jody Wilson-Raybould. He added, ""Mr. Trudeau can no longer, in good standing 
and with a clear conscience, lead this great nation.""
But the only ouster prompted by the scandal was Wilson-Raybould herself, as well as fellow Liberal cabinet 
minister Jane Philpott.
2019: Former premier calls for resignation over blackface photos
When Trudeau's 2019 re-election campaign was derailed by a cascade of photos showing the Liberal leader in 
blackface, it didn't actually prompt all that many resignation calls from official quarters. It was the middle of an 
election, so anybody who would have done so simply figured he would be demoted by voters. But former N.W.T. 
premier Stephen Kakfwi did. ""I think he should come out and be man enough to say, 'There is real consequences 
to holding views and taking actions like this and I, Justin Trudeau, will resign,'"" he told CBC.
2020: The Bloc (and the Tories again) call for resignation over WE Charity scandal
The WE Charity scandal was the one where the Trudeau government sole-sourced a massive contract to WE 
Charity, a group that had paid hundreds of thousands of dollars in speaking fees to Trudeau and his immediate 
family. Scheer was already on the way out as Conservative leader when the details of the scandal first came to 
light, so he threw out one last hail-mary call( https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-scheer-blanchet-call-
on-trudeau-to-resign-over-handling-of-we-charity/ ) for Trudeau's resignation. The prime minister and his finance 
minister Bill Morneau should resign ""for the good of the country,"" said Scheer. And this time he was joined by Bloc 
Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet.
2021: First poll shows majority of Canadians backing resignation
Canadian prime ministers can typically spend almost their entire tenure with approval ratings below 50 per cent. 
But even a hated Canadian prime minister won't necessarily inspire public calls for departure. But after the 2021 
federal election - in which Trudeau's attempt to secure a majority instead yielded a near-identical repeat of the 2019 
election - it was a Maru Public Opinion poll that found Canadians were fed up with the prime minister they had 
just re-elected. Of respondents, 55 per cent said they wanted Trudeau to step aside( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/election-2021/majority-of-canadians-say-trudeau-should-resign-following-
election-believe-country-more-divided-than-ever-poll ) and a new Liberal leader to take charge.
2023: Jean Chrétien's former deputy says resignation is inevitable
John Manley, the former deputy prime minister under Jean Chrétien, didn't outright call for Trudeau to resign 
before the next election. Arguably, Manley did something far worse: He said Trudeau is already doomed, and it 
doesn't really matter if he leaves willingly. ""Change is force of nature in politics,"" Manley told Bloomberg News( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/john-manlet-justin-trudeau-resign-seinfeld ), before citing the ""Seinfeld rule"" - his 
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: A brief history of politicians calling for Trudeau's resignation
personal metric holding that a Canadian prime ministers usually don't last much longer than the nine years that 
Seinfeld was on the air.
IN OTHER NEWS
After years of refusing any concessions whatsoever on the carbon tax, the Liberals recently announced a sudden 
exemption for home heating oil and then sternly warned that no other carve-outs would be coming. The exemption 
was a pretty brazen sop to Atlantic Canada, where the recent imposition of the carbon tax sent Liberal support into 
a tailspin (and where home heating oil usage is wildly disproportionate as compared to the rest of the country). But 
it turns out the NDP had some strong views about this new doctrine of ""East Coasters don't pay carbon tax while 
everybody else does."" This week the NDP teamed up with the Conservatives( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/ndp-
to-back-conservative-carbon-tax-motion ) for a motion that would exempt the tax on all forms of home heating, not 
just the kinds used in Newfoundland and the Maritimes. ""This is an issue of being the adults in the room,"" said 
NDP House Leader Peter Julian, before immediately throwing a barb at the Tories to say that all their other motions 
are ""generally"" crazy and unsupportable.
Green Party co-leader Elizabeth May has never really attempted to be accurate in her characterizations of the Arab-
Israeli conflict (not to mention her party having a bit of a perennial problem with Jews). But on Friday she released a 
statement accusing Israel of ""indiscriminate"" bombings in Gaza. As in; they're just lobbing explosives into the area 
without caring what they hit. This is what Hamas is claiming, but it's not really something repeated by any serious 
analysts of the conflict.
The Supreme Court has once again discovered a new constitutional right. Specifically, they decided that it's ""cruel 
and unusual"" punishment( https://twitter.com/SCC_eng/status/1720437429620871354 ) to prescribe mandatory 
minimum prison sentences for those convicted of child luring. Henceforth, the sentence received by convicted child 
lurers (if one is prescribed at all) will be up to individual judges rather than Parliament. It's not entirely clear what 
kind of imprisonment the Supreme Court actually thinks is constitutional, because they've been doing this a lot. 
Most notoriously, last year the Supreme Court struck down a law that mandated consecutive prison sentences for 
mass murderers. The law held that for every person you killed, you had to spend at least 25 years in jail; so, five 
murders, 125 years in jail. But the Supreme Court ruled that no matter how many murders you rack up, you're still 
up for parole after 25. Their reasoning in that case was similarly that it was ""cruel and unusual punishment"" to 
expect mass killers to die in jail.

Title: FIRST READING: All the Trudeau government's scandals (thus far)
Body: First Reading is a daily newsletter keeping you posted on the travails of Canadian politicos, all curated by the 
National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early version sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Thursday at 
6:30 p.m. ET (and 9:30 a.m. on Saturdays), sign up here( 
https://firstreading.nationalpost.com/p/1?utm_source=Sailthru&;utm_medium=email&;utm_campaign=First%20Rea
ding%20Newsletter%20-%20Mon%20-%20Fri%202021-12-22&;utm_term=PM_Politics_Newsletters ).
TOP STORY
It was only 20 years ago that a Liberal government was brought to the edge of collapse( 
https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/sponsorship-scandal-adscam ) by revelations that they sole-
sourced $4 million in ad contracts to Liberal-friendly marketing firms. And it was 10 years ago that headlines were 
dominated for months by a scandal in which Senator Mike Duffy accepted a $90,000 cheque( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/tasha-kheiriddin-why-the-trial-of-mike-duffy-matters-especially-to-the-conservatives 
) from the prime minister's chief of staff in order to pay back invalid expense claims.
All Canadian governments amass scandals, but the government of Justin Trudeau nevertheless stands out for the 
sheer tonnage of official misconduct. Trudeau remains the only prime minister found to have violated the Conflict 
of Interest Act( https://time.com/5652315/trudeau-conflict-interest-violation/ ), and he's attained the rare distinction 
of having scandals that have attained widespread mention in the foreign press( https://www.bbc.com/news/world-
us-canada-49760160 ). When Canada's Ethics Commissioner stepped down earlier this year, he noted with 
exasperation that he had been forced to investigate Liberal ministers more than two dozen times( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/ethics-commissioner-trudeau-liberals-lapses ) since 2018.
It would be too difficult to list all of them, so here's our best effort at listing the ones that have happened since the 
last federal election in September, 2021.
(As for the main pre-2021 scandals, here's a quick summary: SNC-Lavalin( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/election-2019/the-snc-lavalin-scandal-heres-whats-true-and-whats-false ), 
Aga Khan( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/conservatives-demand-to-know-if-trudeau-used-loophole-to-avoid-
fraud-charges ), We Charity( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/ethics-commissioner-clears-trudeau-in-we-
charity-scandal ), alleged Kokanee groping( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/justin-trudeau-responds-to-
groping-allegation ) and blackface( https://nationalpost.com/news/trudeau-revisits-blackface-embarrassment-during-
black-history-month ).)
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: All the Trudeau government's scandals (thus far)
The Chinese interference scandal
This one has several parts and technically stretches all the way back to 2016, when one of the first scandals( 
https://torontosun.com/2016/12/11/trudeaus-pay-for-play-scheme-can-get-a-lot-worse-2 ) of the newly elected 
Trudeau government surrounded the prime minister's attendance at ""pay for play"" fundraisers featuring Chinese 
billionaires.
But the core of the scandal is a series of CSIS leaks, primarily released through the Globe and Mail, holding that 
the Trudeau government had openly ignored warnings about Chinese attempts to swing the results of the last two 
federal elections. The alleged Chinese efforts weren't massive - a laundered donation here, a disinformation post 
there - but it was apparently being conducted so brazenly from Chinese consulates that it would have been 
relatively easy for Ottawa to shut it down. As to why they didn't, it's not helping the optics of the scandal that the 
Chinese interference was all directed towards getting Liberals elected.
Meanwhile, another CSIS leak hinted that the Chinese government has been openly trying to influence-peddle 
Trudeau almost since he first entered politics in 2008. And just this month came allegations that CSIS also passed 
on a 2020 warning that Chinese agents were attempting to target the Hong Kong family of Conservative MP 
Michael Chong - only for the Prime Minister's Office to ignore it just like everything else.( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/ottawa-summons-chinese-ambassador-over-threats ) Trudeau has 
maintained through everything he was not made aware of China being up to anything unseemly.
The Lucki Affair
One of the most notable results of the Mass Casualty Commission - the probe into Canada's worst-ever mass 
shooting - was how it revealed that RCMP Commissioner Brenda Lucki had tried to interfere in the early stages of 
the massacre's investigation for the explicit purpose of obtaining cover for a planned Liberal gun ban.
As revealed in the Commission-tabled notes of Nova Scotia RCMP Superintendent Darren Campbell, Lucki had 
demanded that investigators make public the types of firearms used in the massacre. The local RCMP refused, 
arguing that withholding the information could help them track the weapons' origins in the United States. To this, 
Lucki berated the Nova Scotia Mounties so hard that Campbell would describe some attendees being brought to 
tears (they were all in the first hours of piecing together a mass-shooting, after all).
And according to Campbell's note - as well as the testimony of a civilian employee in the room that day - Lucki had 
been acting on the direct orders of the federal cabinet( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/first-reading-official-
denials-on-the-lucki-affair-dont-seem-to-be-working ), who wanted the information to justify a planned gun ban. As 
Campbell wrote, ""the Commissioner then said ... this was tied to pending gun control legislation that would make 
officers and the public safer.""
Cabinet ministers keep handing sole-sourced contracts to friends
International Trade Minister Mary Ng said she became so overwhelmed by media requests during the COVID-19 
pandemic that she had to commission $20,000 in media training from a close friend. Even after the Ethics 
Commissioner informed Ng that her actions were pretty clearly a violation of the Conflict of Interest Act, Ng would 
tell a House of Commons committee that she had no idea( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/mary-ng-ethics-
government-contracts ) you weren't supposed to sole-source contracts to friends.
""Media training"" was also the culprit when it emerged in January that a staffer inside the office of Housing Minister 
Ahmed Hussen had paid $93,050 in constituency funds( https://globalnews.ca/news/9424015/hussens-office-93k-
pr-work-foodie-firm/ ) to her sister, who ran a food marketing company called Munch More Media. The Ministry of 
Housing did not need food marketing help, but the idea was that Munch More Media could branch out into political 
PR.
Hiring a cabinet minister's sister-in-law as Ethics Commissioner
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: All the Trudeau government's scandals (thus far)
That exasperated Ethics Commissioner mentioned in the introduction? When the Trudeau government named his 
interim successor, they went with Martine Richard. She was a veteran lawyer in the commissioner's office, but she 
also happened to be the sister-in-law of Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc. Richard would step 
down( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/liberal-cabinet-ministers-sister-in-law-resigns-as-federal-interim-
ethics-commissioner ) after a House of Commons committee decided to probe her appointment for anything hinky.
ArriveCan overspending
This is another one that didn't inherently break any laws (so much as we're aware). It's just another case of the 
government spending way more money on something than would make reasonable sense. ArriveCan - a glitchy 
and oft-criticized mobile app that was mandatory for travellers entering Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic - 
somehow managed to cost $54 million( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/in-two-days-a-single-programmer-
duplicated-arrivecan-an-app-that-cost-ottawa-54-million ).
Software development is expensive, but $54 million was so beyond the pale that in October a team of coders 
decided to stage a ""hackathon"" to see how quickly they could rebuild ArriveCan from scratch. It took them two days. 
Estimates at the time from smartphone app insiders estimated that ArriveCan should conceivably have cost no 
more than $2 million.
IN OTHER NEWS
The arrival of Mother Day's once again peppered the land with miniature culture wars. First, there was a Toronto 
elementary school that apologized( 
https://torontosun.com/opinion/columnists/agar-shame-on-tdsb-for-changing-
schools-mothers-day-message ) for posting an allegedly ""mega exclusionary"" message on its front sign reading ""life 
does not come with a manual it comes with a mom."" And then a Quebec school received backlash from the 
province's Conservative Party after they phased out Mother's Day commemorations in favour( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/controversy-after-quebec-teachers-replace-mothers-day-with-celebration-of-
parents ) of a gender non-specific celebration of parents.
The good news on the Chinese interference scandal is that the People's Republic of China has apparently been 
clandestinely screwing with Canada's internal affairs for more than a generation now. In testimony before a House 
of Commons committee this week, former CSIS senior official Michel Juneau-Katsuya said that( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/china-has-interfered-for-decades-mps-told ) Chinese officials have been 
attempting to influence Canadian policy and elections almost since the beginning of diplomatic relations between 
the two countries. ""We can prove that every federal government from Mr. Mulroney to Mr. Trudeau (has) been 
compromised by agents of Communist China. Every government was informed at one point or another. Every 
government chose to ignore CSIS warnings,"" he said. He then added that up to 70 per cent of Chinese diplomats in 
Canada are spending most of their time on interference and should be expelled.
This is Alberta premier Danielle Smith being whisked out of a press conference by security after it was crashed by 
protesters on Thursday. Both sides in the Alberta provincial election condemned the protest, and as Postmedia 
columnist Don Braid wrote, the whole affair occurred amid a campaign that is particularly worried about the risk of 
violence.
In the final years of the government of Stephen Harper, the power behind the curtain was generally acknowledged 
to be Jenni Byrne, Harper's deputy chief of staff. She also testified before a House of Commons committee this 
week about Chinese interference. While she predictably had strong critiques( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/former-top-harper-staffer-conservative-campaign-lead-says-she-wasn-t-briefed-on-
foreign-interference-1.6394325 ) about the Liberals' handling of the current interference scandal, she denied 
Juneau-Katsuya's assertion that her government had similarly been assailed with warnings about Chinese 
interference that they subsequently ignored.
Governor General Mary Simon has a number of official duties, but she basically has just one job: To represent and 
uphold the monarchy in Canada. So it's a little weird that she recently went on record hinting that Canada should 
maybe consider becoming a republic. ""I think Canada ... has to have a plan and an alternative as to what it is we 
Page 4 of 4
FIRST READING: All the Trudeau government's scandals (thus far)
want as a country,"" she told the Globe and Mail( https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/monarchists-blast-gg-king-
charles-1.6840207 ). The interview also featured her openly criticizing King Charles III for being less popular than 
his mother, Queen Elizabeth II. And this is probably where we should mention that it's near-impossible( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/dont-like-the-monarchy-too-bad-canada-made-it-impossible-to-get-rid-of-them ) for 
Canada to get rid of the monarchy given how strongly it's written into our 1982 Constitution Act.
The Canadian Taxpayer's Federation held their 25th annual Teddy Waste Awards this week, in which they handed 
out golden pigs to government officials who have achieved excellence in the field of overspending. They were many 
top contenders this year, but the top prize (for federal waste, at least) ultimately went to Governor General Mary 
Simon for somehow managing to rack up $100,000 in in-flight catering costs during a flight to Dubai for the world's 
fair.

Title: FIRST READING: Attack of the Laurentian elite!
Body: First Reading is a daily newsletter keeping you posted on the travails of Canadian politicos, all curated by the 
National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early version sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Thursday at 
6:30 p.m. ET (and 9:30 a.m. on Saturdays), sign up here( 
https://firstreading.nationalpost.com/p/1?utm_source=Sailthru&;utm_medium=email&;utm_campaign=First%20Rea
ding%20Newsletter%20-%20Mon%20-%20Fri%202021-12-22&;utm_term=PM_Politics_Newsletters ).
TOP STORY
One of the hallmarks of the Chinese interference scandal has been the realization of just how deeply incestuous it 
becomes at the top levels of Canadian governance.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, the son of a former prime minister (and the grandson of a former cabinet 
minister) retained a former Governor General to probe his government who just happens to be a longstanding 
family friend.
Then, to allay concerns of a conflict of interest, said Governor General sought a legal opinion from Frank 
Iacobucci, a former Supreme Court justice who already has one Trudeau government contract under his belt, and 
was a peripheral figure in the SNC-Lavalin scandal. Iacobucci also happens to be one of Johnston's friends.
And all three men in the above paragraph have at one point been active members of the Trudeau Foundation.
It's this type of constantly interlocking elite social network that has long inspired the term ""Laurentian elite"" or 
""Laurentian consensus.""
In a deeply heterogeneous country of almost 40 million, the idea is that power remains entrenched among a 
wealthy, well-connected cadre of Quebecers and Ontarians all born within easy reach of the St. Lawrence River 
(hence the ""Laurentian"" part of the term).
Coined in 2011 by political journalist John Ibbitson, the term is not necessarily specific to Liberals or Conservatives, 
but it refers to a general notion of an established gentry who see ""Canada"" as a narrow corridor between Montreal 
and Toronto, with everything else afforded the status of distant colonies.
The Laurentian elite are the supposed reason that Quebec interests dominated the national discourse for decades 
at the expense of Western ones. Or why Ottawa will routinely engineer subsidies and protectionist trade policy for 
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: Attack of the Laurentian elite!
the auto and dairy sectors of the Eastern Time Zone - while actively handicapping the oil and gas industries in the 
Mountain and Central Time Zones.
Ibbitson first used the term at a time when it was believed that the powers of such an elite were waning after more 
than 150 years of undisputed Canadian political dominance.
At the time, Prime Minister Stephen Harper had just won a majority government, and Ibbitson was arguing that the 
Laurentians had been sidelined forever by disaffected Westerners bolstered by conservative-minded immigrant 
newcomers.
Instead, a mere four years later, Canada arguably got the most Laurentian Elite-y prime minister it's had yet. 
Canada had been ruled by political scions before, but never by someone who literally grew up in 24 Sussex and 
had spent their childhood shaking hands with the likes of Margaret Thatcher or Queen Elizabeth II.
Ibbitson was the first to admit that he'd maybe forecast( https://www.tvo.org/transcript/2331711/john-ibbitson-back-
to-the-laurentian-consensus ) the death of his Laurentian Elite a bit early. ""Well, we got too cocky, that's for sure,"" 
Ibbitson told TVO soon after the Trudeau government's 2015 majority victory.
The existence of a Laurentian elite may be a simple reflection of the fact that most of Canada does indeed live 
within the St. Lawrence River watershed.
Pair that with the fact that much of Western Canada has now taken to voting Conservative under almost any 
circumstances, and the natural effect is that Canadian politics will become disproportionately focused on pandering 
to the sentiments of swing voters in Toronto and Montreal.
Constitutional scholar Andrew McDougall for one, has noted that even though Stephen Harper was the ostensible 
standard-bearer for the death of the Laurentian elite, his government ultimately acted pretty well within the 
boundaries of the so-called ""Laurentian consensus.""
""Even for someone who identified as a conservative Westerner ... could not stray too far away from the values at 
the Consensus' heart and realistically hope to remain competitive in Ontario and Quebec,"" wrote McDougall in a 
2020 paper( https://journals.openedition.org/eccs/3850?lang=en ).
But the term lives on, usually as an expression of conservative abuse.
At a 2022 reception marking the birth of the province of Alberta, United Conservative Party cabinet minister Ron 
Orr delivered a lengthy speech slamming ""the family compact of Laurentian elites (that) have always skewed the 
deal in their favour.""
And it's been mentioned 11 times in the House of Commons since 2015, the first coming from Conservative MP 
Rachel Harder, when she accused the Liberals of packing the Senate with ""the new aristocrats, the Laurentian 
elites.""
The most recent coming in March from former Conservative Leader Andrew Scheer, in reference to Trudeau's 
retaining David Johnston as his ""special rapporteur"" on foreign interference.
""Could there be anything more emblematic of the Laurentian elite here in Canada than the Prime Minister 
appointing a family friend from his background in the Laurentian Mountains, at his ski chalet, to investigate whether 
or not there should be a public inquiry into his handling of the foreign interference?"" he said.
IN OTHER NEWS
This probably doesn't need to be mentioned, but the NDP has announced that they'll be reacting to the latest 
development in the Chinese interference scandal by doing nothing. For months, the NDP has joined the 
Conservatives in saying that nothing less than a full public inquiry would be needed to probe allegations that the 
Trudeau government sat on their hands through months of intelligence warnings of an ongoing Chinese 
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: Attack of the Laurentian elite!
interference operation. Nevertheless, after former Governor General David Johnston gave the Liberals cover to 
avoid such an inquiry, NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh told CBC that he will not be threatening to withdraw his party's 
support of the Liberal government in order to force an inquiry. Instead, he'll be using ""other tools.""( 
https://www.reddit.com/r/Canada_sub/comments/13q6519/jagmeet_singh_gets_pressed_about_why_he_will_not/?
utm_source=share&;utm_medium=android_app&;utm_name=androidcss&;utm_term=2&;utm_content=share_butto
n )
Johnston's role as an impartial ""special rapporteur"" has been repeatedly called into question due to his 
longstanding personal ties to the Trudeau family. But Terry Glavin points out another big conflict of interest 
regarding the Governor General: Any full-scale probe into Chinese interference might reveal Johnston's own 
uncomfortably close ties to the Beijing regime( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/terry-glavin-david-johnston-
escapes-inquiry-into-his-own-china-dealings ). As Governor General, it was obviously Johnston's job to be nice to 
China whenever asked to do so. But even before becoming the vice-regent, Johnston nurtured close ties with China 
and was instrumental in the setting up of the University of Waterloo Confucius Institute. Pitched as university 
outposts of Chinese ""soft power,"" in recent years the institutes have been shuttered across Europe and North 
America due to their controversially close links to Chinese state authorities.

Title: FIRST READING: Here's all the Liberal memoirs that have bashed Trudeau (so far)
Body: First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ ).
TOP STORY
Former Liberal environment minister Catherine McKenna just released a new book, and attention has focused 
immediately on how it reserves harsh words for her former boss, Justin Trudeau.
And this has happened several times already: A retired Trudeau cabinet minister releases a memoir, and the book 
contains condemnations of Trudeau. What's more, the criticisms are different. Some slam Trudeau's grasp of 
economics. Others blame him for detonating Canada's global reputation. Others blast him as a hypocrite and a 
tokenist.
Below, a cursory guide to Liberal memoirs and their explicitly anti-Trudeau passages.
Run Like a Girl
Catherine McKenna
McKenna served as Trudeau's environment minister during the years when the party's climate policy was still quite 
popular. Climate change regularly ranked as one of Canadians' top political concerns upon the Trudeau 
government first coming to power in 2015, and the carbon tax was initially greeted with acclaim - in sharp contrast 
to the deep ire it would attract in later years.
But while McKenna wrote that she and Trudeau were sympatico on their environmental sensibilities, she developed 
a problem with his constant virtue signalling. She wrote that she particularly objected to his regular boasts about a 
cabinet that was 50 per cent female.
""By making it such a big deal, Trudeau put the spotlight on his own virtue rather than the hard work and expertise of 
the women around him,"" she wrote, adding that this would become a ""recurring issue.""
""The prime minister liked to remind people that he was a feminist. Inevitably, when issues arose with strong 
women in Cabinet or caucus, his commitment would then be called into question,"" she wrote.
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: Here's all the Liberal memoirs that have bashed Trudeau (so far)
McKenna also accused Trudeau of existing in a ""fortress"" in which he ignored cabinet ministers to the exclusion of 
ones he had personally known as children. ""The prime minister was aloof and just didn't seem interested in his 
ministers or caucus members beyond his childhood friends, Dominic LeBlanc and Marc Miller,"" she wrote.
The result? Wrote McKenna, Canada under Trudeau lacked ""leadership"" and the prime minister never built a ""true 
team.""
Indian in the Cabinet
Jody Wilson-Raybould
Given the circumstances of her departure from cabinet, it was clear that Jody Wilson-Raybould's 2021 memoir was 
not going to be kind to Trudeau. Wilson-Raybould was the central figure in the 2019 SNC-Lavalin scandal. Wilson-
Raybould, then the attorney general, objected to Trudeau's attempt to intervene in a bribery-related prosecution of 
SNC-Lavalin, a prominent Quebec engineering firm. In response, Wilson-Raybould was pushed out of both cabinet 
and the Liberal caucus.
Her book gets into point-by-point detail about her heated final meetings with Trudeau, and is among the most poetic 
about highlighting his alleged character flaws.
Wilson-Raybould wrote that Trudeau betrayed ""her deep desire to believe in people"" and that ""this man was not the 
leader I had thought him to be."" His tone is described as ""aggressive and condescending,"" and Wilson-Raybould 
alleges that he attempted to coach her into participating in a cover-up. ""In that moment, I knew he wanted me to lie 
- to attest that what had occurred had not occurred,"" she wrote.
Where to From Here: A Path to Canadian Prosperity
Bill Morneau
As its title suggests, Bill Morneau's 2023 book is mostly policy prescriptions and doesn't delve too much into the 
interpersonal details of his time as finance minister during Trudeau's first five years.
But Morneau describes how he ultimately lost faith in Trudeau's leadership during the chaotic first months of the 
COVID-19 pandemic. Morneau complained that he had often been up against a government where ""policy 
rationales were tossed aside in favour of scoring political points,"" and that this became untenable during the 
pandemic.
As Morneau described it, his people presented COVID relief measures that were moderate and fiscally responsible, 
only to have them discarded in favour of policies that were more expensive and less protected from abuse.
""During the period when the largest government expenditures as a portion of GDP were made in the shortest time 
since the advent of the Second World War, calculations and recommendations from the Ministry of Finance were 
basically disregarded in favour of winning a popularity contest,"" he wrote.
As for Trudeau personally, his ""management and interpersonal communication abilities were sorely lacking,"" wrote 
Morneau. The ex-finance minister also accused Trudeau's office of orchestrating a series of leaks designed to 
undermine him, writing that they seemed to grow in ""both number and degree of malice.""
It wasn't the first time Morneau had publicly slammed Trudeau as an economic illiterate. The year prior, he had told 
a gathering of the C.D. Howe Institute that the Trudeau government had mostly been concerned about redistributing 
wealth rather than creating it. ""There was little attention given to the importance of increasing our collective 
prosperity - let alone developing a disciplined way of thinking and acting on the problem,"" he said( 
https://www.politico.com/news/2022/06/01/morneau-critiques-trudeau-government-policies-00036606 ).
A Most Extraordinary Ride: Space, Politics and the Pursuit of a Canadian Dream
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: Here's all the Liberal memoirs that have bashed Trudeau (so far)
Marc Garneau
After a working life that included becoming the first Canadian in space, Marc Garneau capped it off with six years in 
the Trudeau cabinet, including five years as minister of transport and nine months as minister of foreign affairs. As 
such, Garneau only briefly touched on his political career in this memoir published just seven months before his 
death in June, at age 76.
But those chapters included Garneau's view that Trudeau's foreign policy had prioritized style over substance, 
causing the rest of the world to increasingly ignore Ottawa's input on international issues.
""Unfortunately Canada's standing in the world has slipped, in part because our pronouncements are not always 
matched by a capacity to act or by actions that clearly demonstrate that we mean what we say,"" Garneau wrote( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/canadas-global-reputation-suffering-under-trudeau-garneau-asserts-in-
autobiography ).
The ex-astronaut singled out Trudeau's disastrous 2018 trip to India, which would become widely mocked for the 
prime minister's flamboyant outfits and diplomatic gaffes, such as inviting a convicted Khalistani terrorist to a 
Government of Canada gala.
This and other trips were ""not successful,"" wrote Garneau. ""At a fundamental level, we did not understand who we 
were meeting. We thought we could seduce and were surprised it didn't turn out that way,"" he wrote.
IN OTHER NEWS
Canada-U.S. relations have measurably deteriorated under the joint tenures of Prime Minister Mark Carney and 
U.S. President Donald Trump. But a surreal facet of the decay is that both Trump and Carney have become 
increasingly over-the-top in their praise of one another. Carney has used all of his in-person meetings with Trump to 
deliver an impromptu soliloquy praising the ""transformative"" U.S. leader. And after their Tuesday meeting at the 
White House, Trump posted this flattering image of the pair to social media along with the caption ""It's an honor to 
have the Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney ... We've had a very strong relationship.""
Marineland has threatened to kill marine mammals at its Niagara Falls attraction unless they are provided with 
emergency government bailout funding. In a threat last week that quickly garnered headlines across the English-
speaking world, Marineland's managers said that they would be forced to euthanize 30 captive belugas unless 
Ottawa ponied up the funds for their care and feeding. Marineland's operations have been hit hard by a series of 
federal restrictions on whale captivity passed in 2019, and after the feds blocked a request to transfer the belugas 
to an aquarium in China, Marineland said they will have to consider the ""devastating decision of euthanasia.""

Title: FIRST READING: Here's when a normal prime minister would have resigned
Body: First Reading is a daily newsletter keeping you posted on the travails of Canadian politicos, all curated by the 
National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here( 
https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ ).
TOP STORY
With Prime Minister Justin Trudeau finally setting an end-date on his time as prime minister, he caps off a term 
that can certainly be described as resilient. Trudeau has weathered any number of scandals that would have 
spelled doom for a conventional political leader. By the standards of almost any other democratic peer, Trudeau 
has whistled past crises that would have been a guaranteed career-ender in the likes of Australia, the U.K., New 
Zealand or much of Europe.
Below, a cursory review of some times when Trudeau, if he was normal leader, probably would have already 
resigned.
SNC-Lavalin scandal
This was the first moment in Trudeau's premiership when the ""r-word"" was repeatedly thrown in his direction. The 
2019 SNC-Lavalin scandal was where Trudeau was accused of using his influence to halt a corruption 
prosecution of SNC-Lavalin, a Quebec engineering firm with strong Liberal party ties. The scandal yielded the 
resignation of two cabinet ministers - Jody Wilson-Raybould and Jane Philpott - and a subsequent probe would 
determine that Trudeau had indeed broken the law by seeking to interfere with the workings of the Ministry of 
Justice.
Although SNC-Lavalin has since been joined by a lengthy list of other Trudeau government scandals, this one was 
a big deal at the time. For context, the defining scandal of Prime Minister Jean Chrétien - and one of the 
contributors to his own resignation - had been the Sponsorship Scandal, which involved about $1 million in 
misallocated marketing contracts.
In one of Canada's closest Commonwealth cousins, Australia, prime ministers are typically removed via 
""leadership spills."" As soon as a leader starts to waver, their caucus can vote to declare the position vacant, 
triggering a leadership election. And these are often sparked by little more than a bad poll or a mismanaged 
government file; Tony Abbott was ousted in a spill due in part to controversy over his awarding( 
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: Here's when a normal prime minister would have resigned
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2015/feb/08/chastened-tony-abbott-desperately-fights-off-leadership-
challenge ) the Order of Australia to Prince Philip.
So, a spill would have almost certainly been sparked by a leader caught unilaterally attempting to halt a serious 
criminal investigation for political purposes.
Blackface scandal
It's not just that a cascade of photos of Trudeau wearing blackface makeup came out in 2019, it's that it happened 
in the middle of a federal election campaign. The Liberals were never poised to do great in that election, but there 
remains the possibility that if they'd run a good campaign they could have security a second majority.
Instead - amid swirling international coverage of Trudeau's minstrel past - they permanently dropped into minority 
status.
At a provincial level, there's any number of examples of Canadian politicians resigning after an electoral result that 
they technically won - but which illustrated that they'd lost their edge.
Alberta Premier Jason Kenney resigned in 2022 despite winning a leadership review for the United Conservative 
Party. He deemed that the 51.4 per cent margin was too narrow to continue. Similarly, Ontario Premier Dalton 
McGuinty resigned in 2012 after leading his government into minority status; he stepped down soon after his 
Ontario Liberals lost a byelection( https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ontario-liberals-fall-1-seat-shy-of-
majority-after-byelections-1.1247773 ) that would have restored their majority status.
But Trudeau stayed the course after 2019. He may have hoped to reverse the results, but it was instead the 
beginning of a very long decline both for himself and for the Liberal party.
When he was caught surfing on the first National Truth and Reconciliation Day
U.K. Prime Minister Boris Johnson resigned in 2022, due in part to revelations that his staff had been holding 
alcohol-fuelled parties in defiance of the COVID lockdowns that they were imposing on the rest of the country (a 
scandal known as ""Partygate"").
There were other reasons, but Partygate helped galvanize a growing sense of discontent in Johnson's caucus - and 
it ultimately sparked a wave of cabinet resignations that made Johnson's continued leadership untenable.
If Canada operated under British rules, that moment could well have come in 2021, when Trudeau was caught 
taking a clandestine beach vacation on the first annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, a holiday his own 
government had inaugurated. Trudeau had turned in lacklustre performances in two consecutive federal elections, 
his net approval rating had just taken a plunge( 
https://angusreid.org/trudeau-tracker/ ) from which it would never 
recover - and now he was publicly making a mockery of his government's much-trumpeted issue of Indigenous 
reconciliation.
Instead, the incident yielded no resignations, and not even a Liberal MP calling out his actions.
When polls first started showing the Liberals were doomed
At least among Commonwealth governments, Trudeau has often been compared to New Zealand's Jacinda Ardern: 
A young idealist whose popularity began to plummet once the consequences of her high-minded progressive policy 
began to pile up.
Ardern resigned in January 2023, just at the cusp of polls beginning to show that her government was unpopular 
and unlikely to win the next election( https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/dec/05/support-for-jacinda-ardern-
and-nz-labour-sinks-to-lowest-since-2017-poll-shows ).
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: Here's when a normal prime minister would have resigned
If Trudeau had followed the Ardern route, he would have been gone more than a year ago. As early as September 
2023, polls began to consistently show the Conservatives with a double-digit lead over the Liberals - more than 
enough for the Tories to secure victory in a general election. For each of the subsequent 16 months that Trudeau 
has stayed on, those numbers have only gotten worse for him.
IN OTHER NEWS
This happened just before Justin Trudeau announced his (eventual) resignation: A gust of wind kicked up and blew 
away the pages of his speech.
While Prime Minister Justin Trudeau sort of announced( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/justin-trudeau-
resignation-prime-minister ) his resignation today, he did it in a way that may actually extend his term as prime 
minister. The House of Commons had been scheduled to resume on Jan. 27, at which point all the opposition 
parties had promised to vote yes on a non-confidence vote to bring down the government. Thus, given the usual 
length of federal elections, Trudeau was on track to be forced out of office by about mid-March. Under today's 
pledge, the House of Commons is prorogued until March 24. So, depending on how the leadership race shakes out, 
Trudeau may ultimately get an extra week of prime ministering.
It looks like Jagmeet Singh got his pension. It's been a common Conservative talking point that NDP Leader 
Jagmeet Singh's obsequious support of the Trudeau government has been driven largely by his desire to secure a 
gold-plated House of Commons pension. Singh becomes eligible for the pension on Feb. 25, the date when he'll 
have officially been an MP for six years.
Lest we forget, Trudeau's political demise was hastened in large part by a promise from U.S. President Donald 
Trump to impose 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian imports unless Ottawa could better secure their mutual border. 
The tariff issue has been cited often by Liberals in calling for Trudeau's departure. Anyway, Trump celebrated the 
resignation announcement by again calling for Canada to be annexed.

Title: FIRST READING: The Liberal scandal that may have just guaranteed a third Quebec referendum
Body: First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here.( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ )
TOP STORY
As Quebec lurches ever closer towards a third separation referendum, an old-fashioned Liberal vote-buying 
scandal might have just removed the last barrier to its occurrence.
Pablo Rodriguez resigned as Quebec Liberal leader this week amid two major corruption allegations against his 
party, one of them involving cash-filled envelopes.
Rodriguez maintains he had nothing to do with either of them, saying, ""I regret absolutely nothing.""
But the immolation of the Quebec Liberals only solidifies the likelihood that the Parti Québécois will sweep the 
province's 2026 election. Once in power, PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised he will be pulling out 
all the stops to hold a third referendum on secession from Canada.
Quebec's incumbent government, led by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) under François Legault, is currently 
plumbing new depths of unpopularity. As such, the deeply federalist Quebec Liberals were widely seen as the only 
realistic force to thwart the PQ's ascension.
But under the tenure of Rodriguez, the party's popularity has cratered and given the PQ an overwhelming polling 
lead.
As per a Dec. 17 poll published by the Angus Reid Institute, the PQ is polling at 40 per cent to the Liberals' 18 per 
cent.
It's a far cry from the vote shares the PQ could command in the 1980s heyday of Quebec nationalism, but it would 
still be more than enough for the PQ to secure their most commanding majority in a generation.
In recent weeks, the party has even been rolling out serialized chapters of its ""livre bleu,"" its definitive blueprint for 
what an independent Quebec would look like. Its most recent chapter( https://pq.org/livrebleu/ ) detailed which 
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: The Liberal scandal that may have just guaranteed a third Quebec referendum
countries would receive Quebec ambassadors and which international sporting events would be contested by 
Équipe Québec.
Rodriguez is best known to the rest of Canada as the champion of some of the most sweeping controls ever 
enacted on the Canadian internet. As heritage minister under then prime minister Justin Trudeau, he helped 
push through both the Online Streaming Act and the Online News Act.
The Online Streaming Act empowers federal regulators to impose content controls on online platforms ranging from 
Netflix to YouTube. The Online News Act is why Canadians can no longer share news articles on Facebook.
Rodriguez resigned from federal politics in September 2024, part of an exodus( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/most-telling-indicator-liberals-remain-doomed ) of top Liberals quitting the Trudeau 
government as it lurched towards what was then seen as inevitable electoral oblivion.
He was elected Quebec Liberal leader in June, only for his seven-month tenure to be defined by a string of 
corruption scandals.
The main one being that his very election as leader was secured in an alleged vote-buying scheme, a charge 
currently under investigation( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-liberals-vote-
buying-allegations ) by Quebec's anticorruption police. Another being that a Rodriguez fundraising event featured 
attendees being handed envelopes full of cash( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-
liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-campaign-allegations ) on the understanding that they would donate it to the 
campaign in their name, thus skirting Quebec law on contribution caps.
Even if this all means that Quebec voters are likely to vote in a PQ government, it's a different story when it comes 
to their desire for separation.
Canada's ongoing trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped sovereigntist sentiments to historic 
lows, with even many longtime nationalists publicly declaring their allegiance to Ottawa over Washington.
Probably the most noticeable manifestation of this trend was when the Bloc Québécois - the federal voice for 
Quebec independence - spent the 2025 federal election publicly promising not to threaten secession( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/bloc-quebecois-leader-says-he-wont-threaten-to-overthrow-the-government-anytime-
soon-read-more ) until the trade war had subsided.
As of an October Leger poll, a mere 28 per cent of Quebecers favoured full separation of their province from 
Canada( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/30-years-after-quebec-referendum-majority-of-canadians-see-
canada-as-one-nation-poll ). This would be roughly the same as in Alberta, where separatist sentiment was 
hovering at around 24 per cent.
Nevertheless, there are reports that Ottawa is taking this seriously, with federal officials already drafting plans( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/parti-quebecois-fears-ottawa-will-cheat-in-a-third-sovereignty-
referendum ) on how to thwart the ""Oui"" side if secession once again comes to a vote.
According to Legault, however, there not only won't be a referendum, but the end result of all of this is that he'll get 
to continue being premier.
Although Legault has been quite open in acknowledging his unpopularity, in a year-end interview with Radio-
Canada he predicted that the PQ would ultimately botch their lead so badly that Quebecers would be forced to turn 
back to his CAQ.
Legault used to be a PQ cabinet minister, before founding the CAQ with the explicit goal of attracting Quebec 
nationalists who were tired of organizing and losing referenda. Speaking to Radio-Canada, he predicted that the 
PQ's fever over a third referendum would ultimately prove too much.
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: The Liberal scandal that may have just guaranteed a third Quebec referendum
""The PQ won't stay where it is in the polls,"" he said. ""People will understand that Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is 
synonymous with a referendum, and we don't want that.""
IN OTHER NEWS
The Department of Defence has publicly raised the possibility that it might abandon its order of F-35 fighter jets in 
favour of the Swedish-made Saab Gripen. This is despite the fact that a leaked Canadian Armed Forces scoring 
chart that the F-35 bested the Gripen in every category they tested. But the graph above is from a recent Ekos poll 
finding that a plurality of respondents still like the Gripen anyway.
At the exact same time that two U.S. states are designating the Council on Islamic-American Relations (CAIR) as a 
terror entity, Canada seems to be doing the exact opposite.
The National Council of Canadian Muslims was founded as the Canadian chapter of CAIR, before rebranding in 
2013( https://www.ourcommons.ca/DocumentViewer/en/41-2/SECU/meeting-60/evidence ). In just the last two 
weeks, the NCCM participated in leading a delegation of Canadian MPs( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/canadian-mission-to-west-bank-fabricated-a-political-crisis ) to the Middle East, 
and also received an official goodwill visit from Dan Rogers, the director of CSIS, Canada's main spy agency. 
Rogers also just sent a lengthy apology to the NCCM( https://x.com/nccm/status/1999545114931102041/photo/1 ), 
in response to their complaints that he wasn't sufficiently addressing Islamophobia.
Meanwhile, the U.S. states of Florida and Texas just declared CAIR a ""foreign terrorist organization."" Florida's 
declaration, issued by Governor Ron DeSantis( 
https://www.flgov.com/eog/sites/default/files/executive-
orders/2025/EO%2025-244.pdf ), stated that it was ""founded by persons connected to the Muslim Brotherhood and 
was created, in the words of persons affiliated with CAIR, as 'an official U.S. cover representing the Islamic 
community' to conceal ties to Islamic extremist groups.""
Toronto just completed construction of a $3.7 billion LRT line that is so slow that runners have taken it upon 
themselves to race the train by foot. Above is a screenshot from an Instagram video in which a user known as 
514Runner ran the entire length of the line with a time that was 18 minutes faster than the train itself.
