Title: AI-driven website digs into lobbying; Online tool highlights concerning connections in federal contracts
Body: The new frontier of government accountability could be a colourful, AI-generated image connecting the dots 
between all the different players in one of Canada's messiest procurement controversies.
The Phoenix pay systemwhich was designed to centralize payroll for the federal government but quickly racked up 
a long list of issues including overpayments, underpayments and missed payments - is estimated to have cost 
nearly $5 billion.
The replacement software is now estimated to cost more than $4 billion, putting the total price tag of the calamity at 
nearly $10 billion, according to auditor general Karen Hogan last week.
Now, using the government's lobbying registry, auditor general reports, media stories and govern- ment news 
releases, a new interactive website is drawing a vivid picture of the complicated and frenzied lobbying activity 
beneath the surface of big-money government contracts. And the code can be used to generate a similar map of 
any government contract or program.
For example, click on the ""revolving door"" button on the ""Dayforce × Phoenix Pay System - Lobbying &; 
Relationship Map"" and you'll find people who have moved from government work to related private-sector 
employment.
The website highlights Gianluca Cairo, the former chief of staff to the federal innovation minister, who was in 
government while the Phoenix fiasco played out.
He then joined Ceridian HCM Holding Inc., which was then one of the leading bidders to replace the pay system. In 
the end, Ceridian's Dayforce software won the contract and the federal ethics commissioner cleared Cairo's move, 
as long as he obeyed ethics rules around lobbying the government in his new role.
When Cairo was hired by Ceridian, the Globe and Mail wrote that it was part of the company's ""charm offensive in 
the past two years to make inroads in Ottawa.""
Page 2 of 4
AI-driven website digs into lobbying; Online tool highlights concerning connections in federal contracts
Also in the ""revolving door"" tab of the website is Regan Watts, a former Conservative government staffer who 
logged a series of entries in the lobbying registry for Dayforce. None of the players identified on the website are 
alleged to have broken any ethics rules.
In a written response to National Post, Watts said the website is ""demonstrably inaccurate and lacks even basic 
context."" The tool ""creates the illusion of insight while getting the fundamentals wrong. The reality is the 
organizations I work with see results and governments are better informed, making wiser choices as a 
consequence,"" he wrote.
Cairo did not respond to a request for comment.
But the artificial-intelligence mapping earned rave reviews from government ethics specialist Ian Stedman, a York 
University professor who previously worked for the Office of the Integrity Commissioner of Ontario.
Tools like that can help ethics commissioners across the country explain complex reports in an easy-to-visualize 
format and help Canadians better understand the connections between people, organizations and public contracts, 
Stedman said.
"" This mapping of the characters based on official documents and official reports is absolutely brilliant. It's the kind 
of thing that commissioners ought to be doing with every one of these files for sure,"" he said.
""This visualization of the connections, and the justification and the sources... this should be released with every 
report about conflicts of interest... to make it interactive and digestible and visual,"" Stedman added.
In the case of the Phoenix pay system debacle, the web of players and their connections revealed by the AI-
generated tool shows just how complex these networks are.
""Like this revolving door, the relationships, the fact that it's one ( jumping from one) company to the next, this shows 
you that it isn't easy to just have a surface-level understanding and pick up on how many close relationships there 
are,"" he explained.
To promote transparency, government watchdogs need to ensure the data they publish are searchable, sortable 
and downloadable, so the public and journalists can easily compile and parse the data, Stedman said.
The ethics specialist also said government watchdogs can and should adopt AI tools to help facilitate their 
compliance efforts, such as to verify a public office holder's compliance with a conflict of ethics screen.
Already in 2018, well before large-language models such as ChatGPT and Claude revolutionized coding, then-
federal ethics commissioner Mario Dion also saw the potential for AI-driven tools to aid his office's work. Speaking 
at York University, Dion argued AI could help develop an ""electronic oversight tool"" that would catch compliance red 
flags faster and automatically.
""One day a system could be developed that contains data not only on public office holders and members, such as 
their assets and liabilities, but also on the official decisions they are making or have made. The system would be 
able to automatically generate red flags that would alert the public office holder or member as well as the 
commissioner,"" he said at the time.
In a statement, Melanie Rushworth, a spokesperson with the Office of the Conflict of Interest and Ethics 
Commissioner spokesperson, said the watchdog is always looking at new technological tools to boost its work. But 
she also said the office deals in sensitive and private information that would need to be protected from third parties, 
such as AI platforms.
""This obligation necessarily limits the tools and technologies that could be considered by the Office with 
consideration of our legal obligations, mandate, and risk considerations,"" Rushworth wrote.
Page 3 of 4
AI-driven website digs into lobbying; Online tool highlights concerning connections in federal contracts
In his 2018 speech, Dion said that while the privacy of MPs and public office holders was important, there would be 
ways to have them consent to their information being used by an in-house AI tool.
A key feature of the website is a button that highlights all the lobbying contacts associated with both of the 
government's controversial pay-system contracts. Government officials are highlighted in green and lobbyists are 
red, illustrating the well-travelled path between the world of government relations and the ministers they're trying to 
persuade.
And while the lobbying and relationship map displays the Phoenix pay scandal in Technicolour, it's only the first 
example of the engine powering it. The new tool, built on the AI platform Claude Code, can now find the same 
information for any government contract, lobbying relationship or interaction between a corporation and government 
department.
With some very basic coding knowledge, and using an AI model to do the heavy lifting, a user can launch an 
investigation with a simple command. The program will launch AI agents that dig through the lobbying registry, scan 
media reports and investigate basic facts.
It means Canadians can find ""revolving door"" connections to virtually anything that government money is being 
used for. And it will build a website to display it for posterity - and potenti -al ly to get the attention of opposition MPs 
and journalists.

Title: Alberta First Nation councillor alleges chief sent her a $421K invoice to prevent her from running again
Body: A Federal Court judge has quashed a $421,000 invoice issued to an Alberta First Nation councillor that would 
have kept her from running in the band's election next month.
Fort McMurray First Nation (FMFN) Chief Neil Cheecham and Councillor Christopher Beausoleil sent the invoice to 
Councillor Samantha Whalen this past January ""for repayment of unauthorized compensation improperly paid"" to 
her in 2023. Whalen applied for a judicial review of their decision to send her the bill.
""The circumstances and timing surrounding the issuance of the invoice raises serious issues about the validity of 
the invoice,"" Justice Ann Marie McDonald wrote in the May 19 decision.
""The impact of the invoice, however, is undisputed: it would render (Whalen) ineligible to run for re-election in the 
FMFN election scheduled for June 2026.""
Whalen ""intends to seek re-election in the June 2026 election, however under the Election Regulation, an election 
candidate cannot owe a debt to FMFN or an FMFN entity,"" said the judge. ""Election candidates must provide a 
letter 'signed by the band administrator or chief executive officer of the First Nation,' confirming that the candidate 
owes no debts to FMFN or an FMFN entity.""
The First Nation is governed by a chief and two councillors.
""The evidence filed on this application demonstrates that there is significant animosity between Councillor Whalen, 
and Chief Cheecham and Councillor Beausoleil,"" McDonald said.
""Councillor Whalen has effectively been sidelined in relation to the functions of the FMFN Chief and Council 
duties, and the relationship of the three members who make up the FMFN Chief and Council has broken down.""
The judge points to a lawsuit FMFN filed against Whalen in November 2024 for ""breach of fiduciary duty, breach of 
trust, conversion, and unjust enrichment.""
In the suit filed with the Alberta Court of King's Bench, the Cree and Chipewyan band ""refers to 'an independent 
third party' investigation into Councillor Whalen that concluded in September 2024 and found that Councillor 
Whalen had misused 'Nation funds through excessive and potentially illegitimate expenses,'"" said the decision.
Page 2 of 4
Alberta First Nation councillor alleges chief sent her a $421K invoice to prevent her from running again
""Based on this investigation, in the Alberta action, FMFN alleges that Councillor Whalen claimed expenses that 
'were either not personally incurred by Councillor Whalen, not incurred at all, or unrelated to FMFN business' and 
received 'excessive and unauthorized remuneration' in 2023 for her roles as FMFN Councillor and as the Business 
Development Officer of a FMFN entity.""
The suit, which is ongoing, claims that Whalen ""was wrongly paid '$421,650 in board fees and bonuses based on 
the performance of EcDev Co and other FMFN Companies,'"" said the decision.
Whalen filed a defence with the court in January 2025 ""fully denying the claim.""
In it, Whalen said she ""attended to each and every one of her duties as a FMFN Councillor with transparency, 
good faith, and in alignment with FMFN Bylaws. (Whalen) denies any allegations that she breached her fiduciary 
duty to FMFN, was unjustly enriched, or unlawfully misappropriated money from FMFN.""
After issuing the $421,000 invoice ""on FMFN letterhead"" Cheecham and Beausoleil wrote an ""important update"" to 
community members, said the recent Federal Court decision.
It noted Whalen's invoice was ""for bonus payments improperly paid to her in 2023.""
She responded with a missive to band members this past February.
""It is important that I respond clearly, firmly, and truthfully to protect my reputation and ensure members are not 
misled,"" Whalen wrote.
""First and foremost, the payments being referenced were not bonuses. They were board-related compensation 
issued through established compensation structures and processed through the Nation's financial systems. At no 
time were these amounts issued, recorded, or described as 'bonuses' within the Nation's financial system.""
Whalen said the payments ""were signed and approved through the Board of Directors, including approval by Chief 
Neil Cheecham. That approval shows that compensation was allocated across several Nation entities and included 
payments to multiple officials under the same structure, not just to me. The document further confirms that Chief 
Neil Cheecham also received payments under this same structure. ""
Whalen told band members ""this alleged debt"" could keep her from running in June.
""This is particularly concerning given that the payments in question date back to 2023 and are only now being 
raised in this manner,"" she said. ""The timing creates the appearance of potential election interference, as a 
disputed and unproven claim is being referenced in connection with my eligibility to run.""
FMFN, Cheecham, and Beausoleil argued ""that the decision to issue the invoice is not a decision that can be 
judicially reviewed, because it was a private, commercial, and operational matter by FMFN, and is therefore outside 
the jurisdiction of the Federal Court,"" said the decision.
But according to the judge, ""there can be no doubt that Chief Cheecham and Councillor Beausoleil were acting in 
a public manner when exercising FMFN powers to issue the invoice.""
Fort McMurray #468 First Nation Chief Neil Cheecham in 2023.
Allowing FMFN, Cheecham, and Beausoleil ""to interfere with the FMFN's election process, by hiding behind the 
private nature of issuing an invoice, risks 'undermin(ing) public confidence in the essential integrity of the process,'"" 
McDonald said.
""Further, although the respondents claim that the invoice was a legitimate FMFN decision to formalize debts 
following an independent investigation into Councillor Whalen, the timing of their actions undermines this claim. 
The Invoice was issued four months before the Nomination Meeting for the June 2026 election, but well over one 
year after the investigation concluded and when FMFN filed their lawsuit in the Alberta Courts against Councillor 
Page 3 of 4
Alberta First Nation councillor alleges chief sent her a $421K invoice to prevent her from running again
Whalen. On cross-examination, Chief Cheecham claimed that the invoice was not intended to disqualify Councillor 
Whalen from the June 2026 election, but he conceded that 'we all know (the election was) coming.'""
The judge found ""this is an 'exceptional' case where, even if the issuance of an invoice is a private matter, here it 
has been transformed into a public matter of significance. As such, I find this case falls within the Federal Court 
jurisdiction.""
Whalen argued FMFN, Cheecham, and Beausoleil ""had no authority to issue the invoice because they did not have 
a duly convened meeting and there is no (Band Council Resolution) and, relatedly, she highlights accounting 
irregularities surrounding the invoice.""
She argued that a band lawyer requested and issued the $421,000 invoice, said the decision. ""She also argues that 
the invoice was motivated by bad faith, malice, and for the ulterior motive of blocking her from running in the 
upcoming election.""
The judge was ""satisfied that it was issued at the direction of Chief Cheecham and Councillor Beausoleil,"" said the 
decision.
""Accordingly, the decision to issue the invoice was not made according to the Accountability Bylaw and was not 
made in accordance with the principles of fairness. Therefore, the decision to issue the invoice cannot be upheld as 
a decision made by the FMFN Chief and Council and the decision is hereby quashed.""

Title: Can't shame those who feel no shame; Liberal deputy minister rebuffs ethics chief
Body: The sordid little affair involving Christiane Fox, one of Canada's most senior government officials, in getting an 
acquaintance a job within the public service is made all the more distasteful because of her blindness to her faults 
and her casual disregard for accepting any responsibility.
Worse, it casts a blight over the public service and diminishes the office of the ethics commissioner when Fox, 
currently deputy minister at the Department of National Defence, tries to wave away so easily the fact that she has 
been found guilty of a serious ethical failing.
In a defiant appearance before a House Commons committee on Monday, Fox tried to minimize her involvement in 
the hiring of Bjorn Charles, a Black acquaintance, and all but cast herself as the hero.
The whole matter was about increasing diversity, she said. She had spent her whole career putting diversity at the 
forefront of what she did.
This is supposed to explain why she went out of her way to get Charles a job in 2023 within her then department - 
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada - when he was at that time a gym manager, did not speak French, 
did not know software and had ono government expertise or experience.
Well, she told the committee, in some departments there were ""systemic barriers and there were resistance to 
change. And so genuinely, as a leader, I believe in these issues. I believe it is important to lead by example.""
This was the same saintly defence she used on Konrad von Finckenstein, the ethics commissioner, who was 
having none of it.
It was simply not ""credible,"" he said.
Two witnesses, an acting director general and an office manager within IRCC, testified that the diversity aspect 
wasn't mentioned to them. Even Charles, the man being hired, wasn't told that he was an equity candidate, said the 
commissioner in his report.
""Clearly, the true intent behind her interventions"" was to get him a iob. he said.
Having tried to present herself with the best possible motivation, Fox then blamed underperforming colleagues.
Page 2 of 3
Can't shame those who feel no shame; Liberal deputy minister rebuffs ethics chief
""I have to think about the role that I occupy and whether or not it's best to administer change differently,"" she told 
the committee in relation to the hire, adding, ""But this was a context of trying to change an underperforming unit 
within the department that occupied a lot of my attention.""
Not surprisingly, staff reacted badly to having a non-French speaking, unqualified person foisted upon them.
""Many assumed he had been personally brought in by someone who knew him. Evidence also shows that senior 
staff referred to him as 'the DM's friend',"" said the ethics commissioner, who noted how one person testified that 
morale had been greatly affected. After blaming the underperformers and highlighting her noble motivations at the 
committee, Fox also minimized her relationship with Charles.
He was someone she went to university with 25 years ago, she said.
But in reading the ethics commissioner's report we also find out: Fox's spouse worked as a basketball coach at 
Carleton University and knew Charles as ""part of the university's broader basketball community."" In fact, Charles 
told the ethics commissioner that Fox's spouse was his basketball coach between 2001-2004. Also, he said Fox 
and her spouse had friends in common and that he saw them at barbecues and basketball events every couple of 
years. Fox and Charles were acquaintances rather than friends, as the ethics commissioner found, but neither was 
he some guy she hadn't seen for 25 years.
Fox also downplayed her role in the help she offered. According to her testimony before the committee, she was 
asked by an assistant deputy minister to pass on relevant cvs and she did ""as requested.""
But she did more than that. She sent Charles an internal briefing document to help when meeting officials; she 
spoke to him after his interview and she intervened with staff when they were thinking of offering him a lower 
position.
Staff, said the ethics commissioner, ""felt pressured"" to bring Charles onboard.
What was the outcome? He was hired but a year later, amid ""performance issues,"" he was told his position would 
not be renewed.
But no matter, because Fox came to his rescue again in 2024 in her then new role as deputy Clerk of the Privy 
Council and associate secretary to the cabinet, one of the most senior public servants in Canada.
Charles contacted her to say he was leaving IRCC and she told him to send his resume to her assistant. Fox then 
informed the human resources assistant deputy manager at the Privy Council Office that Charles's resume was on 
its way.
When he was invited into a meeting, Fox met with him and then introduced him to the senior managers.
So a bit more than forwarding an email.
Meanwhile, in November 2024, having been given an expedited Top Secret clearance pass, Charles started 
working as an analyst in the Privy Council Office, the department directly supporting the prime minister and 
cabinet.
From her committee appearance, one senses that Fox - who said she needed to ""reflect"" on her actions - feels 
maligned, misunderstood and her motives misjudged.
However, those reflections should include her apparent disingenuous answers to the committee, her self-
aggrandizing before members and that it was particularly ignoble and shoddy to throw ""underperforming"" 
colleagues under the bus.
She might also reflect that the ethics commissioner found she used her position to improperly get Charles 
preferential treatment thus contravening the Conflict of Interest Act.
Page 3 of 3
Can't shame those who feel no shame; Liberal deputy minister rebuffs ethics chief
However, her lack of regret and her failure to apologize shows she does not accept the report despite 
""acknowledging"" it.
Fox can get away with her facile response, because before her there have been so many others, especially the 
government of the past 11 years, who have treated the ethics commissioner and his office with indifference.
Unfortunately, these people can't be shamed into doing the right thing because they have no shame.

Title: Champagne recuses himself from project
Body: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has been unable to participate in decisions related to the federal 
government's proposed high-speed rail line after setting up an ethics screen last year due to his partner's ties to the 
Crown corporation behind the project.
The screen means the finance minister has had to recuse himself from all discussions related to the Alto proposal 
for an electric rail line between Toronto and Quebec City - which the Carney government considers ""transformative"" 
- because his partner, Anne-Marie Gaudet, became the Crown corporation's vice-president of environment last 
August.
The next month, Champagne wrote a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney informing him of two ethics screens the 
minister had put in place regarding two individuals close to him.
""I am proactively applying a conflict of interest filter to Alto, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Government of 
Canada. This measure is being implemented due to a personal connection to someone close to me in the 
organization, to safeguard against any real or perceived conflict of interest,"" reads the letter, which Champagne's 
office sent to the Star.
The screen is being overseen by Champagne's chief of staff, Ian Foucher, and Deputy Minister of Finance Nick 
Leswick. 
""If the screen is engaged, Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), the Honourable 
Wayne Long will have the delegation of authority,"" the letter states.
The high-speed rail proposal has drawn renewed attention after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called on the 
government to scrap the project, which is estimated to cost between $60 billion and $90 billion. The Liberals, who 
have referred the proposal to its Major Projects Office to fast-track construction, deem the project a ""generational 
investment"" that would boost the country's GDP and create tens of thousands of jobs. 
The other screen Champagne implemented concerns his father, Gilles Champagne, who is the president of 
Bionest Technologies, a Quebec-based company that specializes in sustainable wastewater treatment systems. 
""The conflict of interest filter is a preventive measure to help me fulfil my obligation not to participate in any 
discussion or decision, debate or vote, other than those of a general nature or that affect me in the same way as a 
broad category of people, with regard to my father, president of Bionest Technologies, and Bionest Technologies 
Page 2 of 2
Champagne recuses himself from project
and its subsidiaries and affiliates or related companies, as well as Alto, a wholly owned subsidiary of the 
Government of Canada, with regard to a personal connection with an individual employed by the organization,"" 
the letter says.
The letter notes the ethics commissioner deemed a screen necessary in the case of Bionest Technologies. The 
minister proactively initiated a screen for matters concerning Alto, although only the screen pertaining to Bionest 
appears on the commissioner's public registry. 
The Office of the Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner was not available Monday to explain why.

Title: Channelling Trump a risky move for Stiles
Body: Lock her up!
That classic Donald Trump taunting of Hillary Clinton has found an echo in Ontario. But it's not what you think.
It's true that Doug Ford's Tories have long channelled the U.S. president's playbook. Back in 2018, the premier 
vilified his predecessor, Kathleen Wynne, as corruption incarnate.
Times change. In a role reversal that is turning heads, Ford himself is being threatened with prison time and a 
public inquiry by the New Democratic Party.
NDP Leader Marit Stiles is accusing Ford of corruption and a coverup that require an accounting:
""Don't worry about it Doug, because when I'm premier, I'm going to call a public inquiry into all of this,"" she 
announced this week.
And then the mic drop moment:
""And you know what, maybe you won't get another mandate because you'll be in prison, Doug.""
She paused for a beat, then added: ""Yep.""
As those last words tumbled out - predicting imprisonment for the premier - Stiles pursed her lips hard and dropped 
her gaze downward. As if she were doing a quick mental calculation to gauge whether her rhetoric worked for or 
against her politically.
A TV reporter had already gasped audibly, ""What?""
Journalists quickly asked Stiles if she'd misspoken or truly meant what she'd just said - shades of ""lock him up?"" 
But the NDP leader doubled down, saying anyone who took offence was merely ""clutching their pearls.""
She cited a long-standing RCMP investigation into allegations of inside dealing on the Greenbelt land swap 
scandal, and argued that Ford's latest restrictions on freedom of information were proof he's still trying to hide 
something. Never mind that police subpoenas are far more revealing than any redacted access to information 
documents, or that public inquiries rarely lead to criminal charges - that's for police probes.
Page 2 of 3
Channelling Trump a risky move for Stiles
The point, Stiles insisted, was that ""I'm saying out loud what a lot of people are saying quietly.""
Which seems the very definition of untrammelled Trumpism.
Ford's Tories, who have been under pressure in recent days for a series of political fumbles, couldn't believe their 
luck. Predictably, the premier told reporters the next day he was shocked - shocked! - to hear such 
unparliamentary language from the leader of the opposition.
""That Trump-style rhetoric is unacceptable as far as I'm concerned,"" Ford said with a straight face. ""We aren't going 
to lower ourselves to the Trump-style rhetoric that she's spewing right now.""
This from a politician famed for his personal attacks, most notably against Wynne, when he accused the former 
premier of breaking the law for unspecified financial transactions and inside dealing - none of which added up. 
Ford's allegations back then were outright political fabrications - Wynne's personal reputation remains 
unimpeachable, and no credible allegations of political impropriety have ever stuck.
But it would be untrue and unfair to say Ford crossed a line, then or now. In truth, that Trumpian line had already 
been crossed by the NDP long before, and he was just following in its footsteps.
Righteous New Democrats play the corruption card at every opportunity. In fact, years before Ford's shameless 
smear tactics against Wynne, NDP leader Andrea Horwath led the charge against the Liberal premier of the day.
The attacks were as relentless as they were groundless and pointless. The NDP triggered an Ontario Provincial 
Police probe and criminal prosecution in Sudbury accusing a senior Wynne aide of bribery (she'd asked a defeated 
candidate to step aside so that a new star candidate could help win a local riding, but the prosecution fell apart).
The NDP's recourse to the cops made headlines just ahead of the 2006 federal election, when the federal New 
Democrats issued a mischievous news release announcing an RCMP probe into their complaint of budget 
improprieties by the Liberal finance minister of the day, Ralph Goodale. The allegations later proved spurious, but 
the NDP's well-timed bombshell tarred the Liberals on voting day.
Now, Stiles is telling anyone who will listen that when - if - she becomes the province's next premier, there will be a 
new sheriff in town and her Tory predecessor will be in prison. Just as Ford once implied that his own Liberal 
predecessor would be jailed.
Despite all the awkward allegations stemming from the Greenbelt scandal, the premier has twice won re-election 
resoundingly. The NDP remains a distant third in the polls.
The party that once concentrated on serious and substantive issues - such as welfare reform and judicial due 
process - now plays the corruption card to attract attention. It's not that Ford is necessarily squeaky clean, it's just 
that the court of public opinion may be waiting for the police and law courts to pass judgment, rather than relying on 
the word of another politician.
In all these years, after all these allegations - first against Wynne, now against Ford - the NDP's political playbook is 
a risky play. The opposition's job is holding governments to account, not settling political accounts.

Title: Chomedey MNA issues tearful apology in National Assembly for ethical breach
Body: ""It was not my intention to act in an inappropriate way or go against the rules of the function. I always believed in 
good faith that my acts did not run against the limits,"" a tearful Sona Lakhoyan Olivier told the National Assembly in 
her apology on Thursday, May 14, 2026. Postmedia (Credit: Francis Vachon)
QUEBEC - A tearful and emotional Sona Lakhoyan Olivier apologized to her fellow MNAs on Thursday in the 
National Assembly, saying she assumes the blame for her ethical violations.
But she has not offered her resignation as the MNA for the riding of Chomedey despite numerous calls for her to 
quit, including one from Liberal Leader Charles Milliard.
Rising in the legislature seven days after a blistering ethics commission's report blamed her for two major violations 
of the code( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/provincial-politics/sona-lakhoyan-olivier-violated-
ethics-code-rodriguez-campaign/ ) governing the work of MNAs, Lakhoyan Olivier struggled through tears to speak.
""I want to present my sincere apologies to my colleagues of the National Assembly as well as the public,"" Lakhoyan 
Olivier said.
""I recognize having made an error and gone past certain limits of the code of ethics and behaviour of the National 
Assembly connected to partisan activities.
""It was not my intention to act in an inappropriate way or go against the rules of the function. I always believed in 
good faith that my acts did not run against the limits.""
Last Wednesday, the National Assembly ethics commissioner, Ariane Mignolet, blamed Lakhoyan for ethics 
violations, including using her riding office and personnel to work on the leadership campaign of former Liberal 
leader Pablo Rodriguez( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/provincial-politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-vote-buying-allegations/ ) between April and June 2025.
Mignolet's report goes further, concluding Lakhoyan Olivier violated Article 41 of the code ""in taking a series of 
actions after the investigation opened that had the effect of impeding the commissioner in her functions.""
Page 2 of 3
Chomedey MNA issues tearful apology in National Assembly for ethical breach
""The evidence reveals the MNA discussed the investigation on several occasions with members of her staff to 
convince them of the value of her version of the facts and to dictate eventual responses to the commissioner's 
questions,"" Mignolet wrote.
In addition to the blame, Mignolet recommended the MNA, who was a Liberal before being expelled, be fined 
$8,000. Lakhoyan Olivier now sits as an independent.
Lakhoyan Olivier has been silent ever since, but on Thursday, the last day before the legislature takes a weeklong 
break, she exercised her right to defend and explain herself.
She said she decided to take the necessary time to fully understand and reflect on what she had done wrong.
""Today, I can say I learned from my mistakes,"" Lakhoyan Olivier said. ""This experience leads me to pursue my work 
with even more prudence, rigour and discernment.
""Today, I take note of the commissioner's decision with respect and I accept the sanction it imposes. Without 
commenting on the amount of the penalty, I accept it without contest.
""I will pursue my work at the service of citizens who gave me their confidence. I will continue to assume this 
responsibility with humility, prudence and out of a sense of duty.
""I apologize. I apologize, Marc (parliamentary leader Marc Tanguay).""
Lakhoyan Olivier then rushed dramatically out of the Red Room in tears.
Francis Vachon / PostmediaSona Lakhoyan Olivier leaves the National Assembly in tears after apologizing to 
MNAs for her ethics breach, on Thursday, May 14, 2026.
It's unclear any MNAs were moved by her appeal for clemency.
After she left, the speaker of the house, Nathalie Roy, announced MNAs would vote on the ethics commission's 
report when the legislature reconvenes May 26.
If they vote in favour of the report, the sanctions would be applied. The legislature, however, does not have the 
power to force Lakhoyan Olivier to step down.
Some of her fellow MNAs indicated to the media as they left the room that they would be voting in favour of the 
report.
""I can tell you we will vote in favour of the commissioner's report,"" Premier Christine Fréchette told reporters. ""What 
happened has been well detailed.""
Some seemed shocked by the whole situation.
""It's quite troubling and quite negative for all politicians in Quebec now,"" Ian Lafranière, the domestic security 
minister and deputy premier, told reporters. ""People are looking at us thinking that we play the same game.""
Lakhoyan Olivier's former Liberal colleagues also turned on her. Earlier this week at an event in Sherbrooke, 
Milliard said she should resign.
""I think facts are troubling enough, so I think Sona Lakhoyan Olivier should resign, but it is a resignation (decision) 
which belongs to her,"" Milliard said.
Last Friday, Milliard recommended the party executive take away her membership card( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/provincial-politics/milliard-bans-lakhoyan-olivier-quebec-liberals/ 
) and ban her from the party for life.
Page 3 of 3
Chomedey MNA issues tearful apology in National Assembly for ethical breach
Earlier Thursday, several Liberals said Lakhoyan Olivier is no longer welcome in the party.
""The relationship between Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and our caucus and party are over,"" said Michelle Setlakwe, the 
Liberal MNA for Mont-Royal-Outremont who was also vice-chair of the Rodriguez leadership campaign. ""She 
cannot come back.""
""We think she should resign,"" added Frédéric Beauchemin, the Liberal MNA for the riding of Marguerite-Bourgeoys. 
""It's clear Sona had a problem understanding the rules of the game.""
The Lakhoyan Olivier saga comes as the Liberals continue to struggle to shake off the ethical questions raised 
during the 2025 leadership race.
On Wednesday, Milliard revealed that he had recently met with Quebec's anti-corruption squad (UPAC), which 
asked him questions about the race in which he was one of the opponents to Rodriguez.
""I met them, I answered their questions,"" Milliard told reporters. ""It was all very cordial.""
Officials in Milliard's office said later he was met because he is the current leader of the party and not because he is 
a person of interest in any case.
UPAC announced in December that it was investigating certain ""allegations of reprehensible acts in the Liberal 
party.""

Title: Christiane Fox says she was motivated by advancing diversity when she hired gym manager acquaintance
Body: A deputy minister under fire for breaking conflict of interest rules for hiring an acquaintance and former gym 
manager for a federal government job says she was motivated by advancing diversity.
The government's ethics watchdog found that Christiane Fox, currently the Department of National Defence's top 
civilian official, broke conflict of interest rules( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/deputy-minister-broke-
conflict-of-interest-rules-ethics-watchdog-christiane-fox ) by influencing the hiring of a university peer.
Ethics commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein released a report on Wednesday that found Fox hired Björn Charles 
- whom she knew from when they were both athletes in university - as a project manager in 2023, when she was 
deputy minister of Immigration, Refugee and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).
""This report reminds appointed federal officials at all levels to keep the Conflict of Interest Act in mind whenever 
there's a possibility of influencing a decision,"" von Finckenstein said in a statement. ""They're not allowed to use 
their position to try to influence a decision to further their private interests or those of their relatives or friends, or to 
improperly further another person's private interests.""
But Fox defended her actions in a statement sent to Department of National Defence staff on Friday. Fox did not 
apologize but instead repeated some of the same arguments she made to von Finckenstein.
""My approach was motivated by a genuine desire to bring in outside perspectives, strengthen the performance of 
underperforming teams, and help build a public service that better reflects the people it serves,"" she noted in her 
statement. ""In particular, my efforts were focused on advancing diversity and inclusion across the public service, an 
objective explicitly set for Deputy Ministers.""
Fox has since served as deputy clerk of the Privy Council before moving to her current role as deputy minister at 
DND - a position she was shuffled to by Prime Minister Mark Carney( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-
service/carney-shakeup-senior-ranks-public-service ).
Officials at IRCC felt pressured by Fox to hire Charles in the department's access-to-information division, according 
to the report. He now works as an ATIP analyst in the Privy Council Office (PCO), according to his LinkedIn profile.
Fox and her family attended the same Goodlife gym where Charles worked as a manager before he was hired at 
IRCC, according to the report( https://ciec-ccie.parl.gc.ca/en/investigations-enquetes/Pages/FoxReport-
RapportFox.aspx ).
Page 2 of 3
Christiane Fox says she was motivated by advancing diversity when she hired gym manager acquaintance
The report also said that Fox's spouse was Charles' assistant basketball coach while he attended Carleton 
University from 2001 to 2004.
Von Finckenstein ""concluded that Ms. Fox used her position as Deputy Minister to give Mr. Charles preferential 
treatment, by ensuring he met with departmental officials quickly, seeking updates about his hiring, giving him 
internal information and pushing for a higher job classification.""
Fox was also communicating closely with Charles throughout his hiring process and even helped prepare him for 
his interview with ATIP division officials, including sending him a IRCC briefing document, according to the report.
In her statement released Friday, Fox said she acknowledged ""the Commissioner's findings and take this matter 
seriously. Given the work we are advancing together, I also believe it is important that you have additional context 
about the intent of my actions.""
Fox stated that at IRCC, she ""was given a clear mandate to lead a large-scale cultural and organizational change.""

Title: Complaint last summer spurred probe into councillor OPP investigating politician accused of soliciting money
Body: The complaint that appears to have prompted a police investigation into a Scarborough city councillor was 
referred to law enforcement last summer, according to Toronto's ethics watchdog.
The office of integrity commissioner Paul Muldoon confirmed Tuesday that it received a complaint about Coun. 
Parthi Kandavel on July 8, 2025. The watchdog said it passed the file to the Toronto Police Service two weeks later, 
on July 22.
Toronto police haven't confirmed when they were made aware of allegations against Kandavel, but have said they 
referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police in order to avoid any perceived conflict of interest. The OPP's 
investigation is ongoing, according to the provincial force. 
The authorities and Kandavel haven't divulged the nature of the allegations against him. But as the Star reported 
Monday, the investigation appears to be focused on the councillor's dealings with developers. 
One source, who spoke to the Star on condition of anonymity due to fears of political retribution and professional 
fallout, said they were left with the impression Kandavel wanted a substantial payment to allow a development in his 
ward to proceed. 
Kandavel, who was elected to represent Scarborough Southwest in November 2023, has denied any wrongdoing, 
and has said he has ""strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity."" 
""I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period.
 Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work,"" he said in a statement 
Monday.
The councillor has said he learned of the investigation last Friday. 
The integrity commissioner is responsible for investigating potential breaches of council's code of conduct. 
Page 2 of 3
Complaint last summer spurred probe into councillor OPP investigating politician accused of soliciting money 
from developers
A spokesperson for Muldoon wouldn't provide details of the July 2025 complaint, but said that under the City of 
Toronto Act, the commissioner is obligated to ""immediately refer the matter to appropriate authorities"" if they 
determine there are ""reasonable grounds"" to believe the Criminal Code or other legislation has been violated. 
Under the act, the commissioner must also suspend its investigation pending the outcome of the police probe and 
any resulting charges. 
The commissioner wouldn't say who filed the complaint, or confirm news, reported Tuesday by the Star, that it was 
lodged by a representative of the owners of a development in Kandavel's ward.
 The company's lawyer said that someone acting on behalf of the corporation, called Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., 
complained to the commissioner. The lawyer wouldn't say what the complaint related to, other than to stress his 
clients weren't under investigation. 
The OPP has sought information about the Kennedy development as part of its probe, according to a source.
The company's representative filed the complaint less than two weeks after its development at 708-712 Kennedy 
Rd. went to city council. Staff had previously expressed concerns about the size of the project just south of Eglin- 
ton Avenue, which proposed 682 units in two towers of 21 and 42 storeys. 
On June 9, 2025, the owners offered the city a settlement that would resolve their appeal of the project at the 
Ontario Land Tribunal. They proposed reducing the height of the highest tower by four storeys and providing 1,500 
square feet of non-residential space in the building.
A source, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to share the information, said 
that at council's June 25-26, 2025 meeting, the city solicitor recommended in a confidential report that the city 
accept the offer.
Kandavel moved a motion on the second day of the session amending her advice, however, directing council to 
approve the settlement but attaching a requirement that the developers provide 4,000 square feet of non-residential 
space. 
Last October, the land tribunal sided with the company and said that amount wasn't justified. 
Toronto's municipal election is Oct. 26. Before news of the investigation broke, Kandavel said he planned run for re-
election. He has not yet registered. Nominations opened May 1.

Title: Conservatives say Champagne is avoiding committee study into Alto rail connection
Body: OTTAWA - The Conservatives are accusing the Liberals of blocking a House of Commons committee from 
questioning Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne about his personal connection to the Alto high-speed 
rail project.
Champagne's partner, Anne-Marie Gaudet, is a vice-president of environment at Alto, the Crown corporation 
responsible for the $90-billion rail project that would connect Toronto and Quebec City. She was hired in August 
2025.
Conservative ethics critic Michael Barrett tried to launch a study at the ethics committee to question Champagne, 
the CEO of Alto Martin Imbleau and Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein about 
the minister's relationship with Gaudet and the decisions he's made in government since she was hired.
""We are facing a filibuster that's gone on for more than 12 hours, a Liberal filibuster designed to block basic 
accountability,"" Barrett said Thursday.
John Fragos, a spokesperson for the Office of the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, said in an email that 
it’s up to parliamentary committees themselves to agree on which individuals they’d like to see testify.
""What’s already agreed upon, however, is the understanding that the minister acted proactively and above and 
beyond the guidance outlined in the act to safeguard against the perception of a conflict,"" he said. ""The 
commissioner himself determined as much in August, saying, 'There is no risk of a conflict and no screen is 
required.'""
""The minister opted to recuse himself anyway and had a screen imposed proactively.""
After questions arose in the media about Champagne's connection to Alto, the finance minister's office shared a 
letter he sent last September to Prime Minister Mark Carney and to von Finckenstein.
The letter states that Champagne was proactively implementing a conflict-of-interest screen ""due to a personal 
connection to someone close to me in the organization, to safeguard against any real or perceived conflict of 
interest.""

Page 2 of 3
Conservatives say Champagne is avoiding committee study into Alto rail connection
Champagne's office said the minister has not participated in any discussions or decisions tied to Alto since then. 
His office also said the initial funding for the project was announced in February 2025 and allocated in the main 
estimates in 2025, all before Gaudet was hired.
A compliance officer in the ethics commissioner's office wrote to Champagne earlier this month to say there was no 
risk of a conflict because ""Alto is a Crown corporation accountable to Parliament through the minister of transport 
and as minister of finance you have no decision-making authority over matters of human resources at Alto, you do 
not have an opportunity to further the interest of any specific Alto employee.""
Barrett has formally asked the conflict of interest and ethics commissioner to investigate.
He pointed out that the government included legislation to enable the Alto project in its omnibus budget bill, which 
Champagne introduced and championed in Parliament.
""Why wasn't the bill with respect to the high-speed rail network act brought forward by the transport minister and 
not by the finance minister?"" he asked.
During the ethics committee's last meeting, MPs debated for hours but did not vote on whether the minister should 
appear to answer questions.
The Liberals have four members on the committee, while the Conservatives have four and the Bloc Québécois has 
one. That means opposition members could outvote the government members and request that Champagne 
appear.
""This is the opposite of what the prime minister said that Canadians should expect from parliamentarians at 
committee, and it is counter to the basic accountability that Canadians should demand of all parliamentarians,"" 
Barrett said Thursday.
Earlier this week, Carney told reporters that his new majority Liberal government would engage in serious debate 
and accused the opposition of ""showboating"" and filibustering in committee.
Now that the Liberals have a majority, they could vote in the House of Commons to change the makeup of 
committees. Majority governments historically have held a majority of seats on committees — a key step in the 
legislative process where bills are scrutinized and amended.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published April 16, 2026.

Title: Councillor accused of asking developer for money Kandavel denies wrongdoing as OPP probe interactions with
Body: A Toronto city councillor's dealings with developers appear to be the focus of the police investigation into 
allegations against him. 
The Ontario Provincial Police probe into Coun. Parthi Kandavel was prompted by a watchdog complaint from the 
owners of a development in his Scarborough Southwest ward, according to the company's lawyer, while sources 
allege he sought money in exchange for allowing a different project in the area to go ahead. 
In an email to the Star on Monday, John J. Pirie, a partner at Baker McKenzie LLP, said a representative of his 
clients, Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., made a complaintagainst the councillor to Toronto's integrity commissioner. 
According to Pirie, the commissioner then referred the matter to the Toronto police, without the input of his clients.
The company owns a property at 708-712 Kennedy Road, and has been seeking permission to replace two midrise 
rental buildings at the site with a pair of highrises. Pirie declined to provide details of the complaint, but stressed 
that the company ""is not under investigation.""
Integrity Commissioner Paul Muldoon couldn't immediately be reached for comment Monday. His office previously 
told the Star it ""does not routinely confirm or deny whether he has received a complaint."" 
Meanwhile, a source with knowledge of another development in Scarborough Southwest said they were left with the 
impression that Kandavel wanted a significant financial payment from the proponents to allow the project to 
proceed. 
A second source confirmed hearing the same account. The OPP has reached out regarding the development, 
according to the first source. In a statement in response to the allegations, Kandavel said: ""There has been no 
wrongdoing on my part, which I'm confident the OPP investigation will conclude.""
""I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period. 
Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work.""
The councillor announced in a social media post on Sunday that he was under investigation by the OPP. He 
didn't provide details of the allegations, and said news of the investigation had taken him by surprise when he 
learned about it Friday afternoon. 
Page 2 of 3
Councillor accused of asking developer for money Kandavel denies wrongdoing as OPP probe interactions with 
local builder
He wrote in the post that he had ""worked hard to earn the trust of the people of Scarborough Southwest, which I 
take seriously. I've strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity and will address any allegations 
that suggest otherwise."" 
The Toronto Police Service received the initial complaint about the councillor but referred it to the OPP ""to avoid 
any perceived conflict of interest,"" TPS spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said Monday. City councillors sit on the 
Toronto Police Service Board and vote on its annual budget. Neither the TPS nor OPP has said who filed the 
complaint, or detailed the allegations against Kandavel. The forces didn't immediately return a request for 
confirmation Monday night about who made the complaint.
The Star reported on Sunday that, according to one source, as part of its probe, the OPP had sought information 
about the development at 708-712 Kennedy Road. In 2022, the owners of the property submitted a request for a 
zoning bylaw amendment to demolish the existing 98 rental units at the site and redevelop it. A revised submission 
the company made in 2024 proposed two residential towers of 21 and 42 stories, for a total of 682 units, including 
98 rental replacements. 
The owners appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal in May 2024 after council failed to make a decision within the 
required timelines.
In June 2025, the owners submitted a settlement offer to resolve the OLT appeal, which reduced the height of the 
highest tower by four stories. That month, city solicitor Wendy Walberg submitted advice to council about the 
settlement. While the advice was confidential, according to one source with knowledge of her report, she 
recommended council accept the settlement, which included a concession from the owners to provide 1,500 square 
feet of non-residential uses. Kandavel moved a motion amending her advice however, requesting that the city 
approve the settlement but require 4,000 square feet. 
According to an October 2025 OLT decision, the city and the owners resolved most aspects of the appeal, but 
continued to disagree on the amount of non-residential space. The owner successfully convinced the tribunal it 
didn't need to include as much as Kandavel's motion requested, with the tribunal writing that the city hadn't provided 
evidence for ""why 4000 sq. ft. would be appropriate, how that precise number was good planning, or how exactly 
the development would have to be changed"" to accommodate it.
Kandavel is a former elementary school teacher and Toronto District School Board trustee. He was elected to 
council in a November 2023 byelection, with about 27 per cent of the vote. Earlier this month his office told the Star 
he intends to run for re-election this year, but he has yet to sign up for the Oct. 26 contest. Nominations opened 
May 1. 
A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said Monday she wouldn't answer questions about an active investigation, 
but Toronto residents ""expect every councillor and the mayor to act with integrity.""

Title: CRA tells Laval to pay $1 million to ex-mayor for tax purposes
Body: The City of Laval may be required to pay $1 million to former mayor Gilles Vaillancourt so he can pay taxes on 
money he collected through a municipal corruption scheme.
Mayor Stéphane Boyer is urging the federal government to exercise judgment in the matter, however, describing it 
as an ""exceptional situation.""
""The people of Laval have already paid a heavy price for this fraud,"" Boyer wrote in a statement to The Gazette on 
Monday. ""It would be unacceptable for them to now also be asked to pay taxes on money that was stolen from 
them.""
Vaillancourt, who served as mayor from 1989 to 2012, pleaded guilty in 2016 to participating in a corruption 
scheme that plagued the city for years.
In pleading guilty, Vaillancourt admitted he took part in a conspiracy to use his position as mayor to fill Swiss bank 
accounts with millions of dollars.
He returned roughly $8 million to the city at the time, which was put into a fund aimed at helping disadvantaged 
youths.
Vaillancourt received a six-year prison sentence for the crimes in late 2016. He was granted full parole in 2018.
According to a report by Radio-Canada, the Canada Revenue Agency now wants Laval to pay $1 million to 
Vaillancourt so he can pay taxes on the stolen money.
The broadcaster says the agency first attempted to collect the money from Vaillancourt, but his lawyers argued it 
should come from the city since he returned the stolen funds.
Boyer feels it would be unjust for Laval to do so.
The mayor pointed out that in 2016, the Quebec government returned money Vaillancourt owed to Revenu Québec 
to the city.
He believes the federal government has the option to do the same now.
Page 2 of 2
CRA tells Laval to pay $1 million to ex-mayor for tax purposes
""There is discretionary power to correct this type of exceptional situation. We are asking the federal government to 
exercise this judgment, as the Quebec government did in 2016,"" Boyer wrote.
In an email response, a spokesperson for Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne noted he 
convened a meeting with the CRA commissioner to discuss the matter on Monday.

Title: David Barrick gone after less than 3 months in latest municipal CAO role, weeks after banning Pointer reporter
Body: Less than three months after starting the job, despite his scandal-plagued past and lack of proper experience, 
David Barrick is no longer the Chief Administrative Officer for the Township of South Stormont. 
His abrupt departure from the small eastern Ontario township, quietly announced Tuesday, March 24, has left 
residents, municipal officials and media outlets familiar with Barrick’s numerous scandals questioning what 
occurred behind closed doors. 
South Stormont officials are not providing any details, but the agenda for an emergency council meeting held 
Monday afternoon suggests Barrick was in trouble, days after The Pointer reported that the OPP blocked reporter 
Ed Smith from covering Barrick two weeks ago. 
In a brief statement released Tuesday, about 24 hours after the emergency meeting, the Township announced 
Barrick is no longer the CAO, and expressed gratitude for his work, despite being on the job for less than three 
months. 
“We are grateful for the positive impact David has made on the organization and wish him continued success in his 
future endeavours,” South Stormont Mayor Bryan McGillis wrote in the press release announcing the departure. 
“The Township of South Stormont will offer no further comment on this matter at this time.”
The mayor’s refusal on Tuesday to provide any explanation, came a day after the emergency council meeting. The 
only item on the agenda for the 4:30 p.m. meeting was a closed session discussion about a personal matter 
regarding an identifiable employee, “Specifically: Employee Effectiveness”. There was no other detail about why the 
special meeting to deal with the employee was called. 
Approximately 24 hours later, it was announced that David Barrick is no longer the CAO.
When Brampton council fired Barrick from his CAO role there in 2022, following years of scandal and turmoil, he 
threatened legal action and demanded the City release a letter praising his time with the municipality—despite the 
chaos he caused, which is detailed below. Barrick threatened the City with a $1 million lawsuit if officials did not 
provide him a 36-month severance payment, a positive reference letter and $250,000 in damages for “defamation, 
moral damages, and damages to his reputation”.

Page 2 of 5
David Barrick gone after less than 3 months in latest municipal CAO role, weeks after banning Pointer reporter
“Mr. Barrick requires a public commentary be issued by Council providing a recognition of his very positive service 
and outline of achievements as CAO of the Corporation,” a legal letter sent from Barrick’s lawyer to the City of 
Brampton demanded. “This is vital to Mr. Barrick to try to at least engage in some attempt at repair of his 
reputation.”
The City of Brampton issued a public statement celebrating Barrick’s time with the City. The release was full of 
misleading statements and did not address the numerous controversies he caused or enabled, and there was no 
mention of the reasons council fired him. 
After his departure as CAO in Thames Centre last yesr—a role he held prior to arriving in South Stormont—a 
similar positive statement was released by the municipality. It thanked Barrick for his time, but did not address any 
of the allegations detailed to The Pointer by sources including questionable spending and mass staff departures 
that began after his arrival, following his firing in Brampton. 
Barrick first landed a senior municipal sector job a decade ago at the Niagara Peninsula Conservation Authority, 
despite having no experience. He served as a Port Colborne councillor on Niagara Region’s council at the time, 
and was close to Conservative politicians and insiders who handed him the conservation authority management 
position; Ontario’s Auditor General later reported that his hiring was inappropriate and did not follow proper 
procedures. 
After he was fired, following allegations of mismanagement when he became the conservation authority’s CAO, 
Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown, who had just been forced to quit as PC Party leader for allegedly sexually 
assaulting two young women (he denies the allegations) orchestrated the hiring of Barrick as the city’s CAO, 
despite being woefully unqualified to run the country’s sixth largest city. 
An ongoing investigation into Barrick’s past municipal scandals prompted The Pointer’s reporter Ed Smith to cover 
the March 11 municipal council meeting in South Stormont as part of a series of articles that will examine his 
controversial career, to highlight the breakdown of municipal accountability in Ontario ahead of local elections in 
October. 
On March 11, officers from the Ontario Provincial Police prevented Smith from attending the public council meeting 
inside the municipal building in South Stormont. Two officers positioned themselves shoulder-to-shoulder at the 
entrance and refused him entry.
The officers cited a trespass notice, despite no disturbance or incident. They indicated that prior information had 
been provided suggesting the reporter might pose a threat, repeatedly claiming they had been informed their 
attendance was necessary to stop a “stalker” from entering the building. Officers appeared surprised when informed 
by Smith that he is a journalist reporting for The Pointer. 
They did not explain where the information about a “stalker” had come from, or who specifically had requested their 
presence. 
The OPP’s Sylvain Ladouceur, an administrative Sergeant at the detachment that serves South Stormont, spoke to 
The Pointer Wednesday about the complaint that led to reporter Ed Smith not being allowed inside the town hall 
building on March 11. 
He explained that a request was received by the local OPP from South Stormont Mayor Bryan McGillis prior to the 
public council meeting that day. McGillis informed the OPP that information had been provided to him regarding a 
“history” between David Barrick and Ed Smith, and the mayor requested Smith be denied access to the property 
due to that history. 
Sergeant Ladouceur said the incident report he was reading from does not mention anything about stalking or 
include any details about the history between Barrick and Smith. 
Page 3 of 5
David Barrick gone after less than 3 months in latest municipal CAO role, weeks after banning Pointer reporter
Smith was one of the Niagara residents who obtained documentation through freedom of information requests that 
showed Barrick’s involvement in the Niagara CAO “Inside Job” recruitment scandal that resulted in the hiring of 
Carmen D’Angelo, who had been Barrick’s boss at the local conservation authority.
Controversies in Niagara around a group of Conservative politicians prompted Smith’s advocacy efforts to bring 
accountability to the region, and Barrick who was one of the group of Conservative politicians, was opposed to 
much of the citizen-led advocacy work Smith was a key part of. 
Smith has worked as a reporter for The Pointer since 2023 and recently sent Barrick questions as part of an 
investigation into his hiring and subsequent departure in Thames Centre where he served as CAO. 
Smith has never been accused of stalking and has no recollection of any communication initiated by Barrick. 
The March 11 incident quickly drew attention across Ontario, prompting a flood of messages from municipal 
officials, political observers and concerned citizens, raising questions about transparency, accountability and the 
concentration of administrative power in the municipal sector.
Under the Criminal Code of Canada, providing false or misleading information to police can constitute an offence. 
Section 140, known as public mischief, applies when someone intentionally misleads law enforcement into acting 
on inaccurate information. Other potential offences could include obstruction of justice or fabricating evidence, 
depending on the circumstances. 
Requests for further comment sent to Mayor McGillis and all members of council were not returned. 
Barrick’s departure comes less than three months after he assumed the CAO role in South Stormont. First hired by 
the small municipality in November as the Deputy CAO. He worked with the outgoing chief bureaucrat Debi Lucas 
up until her retirement at the end of last year. Barrick assumed the role of CAO on January 1.
It’s unclear how elected officials in South Stormont were not informed of Barrick’s controversial past and the trail of 
scandal he has left behind in all three of his previous administrative positions.
Barrick first entered municipal administration in 2013. While serving as a regional councillor for Port Colborne, he 
was hired with no experience by Carmen D’Angelo, a friend of his, for a senior position with the Niagara Peninsula 
Conservation Authority (NPCA). Barrick was also an NPCA Board Member at the time. Both men have close 
connections with the Progressive Conservatives. Barrick worked as the NPCA’s corporate services director until 
2018, when he was fired. In a stunning twist which Ontario’s Auditor General would later criticize as improper 
following a scathing investigation into the NPCA’s governance issues, Barrick was briefly rehired as the interim 
CAO of the NPCA. He stepped down after Hamilton and Niagara councillors heavily criticized him for presenting an 
NPCA budget that could not account for more than $2 million in spending. The spending issues got to the point that 
residents protested, demanding he be fired. 
The awarding of his original job at the NPCA was flagged by the Ontario Auditor General as an example of unfair 
hiring practices at the conservation authority.
Barrick was also involved in the corrupt hiring process to get his friend, D’Angelo, the job as the CAO for Niagara 
Region. The scandal was laid bare by the now infamous “Inside Job” investigation by Ontario’s Ombudsman, Paul 
Dubé in 2019. 
Though not mentioned by name in the exhaustive report—Dubé refers to him only by his title—it outlines in detail 
how Barrick worked with other bureaucrats to get D’Angelo the CAO job. Their efforts undermined what was meant 
to be a fair and impartial process. 
After his departure from Niagara, Barrick landed in Brampton through a process controlled by Mayor Brown.
During his time as Brampton’s CAO, Barrick:

David Barrick gone after less than 3 months in latest municipal CAO role, weeks after banning Pointer reporter
• gave $218,000 in City of Brampton contracts (with no public explanation) to a former Niagara ally who was 
unqualified for the vaguely outlined work.
• handed a lucrative contract to handle the municipality’s real estate portfolio to a friend of the mayor whose 
company, which had not even been registered when he was contacted by one of Barrick’s staff about the 
job, had no experience managing such a task. The man was Brett Bell, a long-time Conservative insider 
with connections to Brown.
• shifted the Freedom of Information function and the Internal Audit department–vital tools for public 
accountability over elected officials–under his control.
• ensured the approval of contracts worth over $600,000 to friends of the mayor and a local councillor, 
Rowena Santos. Much of the work was never done. 
• hired inexperienced people without the required education for critical engineering positions
• placed the City’s corporate fraud hotline under the control of close connections he hired
• altered the results of a damning internal audit report 
The situation in Brampton sparked outrage. For the second time in his career residents protested in the street, 
demanding Barrick be fired. 
A majority group of councillors stopped attending council meetings alleging democracy was “under siege"" in the 
city. When those councillors were eventually able to take control of decision-making, Barrick was fired in February 
2022. 
In June of 2023 the municipality of Thames Centre, a town of just under 14,000 about 15 minutes east of London, 
announced it had hired Barrick as the new CAO after a “comprehensive recruitment process”.
Residents and municipal officials from the area who have contacted The Pointer allege turmoil inside town hall 
began almost immediately. Allegations of nepotism include Barrick’s hiring of his old friend Carmen D’Angelo to be 
the town’s treasurer and director of corporate services. Residents also allege improper spending, questionable 
contracts and upheaval among Town staff.
By August of last year Barrick was suddenly gone. In a statement, Thames Centre officials said Barrick resigned, 
but The Pointer has been told by multiple sources he was fired. After Barrick’s departure from Thames Centre, 
D’Angelo also left the municipality. 
Executive search firms appear to be partially responsible for Barrick’s repeated hiring, despite his lack of 
experience and disqualifying past. 
In South Stormont, Barrick’s most recent pit stop, an October 2025 press release from the Town explains Legacy 
Search Partners conducted a “competitive and thorough third-party executive search” that led to his selection as 
CAO. He lasted three months.
When he was hired in Brampton, Feldman Daxon Partners Inc., another executive search firm, recommended him 
for the role. That process was controlled by Brown. An investigation by The Pointer found that during the hiring 
process, Feldman Daxon failed to mention his involvement in the Niagara Inside Job hiring scandal when Carmen 
D’Angelo was handed the confidential interview questions and answers by senior staff, to ensure his selection for 
the CAO job.
The Pointer continues to investigate how Barrick was hired in Thames Centre and South Stormont, and why he no 
longer has a job. 
The OPP told The Pointer that officers will help determine who falsely claimed reporter Ed Smith had been stalking 
Barrick.

Title: Deputy minister broke conflict of interest rules by hiring university peer: ethics watchdog
Body: The government's ethics watchdog has found that Christine Fox, the Department of National Defence's top civilian 
official, broke conflict of interest rules by hiring a university peer.
Ethics commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein released a report on Wednesday that found Fox hired Björn Charles 
- whom she knew from when they were both athletes in university - as a project manger in 2023 when she was 
deputy minister of Immigration, Refugee and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).
Charles was hired in the department's access-to-information division, according to the report( https://ciec-
ccie.parl.gc.ca/en/investigations-enquetes/Pages/FoxReport-RapportFox.aspx ).
Fox has since served as deputy clerk of the Privy Council before moving to her current role as deputy minister at 
DND - a position she was shuffled to by Prime Minister Mark Carney( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-
service/carney-shakeup-senior-ranks-public-service ).
""This report reminds appointed federal officials at all levels to keep the Conflict of Interest Act in mind whenever 
there's a possibility of influencing a decision,"" said Finckenstein. ""They're not allowed to use their position to try to 
influence a decision to further their private interests or those of their relatives or friends, or to improperly further 
another person's private interests.""
The report also found that officials at IRCC felt pressured by Fox to hire Charles at a level that he was not qualified.
Finckenstein ""concluded that Ms. Fox used her position as Deputy Minister to give Mr. Charles preferential 
treatment, by ensuring he met with departmental official quickly, seeking updates about his hiring, giving him 
internal information, and pushing for a higher job classification.""
Fox was also communicating closely with Charles throughout his hiring process and even helped prepare him for 
his interview with ATIP division officials, including sending him a IRCC briefing document, according to the report.
Charles was hired for a casual position at the higher level, and was later hired in a one-year term position.
Fox maintained her role in the hiring process was appropriate, but the ethics commissioner ""did not find these 
claims credible,"" according to the report.
Page 2 of 3
Deputy minister broke conflict of interest rules by hiring university peer: ethics watchdog
Fox's ethics violation took place in the same year that she sat on a deputy minister task team on values and 
ethics inside the public service.
A year later, in 2024, Fox would be promoted to deputy clerk and would spearhead a renewed conversation on 
values and ethics in the public service.( https://www.canada.ca/en/privy-council/services/values-
ethics/messages/message-broadening-values-ethics-conversations-within-organizations-march-2024.html )
In the conclusion of his report, Finckenstein said he did not find Fox's justification for her actions in the process 
were ""motivated"" by the needs of the division Charles was hired to work in.
""Clearly, the true intent behind her interventions was to help Mr. Charles find new employment, and this occurred 
under her watch through the creation of a position in her department to fit Mr. Charles' needs,"" he said.
The Privy Council Office and DND did not immediately provide comment.
IRCC did not not immediately provide comment, either.
More to come.

Title: Deputy minister says she helped hire university peer to address 'client service' skills gap
Body: A deputy minister says she pushed to get an acquaintance hired for a federal government job to help address 
""client service"" in a unit where that skillset was lacking.
Christiane Fox, the top civilian official at the Department of National Defence, faced questions at a Commons 
committee meeting on Monday, April 13, about an ethics watchdog report that found she broke conflict of interest 
rules( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/deputy-minister-broke-conflict-of-interest-rules-ethics-watchdog-
christiane-fox ) by influencing the hiring of a university peer.
Fox repeated her previous comments from a public statement released last week, saying she acted out of ""a 
genuine desire to bring in outside perspectives""( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/defence-watch/christiane-
fox-responds-to-conflict-of-interest ) and advance diversity and inclusion efforts in the department by hiring a 
Black man.
In response to questions from MPs, Fox declined several invitations to acknowledge wrongdoing and instead 
explained her decision-making in greater detail.
""The individual had experience in client service, something that the government struggles with,"" she said. ""We don't 
do client service particularly well, and in this unit, it was obvious that we didn't.""
She added that ""this was a context of trying to change an underperforming unit within the department that occupied 
a lot of my attention.""
Evidence of 'preferential treatment': ethics report
Ethics commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein released a report on April 8, finding Fox influenced the hiring of Björn 
Charles - whom she knew from when they were both athletes in university - as a project manager in 2023.
At the time, she was deputy minister of Immigration, Refugee and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). Fox has since 
served as deputy clerk of the Privy Council before moving to her current role as deputy minister at DND.
According to the ethics commissioner's report( https://ciec-ccie.parl.gc.ca/en/investigations-
enquetes/Pages/FoxReport-RapportFox.aspx ), officials at IRCC felt pressured by Fox to hire Charles in the 
department's access-to-information division. According to his LinkedIn profile, Charles now works as an ATIP 
analyst in the Privy Council Office (PCO).
Page 2 of 3
Deputy minister says she helped hire university peer to address 'client service' skills gap
Fox and her family attended the same Goodlife gym where Charles worked as a manager before he was hired at 
IRCC, the report found. Fox's spouse was Charles' assistant basketball coach while he was a student at Carleton 
University from 2001 to 2004.
The ethics commissioner's investigation also found that Fox's spouse was a ""third or fourth cousin"" of Charles' 
father.
Throughout the hiring process, Fox communicated closely with Charles and helped prepare him for his interview 
with ATIP division officials, including sending him an IRCC briefing document.
Von Finckenstein ""concluded that Ms. Fox used her position as Deputy Minister to give Mr. Charles preferential 
treatment, by ensuring he met with departmental officials quickly, seeking updates about his hiring, giving him 
internal information and pushing for a higher job classification.""
Charles was hired for a casual position and was later hired on a one-year term.
Fox maintained her role in the hiring process was appropriate, but the ethics commissioner ""did not find these 
claims credible.""
Fox 'reflecting heavily'
In her opening statement at the meeting on Monday, Fox briefly addressed the ethics report.
""I take this matter very seriously,"" she said. ""I respect the role of the commissioner and the office, and I need to 
focus on my role as a public service leader and here at National Defence.""
Multiple times throughout the meeting, Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs pressed Fox on the report.
""I wasn't going to bring it up, but since you did,"" said Conservative MP James Bezan, ""can you assure Parliament 
and Canadians that you won't be using your office as a public office holder to further the interests of private 
individuals?""
Fox responded: ""I can assure the committee that I can continue to demonstrate a commitment to public service, to 
build on the strong commitment I've had over my career, and that yes, I will take my responsibility seriously, as I 
always have.""
Later in the meeting, Conservative MP Ned Kuruc said he found Fox's answers ""a little bit jarring.""
""If you don't acknowledge any errors, the Canadian public is going to wonder how you move forward,"" he said.
Fox said she will be ""reflecting heavily"" on how she approaches initiating change as a leader.
She laid out the events from her perspective.
An individual with whom she went to university decades ago reached out with genuine interest to join the federal 
public service. The assistant deputy minister responsible for the program had asked Fox to share resumes for that 
unit. Fox recommended Charles for the role.
In making her decision, Fox said she considered the interest of the candidate, the skills gap at the unit and data on 
the experience of Black men in the public service.
Her ultimate decision, she said, was an effort to change a unit that wasn't performing up to par. Fox added she had 
previously worked in departments where her efforts at embracing diversity faced resistance and systemic barriers to 
change.
At the end of the meeting, Conservative MP Gérard Deltell revisited the issue a final time.
