Title: Mayor Jeff Leal refuses to hear from delegates over his use of racial slur
Body: Peterborough Mayor Jeff Leal walked out of council chambers Monday, refusing to hear from residents addressing 
an integrity report regarding his use of a racial slur.
Two residents had signed up to delegate on an integrity commissioner report that found Leal’s use of the N-word 
 during a guest lecture at Trent University last March “unacceptable,” but not in contravention of council’s code of 
conduct.
“Because of the nature of the delegations this evening, I'll recuse myself,” Leal said before handing over the 
chair’s responsibilities to Deputy Mayor Gary Baldwin, and exiting council chambers as members of the public 
 gallery expressed muffled shock.
Leal made the decision even though the motion before council did not implicate the mayor in any pecuniary or 
other conflict of interest, which would have required him to be recused.
The first delegate, Iyiola Alade, president of the Trent Central Student Association, began by thanking councillors 
Alex Bierk and Joy Lachica for “continuously showing support and allyship to the Black and overall racialized 
community.”
Alade said the findings of the integrity commissioner’s report “shows how far we have to go as a city before 
claiming to be a safe and diverse community.”
The contention that Leal was quoting former U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson was called “a lie” by Alade, and 
the use of the slur was deemed “a direct attack on Black identities and not a mistake.”
“This same mayor, who has been present in Black History Month proclamations over the years and has given 
speeches — clearly, the man is a hoax and only sees his action as a check off for saving face,” Alade added.
Patricia Wilson, executive director of the Community Race Relations Committee (CRRC), addressed councillors 
next, stating that “it is not reasonable for anyone, especially an elected official and former cabinet minister, to 
claim ignorance about the harm of the N-word and the harm that it carries.”

Page 2 of 3
Mayor Jeff Leal refuses to hear from delegates over his use of racial slur
“Saying that you didn't know, in my opinion, is dishonest and a way to further evade accountability for harmful 
 actions,” Wilson said, adding the committee has responded to a record number of racial advocacy cases in local 
school boards in the past year.
“Of those cases, the majority of them involved youth under 12. These youth under 12 were experiencing extreme 
racism in our Peterborough schools. I have kids that are suicidal, because of that word. I have children that are 
scared to go to school, because of that word.”
Following Wilson’s delegation, Coun. Keith Riel asked what more, in her opinion, could council do for the 
community.
Wilson suggested council boost funding for organizations involved in racial advocacy work and councillors attend 
more of the events organized by CRRC and partner organizations.
“I'd love to see more councillors out at some of our events,” Wilson said. “I often see Alex Bierk and Joy Lachica at 
our events, but I would really love it if other folks would come out to our events to actually hear and understand the 
importance of what racialized community members are facing in our community.”
Following the delegations, Leal rejoined his colleagues in council chambers, as one member of the gallery loudly 
and sarcastically welcomed him back into the room.
Despite being in the room, Leal refrained from voting on the first part of the motion, which allowed councillors to 
 receive the report for information, but did not require any action from staff.
Councillors, Leal included, then voted unanimously to ask city staff to amend the council code of conduct to 
explicitly prohibit the use of racial slurs “regardless of context or circumstance.”
The motion came from recommendations by the city’s integrity commissioner, Guy Giorno. It also requires that the 
city’s strategic plan be amended to include anti-racism and race relations under the community and well-being 
pillar of the plan, and that all staff and councillors receive anti-racism, diversity and equity training.
Staff will report back within 60 days of Monday’s meeting about the code of conduct amendment and within 90 
days with an implementation plan for training.

Title: Michael Sabia to appear at ethics committee about Carney's business ties
Body: OTTAWA - The clerk of the Privy Council, Michael Sabia, is set to appear at the House of Commons ethics 
committee concerning the review of the Conflict of Interest Act but questions are expected to be focused on 
Prime Minister Mark Carney's potential conflicts.
Sabia is one of two senior aides to Prime Minister Mark Carney who is authorized to administer his extensive 
conflict-of-interest screen that applies to over 100 corporate entities( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/mark-
carney-conflict-of-interest ) related to Brookfield Asset Management, Brookfield Corporation and Stripe Inc.
The other person authorized to administer this screen is Carney's chief of staff, Marc-André Blanchard, who will be 
testifying at that same committee Thursday afternoon.
Carney's sprawling business ties - and potential conflicts of interest as a result of those ties - have been under 
close scrutiny since he decided to run as Liberal leader.
Prior to entering politics, Carney was chairman of Brookfield Asset Management, which has US$1 trillion in assets 
under management, and also helped lead efforts to raise capital for two major Brookfield clean energy funds. He 
was also on Stripe's board of directors.
On the day he was elected Liberal leader, he put all his assets, other than his personal real estate, into a blind trust. 
He has always maintained he went above and beyond what was required of him as he was to do so within 120 days 
of his appointment as prime minister.
But Conservatives have maintained that Carney's situation is unique, because of the magnitude of his conflicts of 
interest, and should require him to divest his assets.
Former clerk of the Privy Council Michael Wernick has however warned against considering mandatory divestitures 
for politicians during the review of the act.
""My view is that we need more people with private-sector background in politics - not fewer,"" he told the committee 
on Oct. 27.

Title: New files revive false claims about Carney Review shows PM mentioned in news summaries, had no direct
Body: The latest trove of documents related to Jeffrey Epstein reveals to new extents the relationships the notorious sex 
offender held with prominent and powerful figures, from Elon Musk to Bill Gates to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, 
formerly Prince Andrew.
The disclosure has also revived conspiracy theorists' attempts to connect the late financier to a particularly 
prominent Canadian: Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Fringe social media accounts, doubling down on claims they made during the last federal election, are pointing to 
Carney's name cropping up in the records as proof the two men were linked - even though a mere cursory read of 
the records that name Carney show they do not support the claim.
A search of the U.S. Department of Justice's online library containing the Epstein files turns up 69 mentions of Mark 
Carney, dating from 2013 to last fall, all of which have been reviewed by the Star.
The vast majority of incidents are news summaries in which Carney is mentioned in his official capacity as governor 
of the Bank of England. 
There is one email in which Epstein's associates discuss attending an event at which Carney is speaking. There's 
another in which a financial activist mentions the scrutiny Carney was facing at the time regarding a different 
scandal involving an investment firm that went under, taking the life savings of some clients with it.
There is no correspondence between Carney and Epstein, and no suggestion that Carney had any involvement 
with Epstein's crimes. (""The Prime Minister did not know and has never met Mr. Epstein,"" a spokesperson said in 
a statement.)
Other Canadian political figures, including Justin Trudeau and Stephen Harper, also show up in the latest Epstein 
drop for similar reasons.
Carney's mention in the Epstein files, even when it's just via news briefs, fuels a persistent conspiracy theory about 
him, particularly how his time at the Bank of England feeds into narratives about shadowy financial elites, says 
Amarnath Amarasingam, an associate professor who studies conspiracy theories and online communities at 
Queen's University.
Page 2 of 3
New files revive false claims about Carney Review shows PM mentioned in news summaries, had no direct 
connection with sex offender
""A lot of conspiracy theories equate power with nefarious activity and control, so that's a lot of what we are seeing 
here.""
Online conspiracy mongers have tried to link Carney to Epstein as early as the election campaign last summer. 
Much of it was sparked by a photo of Carney standing next to Ghislaine Maxwell, a close Epstein associate, at a 
music festival in 2013.
The photographer who took the photo snapped it for the social pages of a British newspaper that was interested in 
the weekend activities of Carney because he was a newcomer Canadian who'd recently been tapped to run the 
Bank of England. (A source close to Carney told the Star at the time that Maxwell went to school with Carney's 
wife's sister and that she and Carney were ""not friends."")
Despite any actual evidence linking Carney and Maxwell outside of a family connection, the conspiracy gained 
steam thanks to AI-generated images of Carney and Epstein. In spring 2025, there was what the Canadian Digital 
Media Research Network called ""a surge in suspicious posts on social media spreading false claims."" The online 
discourse leaked into the real world, when then-Liberal leader Carney was heckled at a campaign rally in March.
With scrutiny of the American government's handling of the case at a fever pitch, Congress voted last November to 
force the release of the Epstein files. 
They're less a cohesive set of documents than a hodgepodge of records from different departments, including files 
from FBI investigations, unclassified records, communications and court records. There are duplicates and 
redactions - meaning names or photos that have been blacked out - are inconsistent.
Transparency into the online files has some limitations, as some documents, including those that are written by 
hand, are not searchable.
Epstein killed himself in a jail in New York in summer 2019 after being indicted. In 2021, Maxwell was convicted of 
sex trafficking for her role in helping to recruit underage victims and is serving a 20-year prison sentence.

Title: No media at PC convention Some party insiders see ban as bid to prevent questions on controversies
Body: Premier Doug Ford's Progressive Conservatives have banned journalists from covering their convention this 
weekend. In an unprecedented move, the governing Tories are refusing to allow reporters into any part of their 
conference.
""The Ontario PC Party Convention is a closed event and will not be open to media attendance,"" Peter Turkington, 
the party's director of communications, wrote in a terse email Tuesday night.
Turkington's missive came six days after the Star and other news outlets inquired about accreditation for the event 
at the Toronto Congress Centre on Dixon Rd.
In Ottawa for a meeting of the Council of the Federation, Ford defended the decision to keep the press out. ""Well, 
you know something, it's a convention, and I'm out in the media almost every second day, and we'll chat, but this is 
a party convention,"" he said. ""So we're going to keep it as a party convention, but I'm always open to sit down and 
chat with you folks anytime you want,"" he told reporters.
""I'm focusing on this weekend, getting the message out to our Progressive Conservative base in Ontario and telling 
them the plan how we're going to protect themselves, protect the jobs and their communities.""
But some senior Tories, speaking confidentially in order to discuss internal deliberations, questioned the move. 
""This makes no sense to me,"" said one party insider who will be in attendance.
""We've always let you guys (in the media) go to the dinner for the speech,"" the Tory said, noting party brass ""must 
be worried"" about journalists interviewing delegates about controversies like the Skill Development Fund scandal 
or the Greenbelt fiasco.
Another veteran PC member who will also be there this weekend said the ban was ""foolish"" because it generates 
more negative media attention that any convention coverage would. ""This was clearly not thought through,"" said the 
second party stalwart, noting Ford normally welcomes press attention.
Hundreds of Tories will be gathering Friday through Sunday to celebrate their election victory last Feb. 27, paying 
between $99 for youth members and $299 for adults. ""Non-member observers"" will be charged $1,000 to enter and 
those wishing only to attend Saturday's gala dinner can attend for $250.
Page 2 of 3
No media at PC convention Some party insiders see ban as bid to prevent questions on controversies
""This exciting weekend will feature: remarks from Premier Doug Ford and members of the PC Caucus; inspiring 
speakers and policy discussions with fellow members; unforgettable hospitality suites and networking 
opportunities,"" the Tories' website boasts. ""Don't miss this chance to connect, engage, and help shape the future of 
our party. We can't wait to see you there!""
Traditionally, party conventions are at least partly open to reporters with leaders' speeches usually receiving most 
of the news coverage.
Both the official opposition New Democrats and Liberals allowed reporters to cover their September conventions. 
The NDP met in Niagara Falls while the Grits held their event in Toronto.
According to an itinerary published on the Tories' website, there will be a ""welcome reception with caucus"" on 
Friday night followed by a ""state of the party panel"" and an awards ceremony. Saturday's main draw is a 4 p.m. 
""fireside chat"" with Ford followed by a reception and a dinner with the leader.
On Sunday, the party will announce its new executive.
The provincial Tories purposely scheduled their convention to coincide with the federal Conservatives' convention 
that starts Thursday in Calgary. 
That's in part because Ford's team knew federal leader Pierre Poilievre's leadership review would dominate 
weekend political coverage so there would be less interest in - and scrutiny of - the Ontario party's internal 
machinations.
With files from Mark Ramzy

Title: Ontario sues Skills Development Fund -linked company over alleged fraud
Body: TORONTO - The Ontario government has filed a lawsuit against a company it contracted to run a student mental 
health program, alleging fraudulent misrepresentation and seeking to recoup more than $25 million in public money.
Ontario alleges Keel Digital Solutions, through its subsidiary Get A-Head Inc., inflated the number of counselling 
sessions it reported delivering to students, resulting in overpayments of millions of dollars. The company vigorously 
denies the allegations.
Between 2022 and 2025, the company ""provided false and misleading quarterly reports of their corporate 
performance measures,"" which were the basis for its payments, the government alleged in its lawsuit.
""The false reports caused the Crown to pay the corporate defendants millions of dollars that they otherwise would 
not have been paid,"" alleged the claim, which was filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on Wednesday.
The company said it would be filing a counterclaim.
""The government’s lawsuit against Keel Digital Solutions is deeply flawed, built on misstatements and outright 
inaccuracies,"" chief operating officer Jay Fischbach wrote Friday in a statement. 
""Keel Digital has never been involved in any fraudulent activity, and we fully expect the government of Ontario to 
be compelled to retract its claims, apologize, and answer for the recklessness and malice that drove this case.""
Keel Digital Solutions was closely scrutinized during the fall sitting of the legislature as one of the recipients of the 
Ministry of Labour's $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund, a program the auditor general has found was not fair or 
transparent and doled out money to applicants ranked low by bureaucrats. 
Labour Minister David Piccini came under sustained fire from opposition parties calling for his resignation, 
particularly since media reports said one of Keel's lobbyists is a close friend of Piccini's.
That heat only increased after the government announced it had referred the results of an audit on Keel's funding 
from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities to the Ontario Provincial Police, citing concerns dating back to 2023. 

Page 2 of 4
Ontario sues Skills Development Fund -linked company over alleged fraud
Critics questioned why the Ministry of Labour gave Keel $7.5 million in skills development funding for a first 
responder mental health program even after an audit of their student funding had raised concerns within a different 
ministry.
Piccini has said Keel Digital Solutions is one of the applicants that bureaucrats had ranked low but the ministry 
decided to fund. He has defended the practice of granting funding to low-scoring applications, saying that's done 
when they align with government priorities.
Ontario Provincial Police announced last month that they had launched an investigation into Keel's student mental 
health funding.
Liberal parliamentary leader John Fraser said the government's lawsuit seems self-serving, given that the police are 
already on the matter.
""This legal action appears designed to distract from the deeper and far more troubling problems at the heart of the 
Skills Development Fund,"" he wrote in a statement.
""Doug Ford now wants Ontarians to believe his government was swindled. They were not swindled. They were 
caught.""
In the province's lawsuit, Ontario alleges the company filed estimated expenses as opposed to actual expenses, 
failed to report unspent funds and interest earned, and overstated the metrics upon which its funding was based.
Get A-Head reported sessions providing counselling to people other than students as well as training mock 
sessions as student mental health sessions, the province alleges. It also reported the time spent by a counsellor, 
supervisor and student in one session as three separate sessions, the lawsuit alleges.
""(The company's) 2022-2023 final report claimed 42,556 eligible sessions between March 31, 2022 and March 30, 
2023,"" the government wrote in its lawsuit. 
""In actual fact, the Crown has learned that there were only 3,529 unique sessions of any duration during that 
period.""
The province also alleges several executives at the company ""directed, facilitated, and then tried to cover up the 
corporate defendants' false reports"" given to the ministry.
None of the allegations have been tested in court.
The company has previously said it has complied with all laws and contractual obligations and looks forward to an 
apology from the government at the end of the police probe.
Premier Doug Ford and Piccini have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and both have said they remain committed 
to the Skills Development Fund.
Ontario's integrity commissioner, Cathryn Motherwell, has also launched an ethics investigation into Piccini's 
dealings with that fund.
Media reports have said that some beneficiaries of the fund are unions that endorsed the Progressive 
Conservatives in elections and people who have donated to the party.
The auditor general also found that more than 60 of the lower-scoring fund applicants were approved after they 
hired a lobbyist, which had the opposition crying foul over what they called preferential treatment.
The Skills Development Fund gives money to organizations for projects that help hire, train or retrain workers. The 
province says they've so far trained about 700,000 people and of those, 100,000 people found jobs within 60 days 
of completing the program.

Title: Pablo Rodriguez had no knowledge of 'brownies' plan, report concludes
Body: QUEBEC - There is no evidence that Pablo Rodriguez ""participated in or was informed"" in any way of allegedly 
dubious fundraising tactics during his 2025 Quebec Liberal leadership campaign, a retired Superior Court judge 
has concluded.
And after weeks of investigating, Jacques Fournier says there is no way to verify the authenticity or falseness of a 
series of text messages, allegedly between Liberal supporters, suggesting votes for Rodriguez were being 
purchased for the price of a ""brownie"" (slang for a $100 bill).
Le Journal de Montréal broke the story on Nov. 19( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/11/19/il-faut-encore-
payer-pour-que-le-monde-vote-pablo-des-textos-troublants-derriere-la-crise-au-plq ), based on phone text 
messages it had obtained. The Liberals enlisted Fournier to independently investigate.
If anything, Fournier says in his 40-page report handed to the Liberals Wednesday, there is clear evidence the text 
messages are ""only a montage"" cobbled together from other original messages.
None of the texts are clearly dated, so there is no time frame on when they were sent, and there is no way to 
establish their origin, the judge says.
But Fournier also recognizes it is not possible for him to conclude that the texts were false or fabricated by the 
sources used by Le Journal de Montréal, because he did not have access to the entire messages.
As a result, he says he cannot conclude whether someone bought votes or not.
""It is clearly impossible to know the source of something if it did not exist,"" he says.
One thing he does conclude: Rodriguez knew nothing.
""Nothing indicates (Rodriguez) participated or was informed of any (fundraising) irregularities before having 
knowledge of the (Journal de Montréal) article Nov. 19, 2025,"" Fournier concludes in his report, which was released 
to the media.
""None of the revelations that appeared in the newspaper implicate him directly.""
Rodriguez, who resigned as Liberal leader on Dec. 17 after a crisis over the alleged fundraising irregularities 
snowballed into a question of confidence, has always denied any knowledge of what may have been going on( 
Page 2 of 4
Pablo Rodriguez had no knowledge of 'brownies' plan, report concludes
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-campaign-
allegations ) behind the scenes.
In a recent interview with L'actualité magazine( https://lactualite.com/politique/lascension-et-la-chute-de-pablo-
rodriguez/ ), Rodriguez said he was the victim of a party coup d'état to oust him as leader.
The deadline for candidacies to replace him is Friday, with only Charles Milliard an official candidate so far.
Le Journal at no time suggested Rodriguez was aware of what was allegedly going on. The initial article was based 
on text messages between two unnamed people who allegedly worked on the Rodriguez campaign. The messages 
suggested people were being compensated for buying memberships in the party to back Rodriguez.
""Did you have a chance to pick up the member's cards?"" reads one message. ""Yes, it's all done,"" responds the 
other person.
""The money also? ... So everyone will get a paid card this week?""
""Yes. And don't forget we submit the cards only on May 8 in case something goes wrong. So all that will be left is 
that when they have voted they get a brownie (a $100 bill) for voting.
""That's how I won my nomination campaign (for the party) so everyone is aware.
""OK. Perfect. If Pablo does not win, I am finished.""
Le Journal did not name the two individuals texting.
Later, Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau claimed, based on sources, that the two were Liberal Chomedey 
MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and the Coalition Avenir Québec MNA for Fabre, Alice Abou-Khalil, who was 
rumoured to want to leap to the Liberals before the upcoming Quebec election.
Both MNAs strongly denied the allegations( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-vote-buying-allegations ).
In his report, Fournier notes that as a retired judge, he did not have the power to oblige anyone connected to the 
story to testify, as would be the case in a trial. Most of the witnesses he spoke to were willing to take an oath to tell 
the truth.
He also enlisted the services of a private investigator, Anne Cléroux, who helped him gather the data he needed.
Fournier said everyone involved has denied the allegations under oath.
Lakhoyan Olivier told him she learned about the texts on May 6, 2025, the day Le Journal sent them to her asking 
for comment. She confirmed she owned two cellphones, but denied erasing any messages.
She also offered her phone records, but discovered the National Assembly phone supplier did not have a service to 
trace back texts. Her personal phone supplier provided a list showing no messages sent or received on April 12, 
2025, which is the date Le Journal de Montréal quoted.
Lakhoyan Olivier's sister, Zepure Lakhoyan, who raised funds for the Rodriguez campaign, denied any role in the 
alleged texting or any knowledge of a brownie scheme. She provided the judge a copy of her phone records 
showing she had no exchanges on the dates in question.
Lakhoyan Olivier is now sitting as an independent, pending the results of an investigation by the ethics 
commissioner.
Abou-Khalil did not sign a sworn statement, but denied any knowledge of the texts in an email to Fournier.
Page 3 of 4
Pablo Rodriguez had no knowledge of 'brownies' plan, report concludes
The judge said the one other person who, in theory, might have been one of the parties communicating - because 
his first name appears in one of the texts - is federal Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury.
Accompanied by his lawyer, El-Khoury told the judge he had no idea what the texts were about or who the ""Fayçal"" 
named in a text was. He said he was more involved in the federal leadership race than the provincial one at the 
time.
In November, Rodriguez recognized El-Khoury had raised funds for his campaign, confirming a story revealed by 
La Presse. The publication also reported that then-Liberal parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy had words with El-
Khoury during a chance encounter at the opening of the REM's Deux-Montagnes branch that month.
Rizqy reportedly came away with the impression some kind of ""flim-flam,"" or funny business, involving fundraising 
had taken place. It was shortly after that encounter that Rizqy fired her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, a close 
associate of Rodriguez.
That incident sparked the Quebec Liberal crisis that ended with Rodriguez leaving. Rizqy and Hinse are currently 
involved in a wrongful dismissal legal battle.
Fournier also investigated another Journal de Montréal story about the Liberals( 
https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/12/16/campagne-de-pablo-rodriguez--des-enveloppes-de-500-comptant-
pour-rembourser-une-vingtaine-de-donateurs ), published on Dec. 16, 2025, which alleged that during a Rodriguez 
fundraiser on April 12, 2025, a host compensated supporters for contributions to the campaign.
Known as a straw-man system, such an arrangement contravenes Quebec's electoral laws.
It was later reported that the person in question staging the event was wine and port importer Emanuel Cabral( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-campaign-
allegations ), president of Global International Networks Wines &; Spirits. He has admitted in the media to paying 
for some of his employees to donate.
Fournier says the fundraiser seemed to contravene the law, but adds he is limited in what he can say because the 
event is being investigated by Quebec's anti-corruption unit, UPAC.
But Fournier concludes nothing proves it was anything more than an ""isolated and unwise"" initiative launched by 
one person, adding Rodriguez again had no knowledge.

Title: Pablo Rodriguez's replacement as Quebec Liberal leader will be chosen in March
Body: The race to succeed Pablo Rodriguez as Quebec Liberal leader will begin Jan. 12, with the party's new leader 
elected at a March 14 convention, the party announced Tuesday.
The party said the general rules of the race were adopted Monday evening by its executive council and that the 
detailed rules will be made public at a later date.
Rodriguez stepped down last week( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/pablo-rodriguez-future-
quebec-liberals-caucus-meeting-delay ), six months after he was elected leader. It was the shortest leadership term 
in the party's history.
The resignation came amid a growing scandal surrounding Rodriguez's leadership campaign, including allegations 
that some Liberal members were paid $100 - referred to as ""brownies"" because of the colour of $100 bills - to vote 
for Rodriguez, and that some donors to his campaign were reimbursed by a Montreal businessman( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/what-to-know-about-the-quebec-liberal-party-crisis ).
While Rodriguez has not been accused of any wrongdoing, he said he was resigning because he had become ""a 
distraction( https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-speaks-quebec-liberals-resignation )."" He had faced 
calls from inside the party to step down since early December.
The scandal began last month when then-Liberal parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy abruptly fired her chief of 
staff( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ), 
Geneviève Hinse, a close associate of Rodriguez. Rodriguez responded to Hinse's firing by suspending Rizqy and 
then expelling her from the Liberal caucus( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rodriguez-expells-
rizqy-from-quebec-liberal-caucus-as-crisis-grows ). It later emerged that Hinse had been tasked with overseeing 
financing at the fundraiser where donors were allegedly reimbursed, though reports said there was no evidence 
Hinse was aware of any scheme.
The race to succeed Rodriguez will be based on a points system. Each riding will be worth 3,000 points - 2,000 for 
party members age 26 and over and 1,000 for party members age 25 and under - with points assigned to 
candidates based on the percentage of the vote they receive.
Page 2 of 2
Pablo Rodriguez's replacement as Quebec Liberal leader will be chosen in March
Potential candidates will have until Feb. 13 to register and will have to obtain signatures from 750 party members 
and submit a $30,000 deposit.
Charles Milliard, former head of the Fédération des chambres de commerce du Québec, came second to 
Rodriguez in June's leadership vote and has said he's still considering whether he will run again.
Karl Blackburn, the former head of employers' group the Conseil du patronat du Québec and a former Liberal MNA, 
came third on the first ballot in June. He has said he will not run again.
Quebecers are scheduled to go to the polls on Oct. 5 for the province's next general election.
Premier François Legault has said he will seek a third term in office. His Coalition Avenir Québec party is polling in 
third place, behind clear front-runners the Parti Québécois and the Liberals, who have been polling in second place.

Title: PCs suggest A.I. errors in Education Accord originated within government
Body: Newfoundland and Labrador’s education ministry is hinting at the government’s own culpability for more than a 
dozen AI-generated errors that were found in the province’s new Education Accord released in August.
Education and Early Childhood Development Media Relations Manager Lynn Robinson shared a statement from 
the department saying “[t]he inaccurate citations and references generated by AI was unacceptable,” and that the 
government “will ensure that any application of AI within government is subject to strict review, human verification, 
and transparent quality controls.”
The statement also said a new draft of the accord will be publicly released in the new year. The department 
previously said, in October, that work on the updated report would be completed “in the coming weeks,” according 
to CBC.
Labrador-based research and editing firm Brack and Brine was hired “to review all references and citations in the 
Education Accord,” the department’s statement said, adding the report’s “errors will be removed, and we are 
ensuring the integrity of the report has been upheld.”
In August the previous Liberal government released the accord, a decadal roadmap to improving the province’s 
education systems, including K-12 and post-secondary. The report took co-chairs Karen Goodnough and Anne 
Burke—professors in Memorial University’s Faculty of Education—18 months to complete, with input from 
education experts and others. But in September Radio-Canada revealed the 418-page document contained at 
 least 15 fake citations which appeared to be generated by AI, calling into question the $755,000-report’s credibility 
and prompting government to remove it from its website.
Then-Education Minister Bernard Davis defended the report, saying the fake citations “never impacted the body of 
the report or any of the recommendations.” Goodnough and Burke told CBC they “don’t know where the errors 
were made,” and that they “can only assume that it happened with government.”
Until now, the provincial government has not publicly addressed the origins of the report’s fake citations.
Earlier this month The Independent exposed another AI-related scandal, this time with fake citations in another 
major government-commissioned report that cost the province $1.6 million. The Department of Health and

Community Service’s recent Health Human Resources Plan, developed by global accounting and consulting firm 
 Deloitte, contains at least four citations The Independent found not to exist.
The second scandal in under three months related to artificial intelligence use in government policy documents 
has sparked a discussion in the province and elsewhere about the risks associated with improper AI use and the 
value of third party-commissioned policy reports where AI is used.
The province’s Department of Government Services has committed to reviewing government policies and to 
potentially developing new regulations.
On Friday Government Services Minister Mike Goosney said in a statement to The Independent that 
“incorporating this technology into the public service requires oversight and accountability and training for 
employees on the responsible use of AI.”
He said the province’s Office of the Chief Information Officer “delivers in-person training on Microsoft Copilot to 
departments and offers a training course on responsible AI use in government,” while also hosting “an online 
dedicated AI support space with articles, guiding principles, case studies, and best practices related to AI that 
 government employees can avail of.”
Goosney said, going forward, “we will ensure that any application of AI within government is subject to strict review, 
human verification, and transparent quality controls in collaboration with the Office of the Information Privacy 
Commissioner.” 
When the accord was announced in January 2024, then PC Education Critic Paul Dinn said the new study wasn’t 
necessary. “The minister’s desk is full of announcements, studies and reports outlining the problems facing the 
education system in our province,” Dinn, who is now the province’s education minister, said in a statement at the 
time.
“Teachers, parents, childcare workers and other stakeholders have been calling for action for years. Yet the Liberal 
government wants to do another study and kick the can down the road.”

Title: PCs to review A.I. use in government-commissioned reports
Body: Two days after The Independent first reported the presence of fake citations in a $1.6 million government-
commissioned healthcare policy report from Deloitte, Premier Tony Wakeham’s office says Minister of 
Government Services Mike Goosney has been asked to “undertake a review of what guidelines should be put in 
place to stop this from happening in the future.”
A spokesperson from the premier’s office said the directive was given “based on recent examples coming to light 
of AI being used by consultants to generate reports for government.”
On Nov. 22 The Independent reported the existence of at least four sources cited by Deloitte in the province’s 
Health Human Resources Plan which do not exist or appear not to exist. The province’s Department of Health and 
Community Services said it confirmed with Deloitte that the four sources were “incorrect” and that it has “directed 
Deloitte to confirm the accuracy of the citations and literature review.
Deloitte has not responded to The Independent’s questions, but the health ministry said the company told the 
government it “stands by the conclusions and findings in the report.”
On Monday provincial NDP Leader Jim Dinn called on the government to implement “strict regulations” around the 
use of artificial intelligence in government-commissioned reports, adding the use of AI in such reports is 
“disgusting” and “undermining the confidence in our government to do the work necessary to address the issues in 
our healthcare system, and truly throughout the province.”
Last month Deloitte was caught in a similar scandal involving the use of artificial intelligence in a report for the 
Australian government, resulting in the company issuing a partial refund for its mistakes. The provincial 
government and Deloitte have not responded to questions from The Independent around a potential full or partial 
refund for the Health Human Resources Plan, which includes more than 100 occupation-specific 
recommendations for the government to “strengthen and transform health care delivery in Newfoundland and 
Labrador,” then Health Minister Krista Lynn Howell said when the report was released in May.
The Independent asked the Department of Government Services for details on the review of artificial intelligence 
and third-party consultants. We will publish an update once we learn more.

Title: Piccini's future left up in air Ford won't say if minister will keep his job in wake of ethics investigation
Body: Premier Doug Ford is not saying if embattled Labour Minister David Piccini will remain in cabinet in the wake of a 
new ethics investigation into the $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund.
Ford evaded a question about the minister's future Friday in Buffalo, where he signed an agreement with New York 
Gov. Kathy Hochul on advancing nuclear power through potential joint projects.
Asked by a reporter if it were time ""to ask him to step down or for him to be fired,"" the premier pointedly did not 
defend Piccini.
""I know he'll co-operate with the integrity commissioner,"" said Ford, who later walked away and refused to answer 
more questions on the imbroglio at a press conference. 
But he insisted the fund would ""continue on training people.""
His comments came a day after integrity commissioner Cathryn Motherwell announced she would investigate 
complaints from the opposition New Democrats and Liberals about the minister.
""The inquiry is in response to two separate requests from Marit Stiles, leader of the Official Opposition and MPP for 
Davenport and Stephanie Smyth, MPP for Toronto-St. Paul's,"" said Motherwell's spokesperson Juliet Kadzviti.
""The requests asked the commissioner to determine whether David Piccini ... contravened sections of the 
(Members' Integrity) Act in relation to the application and selection process of the Skills Development Fund training 
stream,"" said Kadzviti.
""As the two requests cover similar subject matter, the commissioner has decided to deal with them together under 
one inquiry. 
As required by the act, a report will be filed with the speaker of the legislative assembly of Ontario once the inquiry 
has been concluded.""
Piccini has denied any wrongdoing. In a statement, his office said ""we are continuing to assist the integrity 
commissioner with her work on this file.""

Piccini's future left up in air Ford won't say if minister will keep his job in wake of ethics investigation
Stiles said she expects the ethics watchdog to look closely at low-ranked applications ""that went from the bottom of 
the pile to the top"" on Piccini's desk.
""You have to ask yourself why,"" she added.
""The premier should have the cojones to fire him ... everything he touches now is going to be associated with this 
scandal.""
Smyth, meanwhile, said Motherwell's probe ""is an important first step to getting to the bottom of the rot within the 
fund.""
""The premier and his government are using the Skills Development Fund to reward well-connected insiders, 
donors and lobbyists. This pattern of pay-to-play cannot continue,"" said the Liberal MPP.
""At a bare minimum, the minister should step aside while the investigation is ongoing.""
Earlier this fall, auditor general Shelley Spence issued a special report concluding Ford's Progressive 
Conservatives handed out training funds to poorly rated applicants in a way that was ""not fair, transparent or 
accountable.""
Spence found 670 funding applications ranked ""high"" by bureaucrats were rejected by Piccini.
In the aftermath of that, the Star revealed a secret government database - that the minister still refuses to officially 
release - showing 26 applicants scoring 50 per cent or lower received $36 million from the fund earlier this year.
The Star also disclosed that 17 unions and industry groups that endorsed the Tories in the February election 
received $237 million from the fund.

Title: Picinni is a better buffer than fall guy Ford is in no hurry to fire hapless labour minister, a convenient distraction
Body: Doug Ford faces a growing political problem with a seemingly obvious solution.
That problem is David Piccini, Ontario's embattled minister of labour.
Day by day Piccini sinks deeper into the muck, whence he greased the wheels of the premier's grimy re-election 
machine. He scooped that muck out of the government's so-called Skills Development Fund, which amounted to a 
slush fund - in some cases doling out public money to friendly labour unions that could be counted on to endorse 
the Progressive Conservative government in last February's campaign.
Now, the cheques have come to roost.
Ontario's auditor general has sifted the slush and sniffed the cash. Her audit's bottom line is that the minister's 
math made no sense.
Mysteriously, recent multimillion-dollar submissions with low ratings still merited his signature for approval - more, 
on average, then high-rated applicants. In Piccini's peculiar judgment, it seemed prudent to override the best advice 
of non-partisan civil servants for the worst kind of hyperpartisan vote-buying.
Amid the stench, the opposition smells blood. They are calling for Piccini's head, berating him as a buffoon.
Will Ford decapitate his cabinet minister to save his own skin? Be careful what you wish for, for a buffoon can be a 
buffer.
Ultimately, this is a problem of the premier's own making.
Typically, when you fire the fall guy, the problem fades away. But in Ford's case, his fingerprints are all over the 
skills development and slush dissemination fund.
That's why the premier is loath to let him go. Piccini is more useful as a foil than a fall guy - a convenient target 
(and distraction) for opposition taunts and torments while he watches from a safe distance.
A run-of-the-mill minister, Piccini ran the slush fund but didn't own it. It was the orphaned brainchild of the premier.
Page 2 of 3
Picinni is a better buffer than fall guy Ford is in no hurry to fire hapless labour minister, a convenient distraction 
for premier's critics
But the minister adopted it as his own. As the auditor discovered, Piccini - who cut his teeth as a political aide and 
knows how to sideline the bureaucracy - systematically disregarded the ratings of his ministry's civil servants, 
imposing his own political priorities over their fiscal prudence.
The result, the auditor concluded in a special report last month, was that Piccini's ministry handed out public money 
from the $2.5 billion fund to at least 64 organizations in a manner she deemed was not ""fair, transparent or 
accountable.""
Under fire after the fact, Piccini fends off criticism daily in the legislature by insisting he could see what civil servants 
couldn't fathom - the hidden talents of applicants, the unseen potential of favoured trade unions (whose fidelity 
Ford's Tories could be counted on), the presumed trustworthiness of unproven organizations. Tens of millions of 
dollars have been disbursed on the say-so of a politicized Piccini, empowered by a populist premier in pursuit of 
ever more popularity.
Tempting as it is to decry this as debased, it is par for the course. Every party in power is prone to shovelling cash 
out the door - whether from slush funds or the general treasury - passing the buck from elected governments to 
unelected, unaccountable entities who are entrusted with massive amounts of public money without public scrutiny.
The Ford government isn't the first to give away the store, if not always for political purposes. Remember the 
notorious e-Health and ORNGE scandals that beset previous Liberal governments?
When the provincial auditor poked into Piccini's pig in a poke, her agenda wasn't to expose partisan impropriety but 
governmental incompetence. She had good reason to hypothesize that the downstream problem would be lack of 
fiscal transparency by the building trades and other recipients.
Indeed, the civil servants who scrutinized some of the more dubious applications repeatedly flagged the 
questionable abilities and capacities of Tory-friendly recipients (and others) to meet the high accounting standards 
required for public funding.
In opposition, the Tories frequently complained about government giveaways that amounted to corporate welfare 
for those with their hands out. Now that the shoe is on the other foot, Ford is sitting pretty in the premier's chair.
Even if you set aside any philosophical objection to government grants - corporate or labour, cultural or charitable - 
the lack of proper accountability doubtless keeps the auditor awake at night.
As for Piccini's presumed peril, he can sleep well at night even while the auditor stays up all night. For the moment, 
he is safeguarded by his status as a foil guy, not a fall guy.
Indeed, he's probably the safest minister in a cabinet populated by one too many bumblers and boondogglers for 
Ford to fire in one fell swoop. Perhaps Ford hopes to wait it out until the legislature rises early next month for its 
pre-Christmas break, or possibly the premier is biding his time before a cabinet shuffle if the scandal dies down.
The only certainty is that Ford's Tories remain focused on the politics, not the governance. Yet the root problems 
will return to haunt the premier, because at the end of the day bad government is bad politics.

Title: Pressure mounts on Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez to resign amid crisis
Body: QUÉBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is facing increasing pressure from prominent Liberals to step 
down amid an ongoing crisis within the party. 
But the former federal cabinet minister insists he will remain in office and that he can still win the next provincial 
election. 
""I was elected by the party members because they know I have the experience to beat the (governing Coalition 
Avenir Québec) and beat the Parti Québécois,"" the embattled leader told reporters Thursday morning on the 
sidelines of his party's caucus meeting in Quebec City. ""I'm not going anywhere.""
A day earlier, Quebec's anti-corruption police announced they were launching a criminal investigation of the 
Quebec Liberals, following allegations of vote-buying during the leadership race that Rodriguez won in June.
The news has prompted some Liberals to call openly for the leader's resignation, claiming the ongoing crisis has 
damaged the party with less than a year to go before the next election. 
Former Liberal minister Christine St-Pierre said the anti-corruption unit's investigation is the straw that broke the 
camel's back.
""It's undermining his leadership,"" she said in an interview with The Canadian Press on Thursday. ""It's up to him to 
make the decision, but I urge him to seriously consider the best interests of the party.""
Another former Liberal minister, Serge Simard, called for Rodriguez to step down. 
""The die is cast. The damage is done. So, from this point on, if we want to put this behind the party — a party that 
has done a lot for Quebec, it must be said — we have to stop this now and replace the leader. We have no choice, 
we've reached that point,"" he said. 
Simard supported one of Rodriguez's rivals, Charles Milliard, in the leadership campaign, and is now inviting 
Milliard to re-enter the race if the Liberal leader were to step aside. ""I had confidence in Charles. I still have 
confidence in him,"" he said Thursday. 

Page 2 of 3
Pressure mounts on Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez to resign amid crisis
On Wednesday, Rodriguez's other main leadership rival, Karl Blackburn, told Radio-Canada that the situation is 
""extremely worrying.""
""I think that Mr. Rodriguez, in this context, certainly has to ask himself some serious questions,"" he said. 
Blackburn did not rule out replacing Rodriguez if he were to resign. 
A third former Liberal minister, Jean D'Amour, is also calling on Rodriguez to step down for the good of the party.
""I think the time has come for him to prove his commitment to the party and, unfortunately, to leave. I'm not doing 
this lightly, but I talk to activists, I talk to association presidents, and these people are a little fed up, exasperated 
with the situation,"" he said in an interview with The Canadian Press on Wednesday.
The Liberal caucus was thrown into turmoil in November after former parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy fired her 
chief of staff without consulting Rodriguez. He later expelled her from the caucus, saying she had not explained her 
reasons to him and that she lacked loyalty.
Shortly after Rizqy dismissed her chief of staff, Le Journal de Montréal published text messages suggesting some 
party members who voted for Rodriguez could have received cash rewards. It's unclear whether the two stories are 
connected.
Last week, Rodriguez announced he had expelled a second Liberal member of the legislature, Sona Lakhoyan 
Olivier, from his caucus because of an investigation by Quebec’s ethics commissioner. 
The office of the ethics commissioner said it would examine whether Lakhoyan Olivier used resources from her 
constituency office for partisan purposes during the leadership race. 
Montreal radio station 98.5 FM named Lakhoyan Olivier as one of the two people behind the text messages 
reported by Le Journal de Montréal, but she has denied that claim and has sent a legal letter to station owner 
Cogeco.
The Canadian Press has not verified whether the text messages were authentic.
Rodriguez has said he welcomes the investigations, and he has nothing to hide. He has separately asked a retired 
judge to investigate the claims. 
In Quebec City on Thursday, the mood among Liberal caucus members was downcast, though they have not 
publicly broken ranks with their leader. Liberal Enrico Ciccone said his constituents were beginning to talk to him 
about the controversy. 
""We are in a difficult situation today. We are terribly hurt. We work so hard for the people in our ridings. What we 
want to know is the whole truth,"" he said. 
Another Liberal member of the legislature, Monsef Derraji, reminded reporters that he was not involved in any 
candidate's leadership campaign. ""These are extremely difficult times,"" he said. ""Every day, we learn something 
new.""
But others reiterated their support for Rodriguez. ""I am prepared to go to war with him,"" said Liberal Linda Caron. 
""Nothing wrong was done during the campaign.""
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 11, 2025.

Title: Province sues youth group for $3.29M Non-profit accused of failing to train hundreds of marginalized young
Body: A Toronto youth group is facing a $3.29-million lawsuit by the provincial government over alleged misuse of money 
from the controversial Skills Development Fund.
In a statement of claim dated Dec. 11, the Ontario government says Justice Fund Toronto and its director, Yonis 
Hassan, the not-for-profit's ""sole director, alter ego and directing mind,"" was awarded nearly $4 million by the 
Ministry of Labour in March 2023 to give ""life skills training"" for roughly 800 marginalized young people but failed to 
do so.
Filed in Ontario Superior Court, the lawsuit claims Hassan and the Justice Fund benefited from ""unjust enrichment"" 
of taxpayer dollars. 
Its allegations have not been proven in court. The Star made numerous attempts to contact Hassan, but did not 
receive a response. 
Hassan has had a media presence in recent years, including events with Noah ""40"" Shebib, a music producer and 
friend of the rapper Drake. Shebib, who previously referred to himself as a Justice Fund co-founder, is quoted, 
along with Hassan, in an August 2023 CBC story, saying Drake planned to donate $1 from every ticket sold to his 
""It's All a Blur"" tour to the group.
Hassan is the only director named on the federal corporate records for the Justice Fund. Neither Shebib nor Drake 
face any allegations and neither were named in the lawsuit.
In the 12-page statement of claim, the government alleges that Hassan and his organization ""repeatedly avoided or 
neglected"" visits from Labour Ministry staff investigating ""non-compliance"" of the funding agreement. Justice Fund 
did not file all of the required expenditure reports which, the lawsuit said, led to a government-led forensic audit that 
found ""inappropriate use"" of the SDF money.
Last summer, on July 3, the ministry demanded repayment of $3.29 million. Two weeks later, the Justice Fund filed 
articles of dissolution to shoot down operations which, the government claimed, was a ""breach of trust and 
fiduciary duties."" That action was later cancelled and the organization remains active.
Page 2 of 3
Province sues youth group for $3.29M Non-profit accused of failing to train hundreds of marginalized young 
people
This is the second lawsuit filed by the province in the past two months that seeks repayment of the labour ministry's 
SDF grants.
Both demand millions of dollars paid out by the fund that says it gives grants to programs meant to provide training 
for in-demand jobs - with a focus on supports for ""underrepresented communities."" 
In early January, Keel Digital Solutions and its subsidiary, Get A-Head, were hit with a government lawsuit 
demanding the return of $22.3 million in grants from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities and $3.2 million from 
the Skills Development Fund, with an additional $400,000 in punitive damages.
Keel has said it will fight the lawsuit, promising to take legal action against the government. Last December, the 
Ontario Provincial Police launched a criminal investigation into Keel. 
While the Keel Digital lawsuit was announced by Premier Doug Ford's office, the government did not respond to 
the Star's questions on the Justice Fund statement of claim. 
On its Instagram site, the Justice Fund said it is ""dedicated to supporting communities in conflict with the law.""
Many of its posts speak against inequality in Toronto, noting a city divided, with some living in relative affluence 
while others struggle in communities traumatized by gun violence, poverty and higher rates of incarceration. 
When the funding was approved in early 2023, the agreement said the money was to be used ""only"" for the Justice 
Fund's Creative Pathway's project, which included ""training and wraparound supports"" to help young people find 
employment in creative industries. 
As part of its SDF agreement, Justice Fund was to provide ongoing expenditure reports, audited financial 
statements to the ministry and scheduled visits to the ministry staff. 
But Hassan, the lawsuit alleges, tried to evade oversight and problems began six months after the grant was 
approved. 
Ministry staff reported failed attempts to schedule a site visit, the lawsuit alleges. Hassan responded a day late to 
an official letter citing breach of agreement, the lawsuit said. He promised to file the required reports and offered a 
site visit.
When the government bureaucrat met with Hassan and another man for the planned ""site"" visit, it was not held at 
the group's place of business.
The men showed her an ""incomplete"" website for the program; requested an extension of the funding agreement 
and ""disclosed that they were no longer providing on-site training to their participants,"" according to the lawsuit.
By August 2024, a forensic audit was underway and the following summer, in July 2025, the government sent 
Hassan a ""demand letter"" noting the auditors found ""inappropriate use"" of the SDF money. It sought ""immediate"" 
repayment. But two weeks later, the lawsuit said, the federally incorporated Justice Fund, filed for the dissolution 
that was later reversed.
In the lawsuit, the government lawyer said, ""The defendant's misconduct demonstrates a high-handed, wanton, 
callous and contumelious disregard for the rights and interests of Ontario, resulting in significant losses, both 
financial and reputational.""
According to legal dictionaries, contumelious means ""insolent, rude or to act with disdain.""
None of the money has been repaid, the lawsuit said.
""To date, no response to the demand letter has been forthcoming.""

Title: Provincial government responds to Deloitte report found to contain false citations likely generated by A.I.
Body: The provincial government says Deloitte is standing by its “conclusions and findings” in the Health Human 
Resources Plan report which The Independent found to contain citations that don’t exist.
In an email Saturday afternoon, Department of Health and Community Services Director of Communications Brian 
Scott said the department has “directed Deloitte to confirm the accuracy of the citations and literature review,” and 
that the global consulting firm “has since acknowledged the four citations noted are incorrect.”
As previously reported by The Independent, Deloitte used the four fabricated citations to support claims related to 
recruitment strategies, virtual care, monetary recruitment and retention incentives, and impacts of the COVID-19 
pandemic on healthcare workers.
“Deloitte has committed to expeditiously conducting a full of review of all the citations and will be required to report 
back to government with its findings,” Scott said. “We look forward to them completing their review so we can 
assess how serious an issue this is and take the appropriate steps.”
NAPE President Jerry Earle took to social media Saturday to say the Deloitte report revelations serve “as a 
cautionary note on potential consequences” of using artificial intelligence.
“NAPE has significant concerns about the planned integration of artificial intelligence in our healthcare system,” he 
said, adding the union was “contacted by a [Department of Health and Community Services] official to ensure the 
latest occurrence does not impact the overall Human Resources Plan completed by Deloitte, while also stating a 
comprehensive review is being conducted.”
Earle said that “despite assurances, if public funds are being allocated to private companies, we should expect 
higher standards. If a human employee made this error, it would likely result in disciplinary action. This is 
unacceptable and warrants immediate attention.”
This is the second time in under three months that non-existent academic articles have been found in major 
government-commissioned reports. In September, CBC/Radio-Canada reported that the province’s Education 
Accord, led by a team of researchers from Memorial University, also contained citations which appeared to have 
been generated using artificial intelligence technology.

Page 2 of 3
Provincial government responds to Deloitte report found to contain false citations likely generated by A.I.
That report cost the province more than $755,000. The Deloitte report, which was developed to help guide the 
government toward stabilizing human resources in the health sector, came at a cost of $1.6 million.
Last month Deloitte’s firm in Australia was found to have used generative AI in the production of a report for the 
Australian government. The story made international headlines and the company agreed to reimburse the 
government a portion of the fee.
Deloitte did not respond to The Independent’s questions by the time of publication.
In October Premier-designate Tony Wakeham told the Newfoundland and Labrador Teachers’ Association it was 
“embarrassing to the Liberal government that the Education Accord contains errors,” and that “when a report that 
is supposed to guide the future of education includes mistakes, it creates doubt among readers and undermines its 
credibility.”
The Independent asked the premier and the Department of Health and Community Services if the government will 
be requesting a refund from Deloitte in light of the errors, and if it will consider developing a policy around the use 
of AI in reports it commissions from third parties. They did not answer the questions.
The premier has also not yet publicly addressed the scandal.

Title: Quebec 'brownie bill' would ban vote buying in party leadership races
Body: QUEBEC - The CAQ government moved Friday to plug a hole in the electoral code that, up until now, has made 
vote buying in party leadership races legal.
The bill comes in response to allegations( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-vote-buying-allegations ) that certain Quebec Liberal Party members received ""brownies"" - or $100 bills - 
to support Pablo Rodriguez in his successful run for party leader this spring. The proposed legislation was tabled 
Friday.
The Liberals have since launched an independent investigation( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-liberals-inquiry-vote-buying-allegations ) into the 
matter and Quebec's anti-corruption unit( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-
liberals-vote-buying-allegations ) has interviewed witnesses.
""Before the events of these last weeks, I didn't think it was necessary to table a bill like this one,"" Democratic 
Institutions Minister Jean-François Roberge said Friday after tabling the bill.
Roberge said he had been surprised to learn cash-for-vote schemes were legal in leadership races under Quebec's 
electoral laws.
""It was a blind spot,"" Roberge said. ""I saw this problem, I wanted to fix it.""
The bill would apply both to party leadership races and riding nomination contests. It would make it illegal to either 
offer or accept ""a gift, loan, office, employment or other benefit"" in exchange for a vote. It would impose a maximum 
penalty of $20,000 for a first offence and $30,000 for any subsequent offence.
Trading cash for votes is already illegal during a general election.
Vote-buying allegations surfaced in late November, when the Journal de Montréal published text messages 
between two unnamed people that suggested some voters had been paid $100 each to support Rodriguez.
While the Journal didn't name the individuals, Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau said the exchange was 
between Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and Coalition Avenir Québec MNA Alice Abou-Khalil, who had been 
rumoured to have been trying to join the Liberals ahead of the 2026 election.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec 'brownie bill' would ban vote buying in party leadership races
Both MNAs deny the allegations and have threatened legal action.
On Thursday, Quebec Liberals excluded Lakhoyan Olivier from caucus( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/ethics-commission-investigation-liberal-sona-lakhoyan-olivier-
excluded-from-caucus ) pending an investigation from the legislature's ethics commissioner.
Prior to November, Roberge said he had never heard of allegations of a cash-for-votes scheme in a leadership 
race.
All three opposition parties had indicated ahead of the bill's tabling that they would support the proposed legislation.
""It's a good thing and it should be adopted,"" Liberal MNA André Albert Morin said Thursday. In November, 
Rodriguez had promised the Liberals would support such a measure.
""We were all surprised that it was legal,"" Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez said Friday ahead of the 
bill's tabling. She said that while her party would want to look over the bill first, ""on the principle, we will be in 
favour.""
Parti Québécois legislators had also said they would support the legislation. ""We're surprised that it was not already 
forbidden,"" MNA Joël Arseneau said Friday.
""We never thought that people would be so creative as to say: 'We'll pay you to vote for our leader,'"" Arseneau said. 
""That never crossed our minds.""
Roberge said the government plans to pass the bill through an accelerated procedure, ideally before the session 
ends Dec. 12. ""I had some discussion with other parties and I think we are committed as a group to do so,"" he said.

Title: Quebec 's 'brownie bill' passes, banning vote buying in leadership races
Body: QUEBEC - Legislators rushed through approval of a law Thursday to plug a hole in Quebec's electoral code that, 
until now, had made vote buying in party leadership races legal.
The vote passed unanimously using an accelerated procedure.
Nicknamed the ""brownie bill,"" the legislation responds to allegations that certain Quebec Liberal Party members 
received ""brownies"" - $100 bills - to support Pablo Rodriguez in his successful run for party leader this past spring.
Those allegations have spiralled into a deepening crisis for Rodriguez, who faces calls to resign( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-leadership ) following confirmation 
Wednesday that Quebec's anti-corruption police have begun an investigation( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-upac-investigation ) into his party.
""Unfortunately, there was a gap in the electoral law"" allowing for vote buying, Democratic Institutions Minister Jean-
François Roberge said Thursday after the vote.
""We didn't know about that gap,"" he said, ""and there were allegations about how that gap was used in the Liberal 
party.""
The bill applies both to party leadership races and riding nomination contests, and makes it illegal to either offer or 
accept ""a gift, loan, office, employment or other benefit"" in exchange for a vote.
Such an act was already illegal during a general election.
Members of all four parties in the National Assembly have said they were surprised to learn cash-for-vote schemes 
were legal under Quebec law.
Rodriguez said in November( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rizqy-doubles-down-on-chief-of-
staffs-firing-as-quebec-liberals-set-to-meet-in-montreal ) that he and campaign staff had been under the impression 
that vote buying was illegal during the leadership race. He committed at the time to amending his own party's rules 
to ban the practice if such a measure didn't pass the National Assembly.
Liberals voted for the bill ""because they had an ethics problem,"" Roberge suggested. ""The Liberals wanted to put 
this behind them, and I understand.""

He said he couldn't ""predict everything"" when it comes to other possible gaps in election rules.
""Again and again, (the Liberals) find a new way to cross lines,"" Roberge charged.
