Title: Quebec auto board lied about cost overruns for online platform, inquiry finds
Body: QUÉBEC - Quebec's automobile insurance board lied to the provincial government to conceal exploding costs in 
the creation of the agency's online platform, says a public inquiry into the cost-overrun scandal.
Overseen by Judge Denis Gallant, the inquiry's final report says officials at the auto insurance board — Société de 
l’assurance automobile du Québec — undertook a conscious effort to mislead the public about the total cost of the 
project. 
“The commission concludes, based on particularly significant evidence, that the deceptive information disseminated 
by the (auto board) was not the result of careless errors, but rather a conscious action aimed at hiding the total cost 
of the program from parliamentarians and the government — and therefore from the public,” reads an excerpt from 
Gallant's report published Monday.
In February 2025, Quebec's auditor general reported that the new platform was expected to cost taxpayers at least 
$1.1 billion by 2027 — $500 million more than originally planned. The auditor's report followed the botched rollout in 
February 2023 of the platform, which led to major delays and long lineups at insurance board branches, where 
Quebecers take road tests, register vehicles and access other services. 
In response to the auditor general, Quebec Premier François Legault launched the inquiry last year led by Gallant, 
a Montreal municipal court judge. The judge's role was not to determine guilt, but rather to draw conclusions and 
make recommendations. His report says the online platform project was ""too vast, too ambitious, and had to be 
implemented too quickly.""
Speaking to reporters Monday, Gallant said, ""People deliberately lied throughout this whole affair. We can ask 
ourselves, 'What can we recommend in a case like this?' It's difficult to recommend transparency and honesty, 
since that should be the absolute standard for those working in the public administration.""
Among those named repeatedly in the report was Karl Malenfant, the former vice-president of information 
technology at the auto board. Malenfant held a news conference last week suggesting he was being scapegoated 
for the problem-plagued platform. He said he had nothing to reproach himself for and that the project he led is not a 
fiasco.

Page 2 of 3
Quebec auto board lied about cost overruns for online platform, inquiry finds
Gallant said that despite the agency's actions, members of the government and certain public servants did, at 
various times, obtain reliable information about the problems at the auto board.
The judge noted that in June 2023, Éric Ducharme, then president and CEO of the board, met with Geneviève 
Guilbault, the transport minister at the time, to discuss the status of the contract with the consortium of three 
private firms that were building the platform. During that meeting Ducharme had also told her about the auto board's 
intention to increase the value of the contract for a second time, the report said.
However, Guilbault, who is now municipal affairs minister, has always maintained — including during testimony 
before the Gallant inquiry — that she only became aware of the cost overruns in February 2025. She stood by that 
testimony on Monday, noting in a statement that her focus in 2023 was getting services back to normal and that she 
didn't have any specific recollection of that meeting with Ducharme involving project costs.
Gallant's report adds that Dominique Savoie, the secretary-general of the government, was informed in March 2023 
that costs were increasing, as was Legault's director of communications. The report says one of Legault's political 
advisers was also told about rising costs as early as August 2023. 
""In short, several government representatives were informed in 2023 of the (auto board's) decision to increase the 
value of the contract,"" Gallant wrote, specifying that those amendments did not provide ""a complete history of the 
cost evolution.""
Legault told a Montreal news conference on Monday the results of the inquiry confirm that his government was 
never told the project had reached $1.1 billion until the auditor general's February 2025 report.
""I'm not saying the government was perfect, we could perhaps have been more suspicious, we could have asked 
more questions,"" Legault said, adding, ""the truth is important — that the (auto board) management lied to our 
government for years about the revised cost of the … project.""
Legault said he will look into potential legal recourse against auto board directors who lied, adding that the 
province's anti-corruption police unit, known as UPAC, is investigating the scandal.
Gallant's report includes 26 recommendations, including that the government create a centralized entity specialized 
in IT transformation projects. It said the government's Cybersecurity Department — which includes a unit designed 
to accelerate IT projects — lacks ""structural influence on decisions."" The new entity, he said, should have stable, 
predictable funding, and public bodies should be required to use it for any digital transformation projects. He also 
recommends tightening the governance rules for state-owned corporations and promoting transparency and access 
to reliable information. 
""Learning from failures can only be based on one categorical imperative: the honesty of all public actors,"" Gallant 
wrote. ""Every government official must make a conscious choice to be frank.""
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Feb. 16, 2026.
- with files from Sidhartha Banerjee in Montreal

Title: Quebec Liberal leader calls for external investigation into report on cash for votes
Body: MONTREAL - Pablo Rodriguez is facing his biggest crisis since becoming leader of the Quebec Liberals in June, 
after a news report on Wednesday alleged some party members were paid to vote for him in the leadership 
campaign.
Visibly shaken and combative, Rodriguez repeatedly told reporters he has nothing to hide and that he asked the 
president of the Liberals to investigate the allegations. He also said anyone found to have committed wrongdoing 
would face ""extremely serious"" consequences.
""I was a minister for many years, MP for many years — never did anyone question my integrity,"" Rodriguez said at 
party headquarters in Montreal, referring to his time in federal politics before he left to run provincially.
Rodriguez made the comments in response to a report by Quebecor alleging two people who ""actively worked"" to 
elect Rodriguez as Liberal leader had exchanged text messages suggesting some members would receive cash 
rewards in exchange for their votes.
The news outlet did not identify the names of the people who had allegedly sent the text messages and The 
Canadian Press has not verified whether the messages are authentic.
On Wednesday morning, 98.5 FM reported that Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier and CAQ MNA Alice Abou-
Khalil were the people involved in the exchange of text messages, but the two members of the legislature quickly 
denied the allegations.
""We don't even know if these texts are real or fake,"" Rodriguez said. 
Party president Rafael Primeau-Ferraro said that the party learned about ""very vague"" allegations in April with zero 
documentation. He didn't go into details.
The party executive added that the investigation would be handled by a third party.

Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberal leader calls for external investigation into report on cash for votes
The latest revelations are piling on to other bad news this week for the party and Rodriguez. On Tuesday, 
Rodriguez dismissed Marwah Rizqy from her position as parliamentary leader and suspended her from the caucus, 
citing a ""breach of trust.""
He said he took the decision after learning that Rizqy had fired her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, without 
consulting him first, adding that he had “no idea” Hinse was dismissed.
Rodriguez, who doesn't hold a seat in the legislature, had entrusted Rizqy to serve as the party's leader in the 
national assembly until the 2026 general election. She had endorsed Rodriguez in the leadership race.
It's unclear whether the allegations in the text messages published on Wednesday are related to the drama 
between Rizqy and Hinse.
Rodriguez said the timing of the allegations in the text messages was not lost on him, saying the reports are 
diverting attention from the work the party has been doing to rebuild support among voters, especially 
francophones.
He said since he was elected leader, about 250 people have come forward to run for the party in the 2026 election. 
""The money is coming in … old donors are coming back. For the polls — it's clearly a two-way race and we are not 
far from the (Parti Québécois).""
In recent months the Liberals have been slowly climbing in the polls, with a November Leger survey putting them 
five points behind the first place PQ.
The crisis within the Quebec Liberals reached Ottawa on Wednesday, where a few of Rodriguez's former 
colleagues expressed their support for him.
""Pablo was not only my colleague, he was also my friend. I think he's the right person to manage crises,"" Stéphane 
Lauzon, the Liberal MNA for Argenteuil—La Petite-Nation, told reporters.
“Obviously, Pablo is a great friend. I support him,” added Pontiac—Kitigan Zibi MP Sophie Chatel.
“He’s a longtime colleague I’ve known for a very long time. I trust Pablo,” added Steven MacKinnon, leader of the 
government in the House of Commons.
For his part, Quebec Centre MP Jean-Yves Duclos acknowledged that the matter raises several questions. “I think 
a lot of people are asking questions about the situation, and obviously, I’m one of them, but we’ll see what the 
details are.""
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2025.
—With files from Thomas Laberge and Caroline Plante in Quebec City, and Émilie Bergeron and Frédéric Lacroix-
Couture in Ottawa

Title: Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is resigning
Body: Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez has decided to resign, The Gazette confirmed Wednesday.
Only six months after winning the leadership, the pressure on Rodriguez following a series of allegations of ethical 
problems during his leadership campaign was too great.
Rodriguez is to announce his decision to the caucus later Wednesday. He is expected to meet the media Thursday.
The first sign he would leave came with news that an early-morning meeting of the party's MNAs Wednesday was 
delayed until the afternoon, which fuelled speculation.
La Presse reported( https://www.lapresse.ca/actualites/politique/2025-12-17/crise-au-plq/pablo-rodriguez-remet-en-
question-son-avenir-politique.php ) Wednesday that Rodriguez had called people close to him ""in tears"" Tuesday, 
questioning his future as Liberal leader following a series of events that have rocked the party.
His decision became almost inevitable as soon as it became clear he had lost the support of some members of the 
18-MNA Liberal caucus, which had previously been staunchly behind him.
There had been reports at least two MNAs had planned to ask Rodriguez to resign, but sources said ultimately the 
choice to leave was his alone.
""It was his decision,"" the source said.
Rodriguez, 58, a former federal Liberal MP, will have been leader of the provincial party for only six months, a first 
since it was founded in 1867.
He won the leadership in June( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-
leader ), defeating four other candidates: Charles Milliard, Karl Blackburn, Marc Bélanger and Mario Roy.
Just last Friday at a news conference wrapping up the session at the legislature, Rodriguez vowed to stay on.
""The wind is blowing strongly, but I have a thick skin,"" he said at the time. ""I know why I am here. It's because I'm a 
fighter. A captain does not leave the ship in the middle of the storm.""
One source indicated early Wednesday that Rodriguez's hold on the caucus was no longer a given, following the 
latest allegations about fundraising in the leadership campaign.
Page 2 of 4
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is resigning
""He should do what is best for all of Quebec, the Liberals and for him,"" the source said.
Last week, as he entered an emergency caucus meeting, Nelligan MNA Monsef Derraji, who was neutral in the 
leadership race,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/a-dozen-former-liberal-mnas-and-ministers-call-on-
pablo-rodriguez-to-resign ) refused to say whether he supported Rodriguez.
The latest allegations of ethical shortcomings affecting the party were published in Le Journal de Montréal on 
Tuesday. A series of such reports have now rocked the Liberals for a month.
Tuesday's report said a businessman had reimbursed participants $500 each at a fundraising event that Rodriguez 
attended, in exchange for contributing to Rodriguez's campaign.
Organizers who worked for Rodriguez's leadership campaign said later Tuesday that they had confronted the 
businessman, who allegedly admitted to reimbursing donors.
Both the organizers and a spokesperson for Rodriguez say Rodriguez did not have any knowledge of the alleged 
payments( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-
campaign-allegations ). The organizers have asked Quebec's anti-corruption unit, known as UPAC, to investigate 
the allegations.
Le Journal, La Presse and Radio-Canada have all reported that wine and port importer and producer Emanuel 
Cabral, president of Global International Networks Wines &; Spirits, is the businessman in question. His lawyer, 
Mario Proulx, would not confirm or deny Cabral was involved in the alleged transactions.
Le Journal reported Wednesday( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/12/17/enveloppes-de-500-pour-la-
chefferie-de-pablo-rodriguez--genevieve-hinse-a-signe-comme-responsable-de-levenement ) that Geneviève Hinse, 
the fired chief of staff of ex-Liberal house leader Marwah Rizqy, had been tasked with overseeing financing at the 
fundraiser in question. According to the publication, Hinse's signature could be found on the Élections Québec 
finance report for the event.
There is ""no evidence"" Hinse was aware of the alleged reimbursements, Le Journal reported.
Jacques Martineau, who was spokesperson for Rodriguez's campaign, told Le Journal that Hinse's role in the event 
was ""administrative"" and said she hadn't necessarily organized the event. The Gazette has reached out to Hinse's 
lawyer for comment.
Crisis began one month ago
The Liberals entered crisis mode on Nov. 17, when then-Liberal parliamentary leader Rizqy fired Hinse( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ), her chief 
of staff. Hinse is a longtime associate of Rodriguez, who followed the former federal MP into Quebec politics. 
Rodriguez responded by firing Rizqy from her role as parliamentary leader and suspending her from caucus.
Why Rizqy fired Hinse remains unclear - a point Rodriguez made several times throughout the snowballing crisis.
While Rizqy hasn't spoken about Hinse's removal, she said via a legal letter that Hinse had committed ""significant 
ethical breaches."" La Presse reported that Hinse was fired over the alleged use of parliamentary funds for political 
activities, which is not allowed.
Hinse, for her part, is suing Rizqy for $500,000 and accusing her former boss of firing her without a valid reason.
In early December( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rodriguez-expells-rizqy-from-quebec-
liberal-caucus-as-crisis-grows ), Rodriguez expelled Rizqy from caucus, citing her refusal to meet with him.
Piling onto the conflict with Rizqy is a series of ethics allegations surrounding Rodriguez's campaign for Liberal 
leadership.
Page 3 of 4
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez is resigning
Among the most explosive was a Journal de Montréal report landing just two days after Hinse's removal, alleging 
that certain Quebec Liberal Party members had been paid $100 each to vote for Rodriguez in the leadership race. 
The report was based on screengrabs of an alleged text exchange between two unnamed people who referred to 
payments of ""brownies,"" a slang term for brown-coloured $100 bills, that would be exchanged for votes.
Such payments were not illegal at the time of the leadership race, though Rodriguez said his campaign was 
operating under the assumption that such payments weren't permitted. He maintains he had no knowledge of the 
allegations ahead of the Journal report. The Liberals have since ordered an inquiry into the allegations.
Last week, a bill was passed to plug a hole in Quebec's electoral code, discovered as a result of the crisis, banning 
cash-for-vote exchanges during leadership races( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-
brownie-bill-passes-banning-vote-buying-in-leadership-races ).
Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau said the alleged text exchange about the ""brownies"" was between 
Coalition Avenir Québec MNA Alice Abou-Khalil and then-Liberal MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, prompting denials 
and threats of lawsuits from both politicians. Abou-Khalil was rumoured to have been planning a jump to the 
Liberals, but remains in the CAQ caucus.
While the CAQ said it took Abou-Khalil at her word, the Liberals said they would wait for the results of their 
independent investigation.
Then, in December, Rodriguez suspended Lakhoyan Olivier from caucus pending the results of a separate 
investigation by the legislature's ethics commissioner, in line with parliamentary rules.
The unfolding crisis has also caught the interest of Quebec's anti-corruption unit, which is investigating the 
fundraising allegations.

Title: Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Body: A conversation at the inauguration( https://montrealgazette.com/news/rem-inauguration-day-montreal-deux-
montagnes-branch ) of the Réseau express métropolitain's Deux-Montagnes branch this month may have been the 
unexpected start of the recent crisis within the Quebec Liberal Party, La Presse reported( 
https://www.lapresse.ca/actualites/politique/2025-11-26/crise-au-plq/la-discussion-qui-aurait-tout-bouscule.php ) 
Wednesday.
Drama has been brewing within the official opposition party since early last week, when Marwah Rizqy, 
parliamentary leader and MNA for St-Laurent, fired chief of staff Geneviève Hinse( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ).
In the time since, Rizqy was ousted from her role as parliamentary leader by party leader Pablo Rodriguez; Hinse 
fired back at Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rizqy-hinse-lawyer-letter ) 
with a legal letter, then sued her; and it was revealed that the firing may have been related to the alleged misuse of 
National Assembly funds for partisan activities.
The turmoil in the party comes ahead of the 2026 provincial election, when Rodriguez plans to run for a seat in the 
National Assembly.
Here's a timeline of events thus far:
June 14: Quebec Liberals elect Rodriguez( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-
rodriguez-as-new-leader ), former federal Liberal MP from Montreal,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-
liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-leader ) as the new leader of the party. He won with 52.3 per cent of the 
vote, narrowly overtaking contender Charles Milliard, who received 47.7 per cent of the vote.
June 19: Rodriguez selects Rizqy( https://montrealgazette.com/news/pablo-rodriguez-picks-marwah-rizqy-to-lead-
liberals-in-legislature ) - known for her ability to hold the Coalition Avenir Québec government's feet to the fire - to 
lead the party in the National Assembly since he's not an MNA.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury, highlighted left, and Liberal MNA Marwah Rizqy among a group of politicians posing 
for photos during an inauguration event for the the Deux-Montagnes branch of the REM in Deux-Montagnes on 
Nov. 14, 2025.
Page 2 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Nov. 14: Federal, provincial and local politicians attend a ceremony for the opening of the REM's long-awaited 
Deux-Montagnes branch. A discussion between Rizqy and Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury may have sparked the 
drama that unfolded days later, according to La Presse. El-Khoury denied having a discussion with Rizqy about 
Rodriguez's leadership race and insisted he had no connection to the campaign, but La Presse later discovered he 
had raised funds for Rodriguez.
Nov. 17: Rizqy fires her chief of staff in a short email to members of the Liberal caucus, taking the party by surprise.
""We would like to inform you that Mme. Geneviève Hinse ... is no longer employed as chief of staff of the leader of 
the official opposition as of now,"" the email read.
La Presse reported the dismissal was related to the alleged use of the party's National Assembly budget to pay for 
partisan activities like Rodriguez's recent tour of the regions, which isn't permitted.
Nov. 18: Rodriguez ousts Rizqy as parliamentary leader over the firing of Hinse, claiming he wasn't consulted or 
given an explanation. Hinse was Rodriguez's chief of staff when he was a federal politician and decided to follow 
him into Quebec politics.
Rodriguez's decision to oust Rizqy, ""while difficult, was necessary to ensure the cohesion and the good functioning 
of the Liberal caucus at the National Assembly,"" the party said in a statement.
Rizqy was replaced as parliamentary leader by Pontiac MNA André Fortin. She remains a Liberal but is suspended 
from the caucus until further notice.
Geneviève Hinse in 2019.
Nov. 19: Hinse fires back with a legal letter giving Rizqy 24 hours to admit the ""absence of justified motive"" for the 
firing, warning that she may sue her if she refuses.
In the letter, Rizqy is accused of violating the customs of the party by firing Hinse because such decisions are 
supposed to be made by the party leader.
Before the letter came out, Hinse defended herself in a statement: ""I am obviously hurt by this situation, especially 
since I know nothing justifies my firing.""
The same day, the Journal de Montréal reported( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/11/19/il-faut-encore-
payer-pour-que-le-monde-vote-pablo-des-textos-troublants-derriere-la-crise-au-plq ) Élections Québec was looking 
into text messages insinuating Liberal Party members were paid to vote Rodriguez in as leader.
One exchange reads:
""So, everyone's going to get paid (this) week?""
""Yes. And don't forget, we're only returning the membership cards on May 8 in case something goes wrong. All 
that's left is the voting process and they get a brownie for voting.""
A $100 bill is sometimes referred to as a ""brownie"" in slang.
Cogeco political analyst Jonathan Trudeau claimed the exchanges were between Alice Abou-Khalil, CAQ MNA for 
Fabre, and Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, Liberal MNA for Chomedey, both of whom denied the accusations.
Rodriguez called in an external auditor to investigate the Journal report, saying he had no knowledge of the 
allegations.
""We have nothing to hide,"" he said at the time. ""I have nothing to hide. Nobody has anything to hide.""
Page 3 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
According to the Directeur général des élections du Québec, there are no rules against someone being 
compensated for voting for a candidate in a leadership race (though, it's not allowed in general elections or 
byelections).
Premier François Legault and Rodriguez have both since said they'd be in favour of having the law changed if it's 
considered legal to buy votes.
Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez speaks to media while surrounded by the Liberal caucus in Montreal on 
Friday, Nov. 21, 2025. The caucus was held in the aftermath of vote-buying allegations and other turmoil in the 
party that continued throughout the week.
Nov. 21: Rodriguez says the party might take the Journal de Montréal to court unless it shares more information 
about the alleged vote-buying scheme, requesting the names and phone numbers from the text exchange.
""You cannot just put things like that in a paper and accuse people,"" he said.
Also on this day, Cogeco journalist Louis Lacroix read a letter on air from Rizqy's lawyers to those of Hinse, 
defending the firing. The lawyers declined to share a copy of the letter with The Gazette but confirmed one had 
been sent. According to Lacroix, the letter said the decision was made after reviews of many ""concerning situations"" 
related to the performance of Hinse's duties, conduct and obligations as chief of staff.
""Your client's dismissal was imposed due to significant ethical breaches, particularly with regard to compliance with 
the standards of the National Assembly of Quebec, the internal procedures and expectations related to her 
position,"" the letter said. ""In addition, there were repeated acts of insubordination, including non-compliance with 
clear instructions issued by our client. Notably, your client refused to follow our client's directive to consult with the 
ethics commissioner.""
Lacroix said the letter noted Rizqy couldn't say Hinse had been fired without motive ""because that would be a false 
and erroneous declaration.""
Later that day, Hinse claimed $500,000 in moral and punitive damages against Rizqy. She claims it was Rizqy who 
acted in bad faith and ""completely resisted"" attempts to go to the National Assembly's ethics commissioner to clear 
up operational issues, including what spending should be covered by public funds and what should be considered 
partisan activities paid for by the party.
The claim says Rizqy resisted because she didn't have confidence in the ethics commissioner to ""open such a 
dialogue,"" based on her personal experience with the commissioner and that of her husband, Jacques-Cartier MNA 
Greg Kelley.
""A conflict of personalities developed between the two, fed by Mme. Rizqy's mood swings,"" the claim states.
When Hinse presented a document outlining an operational plan for such spending, Rizqy refused to touch it. It was 
shortly after that incident that she received the letter from Rizqy informing her she was fired.
The claim also notes that if Rizqy apologizes in writing and admits the ""existence of a grave error"" on her part in 
firing Hinse, she would drop the case.
Nov. 23: Rizqy breaks her silence, insisting that she acted within her right and pointing out that she's not allowed to 
discuss human resources matters publicly.
That night, Rodriguez appears on Radio-Canada talk show Tout le monde en parle, saying Rizqy had spoken to 
him about some kind of political ""fling flang"" (or funny business) linked to Ottawa.
Liberal MP Fayçal El-Khoury speaks to reporters before a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill in 
Ottawa in this October 2024 file photo.
Page 4 of 5
Quebec Liberal Party crisis: A timeline of events so far
Nov. 26: In the wake of the La Presse report tying the tension within the party back to the REM inauguration, 
Rodriguez acknowledges that El-Khoury raised funds for his leadership race. He noted El-Khoury's activities were 
legal because he had a campaign certificate permitting him to raise funds.
""He raised money like lots of people,"" Rodriguez said.
El-Khoury did not respond to The Gazette's request for comment Wednesday and refused to answer questions from 
reporters outside the federal Liberal caucus in Ottawa, but told La Presse his comments may have been 
""ambiguous"" last week. He said he assumed he was being asked if he helped acquire membership cards for 
Rodriguez, which he said he didn't. That's why he said he was never involved in the campaign.
He added that his exchange with Rizqy at the REM inauguration was about her decision not to seek re-election next 
year and the fact that she had been an inspiration to his daughter, who is thinking of entering politics.
Later in the day, Quebec's Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirms it is verifying ""allegations of 
reprehensible acts targeting the Liberal Party of Quebec"" but has not yet launched a formal investigation. 
""Following the analysis of this information, we will be able to take a decision to know if we need to go further with 
the investigation or not.""
Rodriguez says he will fully co-operate with UPAC. ""If someone, somewhere, committed an illegal act or contrary to 
our ethics, the truth must come out and we will fully co-operate. If shortcomings are revealed, I will act. There is no 
place for this in the Liberal Party of Quebec. Tolerance zero. Period,"" he writes in a social media post.

Title: Quebec Liberal Party crisis: Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game'
Body: QUEBEC - The day after the province's anticorruption unit confirmed it was meeting witnesses in connection with 
allegations against the Quebec Liberal Party, leader Pablo Rodriguez said his opponents were playing a ""political 
game.""
Speaking to reporters Thursday morning, Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez was playing show and 
tell, holding up a copy of PLQ Inc., a 2019 book that investigated allegations into corruption in the Quebec Liberal 
Party under former premier Jean Charest.
""When we see UPAC and the Liberal Party of Quebec in the same newspaper headline, it reminds us of just one 
thing,"" she said. ""Every day, we wake up and we learn of a new scandal in the Liberal Party of Quebec.""
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Liberal party of a ""culture of corruption,"" which he 
said stemmed from a loyalty to the ""Canadian regime.""
Rodriguez rejected St-Pierre Plamondon's assertion, defining his party as the oldest in Quebec, ""the party of the 
economy"" and ""the party of a just society.""
Québec solidaire's reference to alleged corruption under Charest ""is just their political game,"" Rodriguez said, 
""because they don't have anything else to say.""
First reported in the Journal de Montréal, the Unité permanente anticorruption (UPAC) confirmed Wednesday that it 
was looking into fundraising allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party, but stressed that it hadn't started a 
formal investigation.
The Journal reported Thursday that UPAC had met with Marwah Rizqy, who Pablo Rodriguez removed from her 
post as parliamentary leader after she fired Geneviève Hinse, her chief of staff. Rodriguez maintained Thursday 
that he still didn't know why Rizqy had removed Hinse.
If UPAC proceeds with an investigation, ""we're going to collaborate,"" he promised. ""We have nothing to hide.""
A Pallas Data poll published by L'actualité on Wednesday showed only 13 per cent of Quebecers have a favourable 
impression of Rodriguez - placing him behind Plamondon, Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal and Quebec 
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime - and tying him with Premier François Legault.

Rodriguez is the only leader less popular than his party, the poll said, reporting that 25 per cent of Quebecers 
intend to vote for the Liberals.

Title: Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
Body: QUEBEC - The province's anti-corruption unit (UPAC) has opened a formal criminal investigation into fundraising 
allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party.
But Quebec's Liberal caucus says it stands behind party leader Pablo Rodriguez, despite calls from at least one 
party member that he step aside for the duration of the investigation or even permanently. Rodriguez said he's 
staying on and has nothing to hide.
""We confirm that our verifications are finished and that we are officially opening an investigation,"" UPAC 
spokesperson Mathieu Galarneau said in a statement.
""We will issue no further comment in order to protect as much as possible our actions and to respect the rights of 
the persons involved.""
On Nov. 26, the police force said( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-liberals-vote-
buying-allegations ) that it was looking into allegations of what it called certain ""reprehensible acts"" targeting the 
Liberal party.
UPAC did not provide details on what is motivating the investigation, but there have been allegations on the 
possible use of National Assembly funds for partisan reasons in the Pablo Rodriguez leadership race.
Rodriguez, who is now leader of the Liberals( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-resignation-petition ), rapidly issued a statement on social media.
""It's important to get to the bottom of things,"" Rodriguez said. ""The Liberal Party of Quebec and all of its members 
will fully co-operate (with UPAC). If someone has committed an illegal act, the truth will come out and, as leader, I 
will act without hesitation.""
Later, meeting reporters at the legislature, Rodriguez emphasized that UPAC was not specific on what it is 
investigating.
""For us it's important to get the truth and all the truth,"" Rodriguez told the media. ""If people did anything wrong, then 
they'll pay the price, they'll suffer the consequences.""
Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
He said he saw no reason to step aside pending the results of the investigation.
""It's not about me,"" Rodriguez said. ""I'm there, I'm duly voted on by the members. There's nothing that I have done 
wrong. I can assure them (at UPAC) and all Quebecers that we'll get to the bottom of this.""
UPAC revealed it was having conversations with individuals the day La Presse reported news of a discussion that 
had taken place between then Liberal parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy and federal MP Fayçal El-Khoury on 
Nov. 14 at the launch of the Deux-Montagnes REM extension.
El-Khoury had initially insisted he had no involvement in the Rodriguez campaign, but it was revealed later he had, 
in fact, raised money for it. The exchange caught the eye of Quebec's chief electoral office, various media have 
reported.
La Presse has since revealed that UPAC, the Unité permanente anticorruption, met with Rizqy after Rodriguez 
excluded her from the Liberal caucus in connection with her decision to fire her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, a 
close associate of Rodriguez.
Last week, Rodriguez permanently expelled Rizqy from the Liberal caucus( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rodriguez-expells-rizqy-from-quebec-liberal-caucus-as-crisis-
grows ). He said she has refused to explain the firing beyond her initial statement to him about some kind of ""fling 
flang"" (fishy business) in the party's use of public money for partisan reasons.
The story took on a further air of mystery when the Journal de Montréal last month published text messages( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rizqy-doubles-down-on-chief-of-staffs-firing-as-quebec-
liberals-set-to-meet-in-montreal ) between two unnamed people suggesting Liberal members had been paid $100 
(referred to as a ""brownie"" in the messages) for voting in favour of Rodriguez in the leadership race last spring.
The practice is not illegal under Quebec's electoral laws, but legislation tabled last week( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-brownie-bill-vote-buying-ban-leadership-races ) 
designed to plug that loophole is expected to be voted into law on Thursday, with support from all parties.
News of the UPAC investigation, however, sent another shock wave through the Liberal ranks. Most Liberal MNAs 
entered an emergency party caucus meeting at the legislature Wednesday without talking to reporters. One did.
""We had a leadership race, we will respect this leadership race,"" said Mille-Îles Liberal MNA Virginie Dufour. ""Our 
leader is Pablo Rodriguez. I repeat, we want to get to the bottom of things. If people did illegal things, we want to 
know why.""
Later, one person who is unhappy with Rodriguez emerged from the shadows to call for his head or for him to at 
least step aside for the duration of the UPAC investigation.
""I ask the party to immediately suspend Mr. Rodriguez for the duration of the investigation,"" Alexandre Tremblay-
Michaud, a lawyer and the former president of the Outremont Liberal riding association, told The Gazette.
""If Mr. Rodriguez has the interests of the party at heart, he should resign.
Until now, Tremblay-Michaud had been discreet, but he has been linked to a group of Liberals who wanted to 
organize a party general council in January where Rodriguez would face a confidence vote.
On their way out of the caucus, however, Liberals closed ranks around the leader, but some still appeared shaken 
by the news.
""We had a good caucus, good conversations,"" Liberal whip Marc Tanguay told reporters. ""What is happening is 
serious. We are unanimous behind our leader Pablo Rodriguez. We will get through this. We have a job to do.""
""We're behind our leader, we're behind our leader,"" said Mont-Royal-Outremont MNA Michelle Setlakwe.
Page 3 of 3
Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
""I have full confidence in Mr. Rodriguez,"" said Pontiac MNA André Fortin. ""I have full confidence in his integrity.""
""Are we worried? Yes,"" said Nelligan MNA Monsef Derraji. ""We are all very worried. But today, as legislators, we 
are not going to start putting anyone on trial. We must wait for the results (of the investigations) before drawing 
conclusions.
""Personally, I am fed up with what I am seeing. I am very worried.""

party member that he step aside for the duration of the investigation or even permanently. Rodriguez said he's 
staying on and has nothing to hide.
Late Wednesday, however, one of the candidates Rodriguez defeated in last spring's leadership race, Karl 
Blackburn, invited Rodriguez to think about his political future and the damage the current chaos is causing the 
Liberal brand this close to the 2026 general election.
""It's clear the situation the party finds itself in is extremely worrying,"" Blackburn said in an interview with Radio-
Canada. ""I think in this context Mr. Rodriguez must certainly ask himself the right questions.""
Blackburn, the former president of the Conseil du patronat( https://montrealgazette.com/news/karl-blackburn-kicks-
off-bid-for-quebec-liberal-leadership-denounces-caqs-identity-politics ) who placed third in the leadership race, 
noted that questions being raised in the media ""seem to concern the leadership race and the leadership race of Mr. 
Rodriguez, and that does not bode well.""
He insisted he is not the one who is going to start a movement to get rid of Rodriguez but also said he thinks the 
party was in a better electoral position last June after the leadership race( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-leader ) than it is now.
""That's far from being good news,"" Blackburn said. ""But, unfortunately, all of this negative perception surrounding 
the leadership of Mr. Rodriguez hurts the Liberal Party of Quebec. I make a distinction between the Liberal Party of 
Quebec and the leadership race.""
Blackburn's explosive comments came at the end of a chaotic day at the legislature for the Liberals following news 
of the UPAC investigation.
""We confirm that our verifications are finished and that we are officially opening an investigation,"" UPAC 
spokesperson Mathieu Galarneau said in a statement.
Page 2 of 4

""We will issue no further comment in order to protect as much as possible our actions and to respect the rights of 
the persons involved.""
On Nov. 26, the police force said( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-liberals-vote-
buying-allegations ) that it was looking into allegations of what it called certain ""reprehensible acts"" targeting the 
Liberal party.
UPAC did not provide details on what is motivating the investigation, but there have been allegations on the 
possible use of National Assembly funds for partisan reasons in the Pablo Rodriguez leadership race.
Rodriguez, who is now leader of the Liberals( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-
rodriguez-resignation-petition ), rapidly issued a statement on social media.
""It's important to get to the bottom of things,"" Rodriguez said. ""The Liberal Party of Quebec and all of its members 
will fully co-operate (with UPAC). If someone has committed an illegal act, the truth will come out and, as leader, I 
will act without hesitation.""
Later, meeting reporters at the legislature, Rodriguez emphasized that UPAC was not specific on what it is 
investigating.
""For us it's important to get the truth and all the truth,"" Rodriguez told the media. ""If people did anything wrong, then 
they'll pay the price, they'll suffer the consequences.""
He said he saw no reason to step aside pending the results of the investigation.
""It's not about me,"" Rodriguez said. ""I'm there, I'm duly voted on by the members. There's nothing that I have done 
wrong. I can assure them (at UPAC) and all Quebecers that we'll get to the bottom of this.""
UPAC revealed it was having conversations with individuals the day La Presse reported news of a discussion that 
had taken place between then Liberal parliamentary leader Marwah Rizqy and federal MP Fayçal El-Khoury on 
Nov. 14 at the launch of the Deux-Montagnes REM extension.
El-Khoury had initially insisted he had no involvement in the Rodriguez campaign, but it was revealed later he had, 
in fact, raised money for it. The exchange caught the eye of Quebec's chief electoral office, various media have 
reported.
La Presse has since revealed that UPAC, the Unité permanente anticorruption, met with Rizqy after Rodriguez 
excluded her from the Liberal caucus in connection with her decision to fire her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, a 
close associate of Rodriguez.
Last week, Rodriguez permanently expelled Rizqy from the Liberal caucus( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rodriguez-expells-rizqy-from-quebec-liberal-caucus-as-crisis-
grows ). He said she has refused to explain the firing beyond her initial statement to him about some kind of ""fling 
flang"" (fishy business) in the party's use of public money for partisan reasons.
The story took on a further air of mystery when the Journal de Montréal last month published text messages( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/rizqy-doubles-down-on-chief-of-staffs-firing-as-quebec-
liberals-set-to-meet-in-montreal ) between two unnamed people suggesting Liberal members had been paid $100 
(referred to as a ""brownie"" in the messages) for voting in favour of Rodriguez in the leadership race last spring.
The practice is not illegal under Quebec's electoral laws, but legislation tabled last week( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-brownie-bill-vote-buying-ban-leadership-races ) 
designed to plug that loophole is expected to be voted into law on Thursday, with support from all parties.
Page 3 of 4
Quebec Liberals close ranks as UPAC opens criminal probe into vote-buying allegations
News of the UPAC investigation, however, sent another shock wave through the Liberal ranks. Most Liberal MNAs 
entered an emergency party caucus meeting at the legislature Wednesday without talking to reporters. One did.
""We had a leadership race, we will respect this leadership race,"" said Mille-Îles Liberal MNA Virginie Dufour. ""Our 
leader is Pablo Rodriguez. I repeat, we want to get to the bottom of things. If people did illegal things, we want to 
know why.""
Later, one person who is unhappy with Rodriguez emerged from the shadows to call for his head or for him to at 
least step aside for the duration of the UPAC investigation.
""I ask the party to immediately suspend Mr. Rodriguez for the duration of the investigation,"" Alexandre Tremblay-
Michaud, a lawyer and the former president of the Outremont Liberal riding association, told The Gazette.
""If Mr. Rodriguez has the interests of the party at heart, he should resign. I think it is a minority of Liberal members 
who still have confidence in Pablo Rodriguez.""
Until now, Tremblay-Michaud had been discreet, but he has been linked to a group of Liberals who wanted to 
organize a party general council in January where Rodriguez would face a confidence vote.
His comments were followed by reports that a letter calling for Rodriguez to resign has started to circulate among 
Liberals asking for the resignation of Rodriguez. It is only identified as a letter from former Liberal MNAs. No names 
are included.
""Can the current leader steer the Liberal through such a critical period?"" the letter seen by The Gazette says. ""Does 
he have the necessary leadership to lead us to a victorious campaign? Unfortunately the events of the last few 
months tell us no.
""We measure the quality of a leader based on the way he handles adversity and gets out of problem situations. He 
has pushed the party into a slump which harms the recruitment of candidates. We think it would be in the interests 
of the Liberal Party that Pablo Rodriguez resign without delay. We are not in a position to manage an election under 
such conditions.""
In the interview, Blackburn denied he had anything to do with the letter.
On their way out of the caucus, however, Liberals closed ranks around the leader, but some still appeared shaken 
by the news.
""We had a good caucus, good conversations,"" Liberal whip Marc Tanguay told reporters. ""What is happening is 
serious. We are unanimous behind our leader Pablo Rodriguez. We will get through this. We have a job to do.""
""We're behind our leader, we're behind our leader,"" said Mont-Royal-Outremont MNA Michelle Setlakwe.
""I have full confidence in Mr. Rodriguez,"" said Pontiac MNA André Fortin. ""I have full confidence in his integrity.""
""Are we worried? Yes,"" said Nelligan MNA Monsef Derraji. ""We are all very worried. But today, as legislators, we 
are not going to start putting anyone on trial. We must wait for the results (of the investigations) before drawing 
conclusions.
""Personally, I am fed up with what I am seeing. I am very worried.""

Title: Quebec Liberals lose two caucus members in a week as crisis continues
Body: QUÉBEC - The Quebec Liberals have lost two members of their caucus within a week and are facing multiple 
investigations as a crisis within the party shows no sign of abating.
The Liberals have been dogged by controversy for nearly three weeks, with one recent poll showing the party and 
its leader, former federal cabinet minister Pablo Rodriguez, have taken a substantial hit in public opinion. 
""Everything that's coming out now, it's preventing us from doing our best work,"" Monsef Derraji, a Liberal member of 
the legislature, told reporters in Quebec City on Friday. ""I'm tired of hearing all these stories every day.""
His comments came after Rodriguez announced Thursday evening that he had expelled a Montreal-area member 
of the legislature, Sona Lakhoyan Olivier, from his caucus because she is under investigation by Quebec's ethics 
commissioner. 
The office of the ethics commissioner announced it will investigate whether Lakhoyan Olivier used resources from 
her constituency office for partisan purposes during this year's Liberal leadership race, which Rodriguez won in 
June. 
""Under the circumstances, I have decided to exclude her from the Quebec Liberal Party caucus for the duration of 
this investigation,"" Rodriguez said on X. 
Lakhoyan Olivier wrote on social media Thursday that she has always followed the rules and will co-operate fully 
with the investigation.
At a press conference on Friday, Marc Tanguay, the party's chief whip, said it's customary for members of the 
legislature to be removed from their caucus while they're subject to ethics investigations. 
Another Liberal, Désirée McGraw, told reporters the Liberal caucus remains ""100 per cent"" behind Rodriguez. 
Still, that caucus now numbers just 18 people after Rodriguez expelled his former parliamentary leader, Marwah 
Rizqy, earlier this week, saying she lacked loyalty to him and to the party. 
Rizqy kicked off the crisis in the Liberal ranks when she fired her chief of staff last month. Rodriguez says she did 
not consult with him about the decision and has not explained her reasons. 

Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals lose two caucus members in a week as crisis continues
The Liberals are also facing allegations of possible vote-buying during the leadership race. Last month, Le Journal 
de Montréal published text messages suggesting some party members who voted for Rodriguez could have 
received cash rewards.
Montreal radio station 98.5 FM named Lakhoyan Olivier as one of the two people behind those text messages, but 
she has denied that claim and has sent a legal letter to station owner Cogeco.
The Canadian Press has not verified whether the text messages were authentic. It's also unclear whether the firing 
of Rizqy's chief of staff and the vote-buying allegations are connected. 
Rodriguez has asked a retired judge to investigate the allegations, and says anyone involved in such activity will be 
kicked out of the party. Quebec's anticorruption police have also said they are looking into the controversy. 
The crisis for the Liberals comes as the party tries to regain the support of Quebec voters, particularly 
francophones outside Montreal, ahead of next year's election. With the governing Coalition Avenir Québec polling 
badly, the Liberals are positioning themselves as the alternative to the Parti Québécois, which is promising a 
referendum on independence by 2030. 
But a recent Léger/Québecor poll showed the Liberals losing ground as the controversy drags on. The survey put 
the Liberals at 21 per cent, compared to 39 per cent for the PQ.
On Friday, the Quebec government tabled new legislation to ban vote-buying in leadership and nomination races. 
To the surprise of many lawmakers, Elections Quebec recently revealed that the province’s Elections Act does not 
prohibit people from making donations in exchange for votes in those campaigns. 
The bill, which has the support of the opposition parties, includes fines of up to $10,000 for a first offence and up to 
$30,000 for repeat offences within 10 years. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Dec. 5, 2025.
-- By Maura Forrest in Montreal with files from Thomas Laberge in Quebec City

Title: Quebec Liberals set stage for 'rigorous and impartial' inquiry into vote-buying allegations
Body: QUEBEC - The Quebec Liberal Party has outlined the scope and set a deadline for its independent inquiry into 
allegations of vote buying in its most recent leadership race.
In a statement, the party said its executive entrenched the mandate for the inquiry at a meeting Friday. It is to be 
headed by retired Superior Court Judge Jacques R. Fournier. The party has set a Jan. 31, 2026 deadline for the 
inquiry to be completed and the report filed.
The Liberals have promised to make the report public.
""The integrity of our party is not negotiable,"" Liberal Party president Rafael Ferraro said in a statement Friday to the 
media. ""With the official entrenchment of the mandate by the executive, the independent inquiry can proceed 
without delay. We want all the light to be shed on this in a rigorous and impartial way.""
Fournier's mandate includes determining if payment to try to influence votes occurred, to identify the persons 
allegedly involved, the monetary amounts and the number of votes.
Fournier is asked to reveal any potential violations of the electoral law, the Quebec Liberal Party's code of ethics 
and the rules of the leadership in place at the time, and to establish whether any of the leadership campaign teams 
were aware or participated in such actions.

liberals-rodriguez-vote-buying-allegations ) following an article in the Journal de Montréal detailing a series of text 
messages between two unidentified parties who seems to be discussing vote buying in last spring's leadership race 
to replace Dominique Anglade.
The race was won by former Liberal MP Pablo Rodriguez,( https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec-liberals-
choose-pablo-rodriguez-as-new-leader ) who heads the party today.

Title: Quebec Liberals: Rodriguez denies knowing campaign donors allegedly reimbursed with cash
Body: Campaign organizers for Quebec Liberal Party Leader Pablo Rodriguez say they are filing a complaint with the 
province's anti-corruption squad over a fundraising event where a businessman allegedly reimbursed guests for 
making campaign contributions.
The campaign said in a statement Tuesday that Rodriguez had no idea the businessman had done that, and 
confronted the latter after the Journal de Montréal( https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2025/12/16/campagne-de-
pablo-rodriguez--des-enveloppes-de-500-comptant-pour-rembourser-une-vingtaine-de-donateurs ) reported on the 
event which took place last April.
""When confronted, this person admitted they had, on their own initiative, reimbursed some of their own employees 
who did not have the means to participate in the event,"" campaign organizers said.
While Rodriguez did attend the event, the organizers said neither he nor his campaign had any idea that guests or 
donors had been reimbursed.
""This is unacceptable, unethical, contrary to the rules in place at the time, and was never part of the campaign's 
practices,"" the statement said. ""It was carried out without authorization, without instructions and completely without 
the knowledge of Pablo Rodriguez and his team.""
The move comes after the Journal reported that guests at the event had received envelopes with $500 cash in 
exchange for donating the same amount to Rodriguez's campaign. A spokesperson for Rodriguez told The Gazette 
he was ""absolutely not"" aware of any alleged transactions.
According to the Journal, the ""businessman"" who hosted the event decided that some guests would receive $500 - 
the maximum contribution amount allowed to a candidate during a leadership run - as repayment for having 
donated to the campaign. The Journal reported interviewing the businessman, promising not to disclose his name, 
as well as other sources who were ""well aware"" of the alleged payments.
While the Journal said that the businessman maintained that between two and four people received such payments, 
it reports having spoken to other sources who said that around 20 people received envelopes of cash.
The report is only the latest in a series of allegations that have plagued Rodriguez's leadership campaign for weeks.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec Liberals: Rodriguez denies knowing campaign donors allegedly reimbursed with cash
In November, the Journal reported allegations that certain Liberal Party members were given ""brownies"" - a slang 
term for $100 bills - in exchange for voting for Rodriguez to become Quebec Liberal leader. Quebec's anti-
corruption police are now investigating the provincial Liberals and the party itself has launched an independent 
inquiry into the allegations.
Meanwhile, two letters - one calling on Rodriguez to resign and the other supporting him as leader - have been 
circulating among Liberal ranks. The party's youth wing has confirmed it won't sign the letter in support of 
Rodriguez.
""This is not a position against or in favour of him,"" said Noah Faour-Charpentier, the youth wing's vice-president of 
communications. ""Given the facts that are held up against Rodriguez... we see it fit to maintain a neutral position.""
""We're trying to protect the institution"" of the Quebec Liberal Party, Faour-Charpentier said.
Rodriguez is unlikely to survive the ongoing crisis facing his leadership, said Dónal Gill, assistant professor of 
political science at Concordia University. ""We could be looking at a resignation (in) early January, probably,"" he 
said.
It isn't clear ""what can be done to salvage what's left of any kind of momentum (the Liberals) had without Rodriguez 
going,"" he said.
Gill said the Liberals have long been associated with corruption and conflict-of-interest allegations ""in the minds 
of many middle-ground and swing voters in Quebec,"" dating as far back as the premiership of Robert Bourassa.
Liberals need a clean break from the allegations now swirling around Rodriguez, Gill said, and ""the only way to 
make that break is to say goodbye to the leader.""
Leaders throughout history and of all stripes tend to cling on longer than benefits their party, he added. In such 
situations, ""everybody knows it's over"" but the leader themselves.
For the Liberals, ""the laws of political gravity are dragging this party downward and it is Pablo Rodriguez that is the 
chief anchor,"" Gill said.
Rodriguez ""won the leadership race largely on the basis of his status as a kind of a big fish in the federal game,"" he 
said.
During the campaign, and since, Rodriguez hadn't ""exactly been putting forth new and dynamic and different kinds 
of thinking about what Quebec should be,"" Gill said, suggesting that replacing Rodriguez as leader could offer the 
Liberals an attempt at renewal.
To present a viable alternative to the Parti Québécois, which leads in recent polls, Gill said the Liberals now ""need 
someone with a little bit more energy, a little bit more enthusiasm and vigour than Rodriguez was showing.""

that is the chief anchor,"" Gill said.
Rodriguez ""won the leadership race largely on the basis of his status as a kind of a big fish in the federal game,"" he 
said.
During the campaign and since, Rodriguez hadn't ""exactly been putting forth new and dynamic and different kinds 
of thinking about what Quebec should be,"" Gill said, suggesting that replacing Rodriguez as leader could offer the 
Liberals an attempt at renewal.
To present a viable alternative to the Parti Québécois, which leads in recent polls, Gill said the Liberals now ""need

Title: Quebec promises to punish guilty parties in SAAQclic fiasco
Body: QUEBEC - Saying she is just as angry as other Quebecers over the SAAQclic fiasco, the president of the treasury 
board Tuesday vowed to use every lever at the government's disposal to discipline and punish the guilty parties.
""Like all Quebecers, I am outraged over the revelations of the commission,"" France-Élaine Duranceau, who is 
responsible for the public sector, told reporters Tuesday. ""Like all Quebecers, we want to punish those who are 
guilty.
""Real people, in the private sector, had they done something like this would have lost their jobs,"" she added. ""We 
can't tolerate that in the public sector, someone who lies, someone who transmits false information or acts like the 
rules don't apply to them, gets out of it without any impact.""
It was the government's first official reaction to the Gallant commission, which concluded the Société de l'assurance 
automobile du Québec lied( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-management-lied-to-
quebec-gallant-commission-report ) over a period of 10 years on the cost overruns and progress of its shift to the 
SAAQclic digital platform.
She was accompanied by the current Minster of Transport, Jonatan Julien, as well as Quebec's Minister for 
Cybersecurity and Digital Technology, Gilles Bélanger.
On Monday, Premier François Legault said his government was looking at all legal recourse against the 
management of the SAAQ( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-public-inquiry-report-
legault-caq ) allegedly involved in the scandal.
Duranceau on Tuesday added the possibility of imposing disciplinary measures on employees of the state-owned 
corporation and bureaucrats who played a role in the project.
She set out range of possible sanctions.
""We are going to be looking at what's feasible on the legal side and on the disciplinary side,"" Duranceau said.
""We can talk of suspension without pay, a demotion in their functions or have negative notes added to their 
(personnel) files, which would impede their advancement,"" Duranceau said.
Page 2 of 3
Quebec promises to punish guilty parties in SAAQclic fiasco
Julien, the minister responsible for the SAAQ, added that in his view the current CEO of the SAAQ, Serge 
Lamontagne, has ""carte blanche,"" to act in any way he sees fit to act on the recommendations of Gallant as well.
Julien even identified some people who could be targeted by the government, including the former CEOs of the 
SAAQ, Nathalie Tremblay and Denis Marsolais (both since retired) as well as the architect of the digital platform, 
Karl Malenfant.
Malenfant in particular was criticized by commissioner Denis Gallant for his manner of controlling the project.
The SAAQ employs 5,000 people in Quebec.
On Tuesday, Duranceau announced the government is creating a follow-up committee to act on the 26 
recommendations for action included in the Gallant report.
Duranceau's announcement came a day after the SAAQ presented its ""sincere apologies"" for the failure of its digital 
platform launch in 2023 and has vowed to do better to regain the confidence of Quebecers.
In a statement issued late Monday following the publication of the report, the SAAQ said it will spare no effort to 
conform to the recommendations of the report.
""The SAAQ today wants to express its sincere apologies to all Quebecers for the failures that contributed to 
undermining the confidence of Quebecers in their institutions,"" the government agency said.
The SAAQ says it plans to fully co-operate with the government and notes it has enacted specific actions aimed at 
improving its governance.
""We have put in place new strategic controls, elaborated an action plan in contractual management, reinforced the 
framework for contract management and revised the profiles and competency requirements in the nomination of 
upper managers and the board of directors.""
The apology and pledge to do better followed publication of a report Monday that revealed the SAAQ had been 
lying for years to the government about the real costs of the platform.
Instead of costing $458 million over 10 years, the final price tag will be $1.1 billion.

Title: Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game' amid corruption suggestions
Body: The day after the province's anticorruption unit confirmed it was meeting witnesses in connection with allegations 
against the Quebec Liberal Party, Leader Pablo Rodriguez accused his opponents of playing a ""political game.""
Earlier Thursday, Québec solidaire MNA Alejandra Zaga Mendez showed reporters a copy of PLQ Inc., a 2019 
book that investigated allegations of corruption in the Quebec Liberal Party under former premier Jean Charest.
""Every day, we wake up and we learn of a new scandal in the Liberal Party of Quebec,"" she said. ""When we see 
UPAC (Unité permanente anticorruption) and the Liberal Party of Quebec in the same newspaper headline, it 
reminds us of just one thing.""
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon accused the Liberal party of a ""culture of corruption,"" which he 
said stemmed from a loyalty to the ""Canadian regime.""
Rodriguez rejected St-Pierre Plamondon's assertion, defining his party as the oldest in Quebec, ""the party of the 
economy"" and ""the party of a just society.""
Québec solidaire's reference to alleged corruption under Charest ""is just their political game,"" Rodriguez said, 
""because they don't have anything else to say.""
UPAC confirmed Wednesday that it was looking into fundraising allegations involving the Quebec Liberal Party, but 
stressed it hadn't started a formal investigation.
Le Journal de Montréal reported Thursday that UPAC had met with Marwah Rizqy, who was removed from her post 
as parliamentary leader by Rodriguez last week after she fired her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse.
""It's Marwah who decided to call in UPAC from what I understand,"" Rodriguez said, reacting to the report. ""You 
know more than me,"" he added. He said he still didn't know why Rizqy removed Hinse from her role.
If UPAC proceeds with an investigation, ""we're going to collaborate,"" he promised. ""We have nothing to hide."" In an 
email to The Gazette, UPAC said privacy rules prevent it from confirming whether officers had met with Rizqy.
Page 2 of 3
Rodriguez accuses opponents of playing a 'political game' amid corruption suggestions
The Liberal scandal has been centre stage for over a week, and now includes the conflict between Rizqy and 
Hinse, the involvement of anticorruption police, and allegations that some party members received $100 each to 
support Rodriguez in his successful run for leader.
Regardless of whether allegations against the Liberals prove true, ""these things stick,"" said McGill University 
political scientist Daniel Béland.
Corruption allegations have ""tainted"" the Quebec Liberals' image ""for a long time,"" he said, in part because of the 
Charbonneau Commission, which investigated corruption in the construction industry.
The Parti Québécois ""has been saying for a long time that the Liberals are corrupt,"" Béland said, so ""it makes 
sense for the PQ to return to this"" now.
""For them, it's a great opportunity,"" he said. ""Whether it's true or false, it's almost irrelevant at this stage.""
On Wednesday, Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette also weighed in, calling Rodriguez's party ""the same old 
Liberal party"" rife with ""the same illegal practices, the same ethically questionable practices.""
A Pallas Data poll published by L'actualité on Wednesday showed only 13 per cent of Quebecers have a favourable 
impression of Rodriguez - placing him behind St-Pierre Plamondon, Québec solidaire's Ruba Ghazal and Quebec 
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, and tying him with Premier François Legault.
""The polling numbers are really bad,"" Béland said. While Legault's score might be expected given his seven years 
in power, 13 per cent favourability for the new leader of the biggest opposition party is abysmal, he said.
""The question for the (Liberals) is whether there's still time to change leaders before the next provincial election,"" 
Béland said. ""Or you stick with Pablo Rodriguez knowing that he's not well perceived by the population.""
Rodriguez is the only Quebec leader less popular than his party, the Pallas Data poll showed. According to the poll, 
25 per cent of Quebecers intend to vote for the Liberals.

Title: Rodriguez permanently expels Rizqy from Quebec Liberal caucus as crisis grows
Body: QUEBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Pablo Rodriguez has expelled Saint-Laurent MNA Marwah Rizqy from caucus 
as the crisis in the provincial party continues to grow.
Until now, Rizqy had only been suspended from caucus for an undetermined period of time( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/genevieve-hinse-pablo-rodriguez-quebec-liberals ) following 
her decision to fire her chief of staff, Geneviève Hinse, a close associate of Rodriguez, on Nov. 17.
Rodriguez suspended her initially for not explaining her decision to fire Hinse and for not consulting Rodriguez or 
party officials in advance.
During a news conference at the legislature Tuesday, Rodriguez didn't mince his words, repeating what he said 
earlier in a statement: His patience has run out.
He said Rizqy's actions and silence are harming the party, which also finds itself mired in a crisis over allegations of 
vote buying( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-liberals-inquiry-vote-buying-allegations ) 
in last spring's leadership campaign.
""I asked to talk to her,"" Rodriguez said. ""She refuses to do so. She has chosen to turn her back on her party.
""Enough is enough. In the last two weeks, she has caused a lot of damage to the Liberal Party of Quebec. She 
caused damage to all of the team. In choosing to act alone, she has chosen to place herself above the party. And 
let me say there is nothing more important than the party.
""She made her choice. I made mine. The distractions are over. Now we will concentrate on what really matters: the 
priorities of Quebecers.""
On social media, Rizqy broke her silence but limited herself to few lines( 
https://www.facebook.com/marwahrizqymtl/posts/pfbid0KDJQ6AP92smMZAMHHtE3o2cLqEsDLXcWSQqJgRDZ2K
Ef9N2nFmfMgtj8P7Fhq2iDl ) in which she took note of Rodriguez's decision.
""Since the day I was elected as the MNA for Saint-Laurent, I have represented my fellow citizens with devotion and 
rigour,"" she wrote. ""I want to repeat and assure them I will continue to represent them at the same level as an 
independent MNA.""
Page 2 of 3
Rodriguez permanently expels Rizqy from Quebec Liberal caucus as crisis grows
But for the first time, Rodriguez addressed the issue of the future of Rizqy's husband, Greg Kelley, who is also an 
MNA and represents the riding of Jacques-Cartier. Rodriguez said Kelley will remain a member of the Liberal 
caucus even with Rizqy out.
""I just reached out (to Kelley) to say, 'Listen, I know this tough,"" Rodriguez said. ""This changes nothing between the 
two of us.""
And trying to move forward, Rodriguez announced he has begun discussions with Hinse, who was his chief of staff 
when he was a federal MP, for her to return to her previous functions as chief of staff, this time for the new Liberal 
parliamentary leader, André Fortin.
""I checked with madame to see if she is interested,"" Rodriguez said. ""She said, 'give me some time to think about it 
because it has been a very difficult time. Nothing is indicated that she did anything wrong.""
Hinse is suing Rizqy for $500,000( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-liberals-rizqy-
hinse-lawyer-letter ), accusing her of firing her for no valid reason.
But another controversy continued to haunt Rodriguez and the Liberals.
After several articles in the Journal de Montréal with allegations of vote buying in the Liberal leadership race last 
spring, the newspaper Tuesday alleged an entrepreneur contributed $500 to the Rodriguez campaign at the request 
of a businessman and friend who thought he could get government contracts in return.
Such a practice violates Quebec's electoral laws.
The Liberals have already asked a former Superior Court Judge, Jacques R. Fournier, to investigate the 
allegations( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebecs-liberals-inquiry-vote-buying-allegations ). 
His report is due Jan. 31, 2026.
""If reprehensible acts are confirmed as a result of this investigation, there will be consequences,"" Rodriguez told 
reporters. ""I will repeat, and I have said it many times, I will kick these people out.""
But the pressure on the Liberals is starting to show. Arriving for their Tuesday noon caucus, a number of MNAs said 
the endless stories about party ethics is exasperating to them as they try to do their work of questioning the 
government's work.
""I am mad, I'm in a hell of state,"" Marquette MNA Enrico Ciccone told reporters standing at the door of the caucus. 
""There seems to have been something criminal that happened today. Stop them please. Put them in jail, send them 
as far away as possible form our gang because we are fed up.
""I am fed up,"" added Nelligan MNA Monsef Derraji. ""I hope we will soon close all these files. We have so many 
things to do here.""
Chomedey MNA Sona Lakhoyan Olivier said she is angry at all those who speak to the media ""under the cover of 
anonymity.""
""We're here to do a job, to represent our constituents, and get on with our day,"" said D'Arcy-McGee MNA Elisabeth 
Prass, urging anyone who possesses any evidence of wrongdoing to come forward.
""I want to know the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth,"" added Acadie MNA André A. Morin.
But some of the other parties continued to hammer away at the Liberals.
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he believes the issue of ethics is a ""generalized cultural 
problem"" with the Liberals.
Page 3 of 3

He said that explains his recent attempt to reach out to Quebec anglophones( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/canada_news/canadian_politics/a-pq-government-will-be-sensitive-to-
anglophones-needs-leader-says ) to tell them they have another option than voting Liberal.
Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime has launched a similar effort( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-conservatives-make-play-for-anglo-vote-liberal-crisis 
), buying advertising in English newspapers pledging 'No referendum, no corruption.""
Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal said she finds the sheer number revelations about the Liberal 
""dizzying.""
