Title: Who will end the debate? Political gridlock continues in the House of Commons
Body: OTTAWA - Federal political parties appear to be locked in a game of chicken in an increasingly precarious 
Parliament over a debate that has stalled almost all business in the House of Commons.
The Conservatives have vowed the debate will continue until the Liberals hand over unredacted documents to the 
RCMP about a green-tech foundation that was found to have misspent government money.
The debate has now stretched into its second week.
""I could sit down right now and everything would be done, if they just gave the documents,"" Conservative MP Kyle 
Seeback said in the House of Commons Monday. 
""The Liberals could end this entire thing.""
The Speaker ruled last week that the Liberals did not comply with an order from the House to hand over the 
documents related to the green-technology foundation, known as Sustainable Development Technology Canada. 
The foundation was abolished after the auditor general found dozens of cases of conflict of interest and several 
cases of money going to ineligible projects this summer. 
But House Speaker Greg Fergus also said the issue is complicated and should be studied at committee, and the 
government maintains it should not provide documents to police.
The Liberals could put forward a motion to end the debate, but they would need the support of another party to 
force the House to move onto other business.
Liberal House leader Karina Gould's office says it's up to the Conservatives to end the ""filibuster.""
The Conservatives are poised to make the documents a possible focus of their next attempt to topple to the House 
and trigger an election.
On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre gave notice that he plans to put forward another non-confidence 
motion. 

Page 2 of 3
Who will end the debate? Political gridlock continues in the House of Commons
The wording of the latest motion takes aim at the government for the green-tech foundation and the inflated cost of 
the ArriveCan app, all while Canadians are suffering financially.
""As Liberal insiders are lining their pockets, millions of Canadians are lining up at food banks,"" the Conservatives 
said in the motion, which the party could bring forward for a debate the next time it is scheduled to have an 
opposition day.
The number of opposition days allotted in each sitting is decided at the beginning of a session, but the government 
decides when they are scheduled. 
The Conservatives are set to have another three opposition days before the holiday break in December, but the 
next date cannot be set while MPs are still in the midst of the privilege debate. 
Unlike the last two non-confidence motions put forward by the Conservatives this fall, the Tories have a greater 
chance of winning support from the Bloc Québécois, putting the government at greater risk of falling.
Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet has said he plans to start negotiations with the other parties this week to bring 
down the government if the Liberals do not agree to his party's demands. The Bloc wants financial support for a bill 
to increase old age security payments for seniors under the age of 75, something that would cost an estimated $16 
billion over five years.
Jean-Yves Duclos, the government's Quebec lieutenant, showed no signs of acquiescing to that request on 
Monday as he reiterated concerns with the Bloc's bill.
""It gives affluent pensioners like I will be in a few years more money sometimes than the low-income senior in my 
riding who has to make ends meet with a pension income of $20,000 per year,"" Duclos said.
""That's not the right way to focus on vulnerable seniors.""
The New Democrats said they have not yet been approached by the Bloc, and they will decide how to vote on a 
case-by-case basis.
The Liberals maintain that the House of Commons should not provide documents to the RCMP for their 
investigation into spending at Sustainable Development Technology Canada. They have said police need to go 
through proper channels for their investigation, otherwise the actions of the House could infringe the right to due 
process.
The RCMP received redacted versions of the documents the government already provided to the House in August, 
but have raised doubts about whether they can legally use documents handed over by Parliament as part of an 
investigation. 
""The RCMP will continuously assess information and documents that may give rise to a reasonable expectation of 
privacy, which is important to ensuring that all applicable legal standards are upheld during this review,"" the police 
agency said in a statement Friday. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2024.

Title: Witnesses against former city councillor will testify remotely
Body: More than two dozen witnesses against former Calgary city council member Joe Magliocca will be permitted to 
testify remotely via video links from across the country and beyond.
Defence counsel Aryan Sadat, after reviewing an affidavit from an RCMP officer and statements from the 
prospective witnesses, told Justice Gord Wong on Friday he was no longer opposing Crown prosecutor Aaron 
Rankin's application to have most of his case presented via remote testimony.
On Monday, at the start of Magliocca's Calgary Court of Justice trial, Sadat indicated he had instructions from his 
client to oppose proceeding in such a manner, arguing Rankin had not produced evidence supporting his 
application.
The lawyer asked to adjourn the case to Friday to determine his position on the bid and in the interim Rankin had 
lead RCMP investigator David Mitchell prepare an affidavit, which included witness statements.
Sadat's initial reaction to that document was to ask Justice Gord Wong to recuse himself from the case, suggesting 
the statements could influence the judge's decision in the case.
""It can put you in an improper position,"" Sadat said, before Wong summarily dismissed the recusal application.
Magliocca, 59, faces charges of fraud and breach of trust by a public officer over allegations he was reimbursed 
for expenses at outof-town functions that weren't actually incurred.
Magliocca's trial is set to run until Sept. 26. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2024 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: Woman faces fraud charges after theft from Nova Scotia premier's riding association
Body: NEW GLASGOW, N.S. - Police in New Glasgow, N.S., say a 44-year-old woman faces fraud charges after funds 
went missing from the Pictou East Progressive Conservative Association.
New Glasgow Regional Police began the investigation on Oct. 7, after Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston reported 
that an undisclosed amount of money had gone missing from his riding association’s account.
Police allege that a volunteer who was acting as treasurer had withdrawn funds from the association’s account 
between 2016 and 2024.
The force says it arrested Tara Amanda Cohoon at her Pictou County, N.S., residence on Oct. 11.
They say investigators seized mobile electronic devices, bank records and cash during a search of the home.
Cohoon has since been released and is to appear in Pictou provincial court on Dec. 2 to face charges of forgery, 
uttering a forged document, theft over $5,000 and fraud over $5,000.
Police say their investigation remains ongoing.
Houston revealed the investigation to reporters on Oct. 9, saying he felt an “incredible level of betrayal” over the 
matter.
The premier also said a volunteer he had known for many years had been dismissed from the association and the 
party.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2024.

Title: 'Auto-correct'blamed for 'other Randy'in probe of minister; Boissonnault focus of ethics committee
Body: Employment Minister Randy Boissonnault is slamming his former business partner for failing to clear his name in a 
House of Commons committee's quest to discover the identity of ""the other Randy.""
Stephen Anderson, who co-founded Global Health Imports (GHI) with Boissonnault at the start of the pandemic in 
2020, testified at a rare summer meeting of the ethics committee on Wednesday in a white suit with black Christian 
Louboutin boots and a Louis Vuitton bag.
At issue is whether Boissonnault remained an active participant in the medical supply business he co-owned after 
he was appointed to cabinet, which would have violated ethics rules. Anderson repeated several times that he 
never discussed business with Boissonnault after his re-election as an MP in 2021.
The ordeal started when Global News obtained text messages showing that Anderson had passed along an urgent 
message from a certain ""Randy"" to the owner of a personal protective equipment company for a wire transfer of 
$500,000.
The exchange was dated Sept. 8, 2022, which is almost a year after Boissonnault was first sworn into cabinet as 
associate minister of finance and of tourism. Last summer, he became minister of employment, workforce 
development and official languages.
The Conflict of Interest Act prohibits public office holders from engaging in certain outside activities, including 
managing or operating a business or commercial activity. Any business holdings are required to be divested or put 
into a blind trust.
For more than an hour on Wednesday, Anderson attempted to deny that the ""Randy"" that he was texting at the time 
was Boissonnault.
Anderson started off by saying that the name ""Randy"" was an ""unfortunate auto-correct"" and that he would be able 
to only reveal the person's real identity in-camera, as he said the individual's personal situation could be negatively 
affected by media exposure.
Page 2 of 3
'Auto-correct'blamed for 'other Randy'in probe of minister; Boissonnault focus of ethics committee
Conservative ethics critic Michael Barrett said he had in fact uncovered nine separate text messages, which the 
National Post has not seen, from Anderson referencing an individual named ""Randy.""
He said one of them referenced ""Randy"" being in Vancouver - at the same time as Boissonnault was part of the 
cabinet retreat in that city.
""Are you saying that ... every one of those nine (text messages) is an auto-correct?"" asked Barrett.
Anderson answered with a defiant ""yes.""
""I don't believe you,"" said Barrett. ""Your story doesn't add up.""
Later, Anderson admitted that he lied to a Global News reporter about the other ""Randy"" being head of logistics at 
GHI.
""I appreciate that. I actually do. Maybe it's the first truth I've heard today,"" said NDP ethics critic Matthew Green.
In the end, Anderson muddied the waters even more, to the point where the Conservatives and the NDP now 
believe that the ""Randy"" in the texts is indeed Boissonnault.
""Objectively, given the information I have, there's no other conclusion to make,"" said Green.
Members of the committee agreed to ask Anderson to not only reveal the real identity of ""Randy"" by Friday at noon, 
but also to force him to hand over phone records and text message records. They also agreed to have Boissonnault 
testify once more in September.
In a statement, Boissonnault said he was ""deeply troubled and disappointed"" by Anderson's testimony.
""I have unilaterally surrendered my shares of GHI for no compensation, and am no longer a shareholder. As the 
records I've given to the committee show, I have had no involvement whatsoever with the operations of GHI since 
September 2021,"" he said.
""If Mr. Anderson has subsequently been using my name without my consent to gain influence, he should simply 
explain that to the committee.""
Boissonnault came into politics as an Edmonton MP in 2015, claiming to be a successful entrepreneur, journalist 
and political commentator.
But in recent months, investigative reporting by Global News uncovered some ethical concerns over Boissonnault's 
business links to Anderson, while Quebec-based newspaper Le Devoir cast doubts on Boissonnault's claim that he 
worked as a journalist.
For weeks, the Conservatives have been sharing memes about ""the other Randy,"" joking that it is in fact 
Boissonnault with fake glasses and a moustache. Their latest mockery on Tuesday involved a play on the popular 
internet parody song ""Looking for a Man in Finance.""
Boissonnault has always denied that he is the ""Randy"" mentioned in the text message.
To date, the ethics commissioner has said there are no grounds to investigate the minister further.
In a letter dated June 25, Konrad von Finckenstein said he was satisfied that Boissonnault had had no contact with 
Anderson regarding their medical supply company after reviewing call logs from his three devices and screenshots 
of messages exchanged that date.
But the Conservatives and the NDP said that there are many other ways that people can communicate other than 
calls or text messages.

Title: 'Nothing to hide,' in Greenbelt probe, premier insists RCMP interviews witnesses linked to Ford government in
Body: RCMP detectives investigating the $8.28-billion Greenbelt land swap scandal are interviewing witnesses linked to 
Premier Doug Ford's government.
As first disclosed by the Star, current and former Progressive Conservative aides are sitting down with the Mounties 
to discuss Ford's controversial 2022 decision to open up 7,400 acres of the two-million-acre Greenbelt to housing 
development.
""We have nothing to hide,"" the premier told reporters in Thunder Bay on Friday, three hours after the Star broke the 
news.
""Come in and do whatever you have to do ... but I want full co-operation - they know that - because there's nothing 
to hide there. Let's get on with it,"" said Ford.
Interviews with members of the RCMP ""O"" Division's Sensitive and International Investigations unit, the elite 
Ottawa-based branch that probes political crimes and corruption, are being held at the force's Greater Toronto 
Area detachment.
In a statement Friday, Ford's office confirmed that aides and former staffers were being interviewed.
""We've always said we would co-operate. That co-operation would include the premier and current or former staff 
conducting interviews as witnesses, which are currently underway,"" the premier's office said. ""Any further 
questions should be directed to the RCMP.""
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police would only ""confirm that the investigation is ongoing.""
But officials close to Ford said the premier has not yet been approached by the RCMP.
The Star is not identifying anyone who has been contacted by the Mounties because they are not authorized to 
discuss what they are telling - or will tell - detectives. 
But sources say the RCMP appears to be focusing on potential witnesses, rather than anyone actually suspected of 
wrongdoing.
Page 2 of 3
'Nothing to hide,' in Greenbelt probe, premier insists RCMP interviews witnesses linked to Ford government in 
criminal probe
The revelation came on the first anniversary of the auditor general's explosive report into the land swap that 
ultimately triggered the police investigation.
Ford scrapped his Greenbelt land-swap scheme last Sept. 21 in the wake of an Aug. 9 report by then-auditor 
general Bonnie Lysyk that found developers connected to his Progressive Conservatives had been ""favoured"" in 
the government's surprise move to allow houses to be built on the environmentally sensitive land.
Lysyk, who told the Star this week she has not been contacted by the Mounties, said the rezoning ballooned the 
value of the 15 properties in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area to $8.28 billion.
Her 97-page report - and a subsequent review by integrity commissioner J. David Wake released on Aug. 30, 2023 
- appear to be serving as guidebooks for the RCMP investigation.
Some of the witnesses now being interviewed were named by Wake in his 166-page report.
He interviewed 62 people - most of whom were in the presence of their legal counsel - during the course of his 
review.
News that the RCMP investigation is heating up comes as Ford, whose Tories have a large lead in public opinion 
polls, has been considering an early election call next year instead of waiting for the scheduled June 2026 vote.
Last month's Abacus Data tracking poll found his PCs at 44 per cent - their highest level of support in more than 
two years - with Bonnie Crombie's Liberals at 26 per cent, Marit Stiles's New Democrats at 19 per cent and Mike 
Schreiner's Greens at seven per cent.
Abacus surveyed 1,000 Ontarians July 16-21 using online panels based on the Lucid exchange platform. While opt-
in polls cannot be assigned a margin of error, for comparison purposes, a random sample of this size would have 
one of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
Two of Ford's ministers and two senior political aides resigned last summer after the Lysyk and Wake reports.
With his popularity plummeting last September, the premier reversed course on his Greenbelt scheme.
""It was a mistake to open the Greenbelt. I'm very, very sorry. I made a promise to you that I wouldn't touch the 
Greenbelt. I broke that promise,"" Ford said on Sept. 21.
""As a first step to earning back your trust, I'll be reversing the changes. We moved too quickly and we made the 
wrong decision ... it caused people to question our motives,"" he said.
But Stiles said ""one year after the auditor general's revelations about Ford's Greenbelt grab, he hasn't learned a 
thing.""
""You deserve a government that tells the truth. That cares about regular people and does right by them. A 
government that isn't under criminal investigation,"" the NDP leader said.
Crombie said Friday was ""a sad day for the people of Ontario, who deserve and need so much more than a 
government embroiled in criminal investigation.""
""The people of this province need to know exactly how Doug Ford was involved in this scandal. Ontario deserves 
better,"" the Liberal leader said.
Schreiner, for his part, maintained ""the premier has not learned from the Greenbelt scandal.""

Title: 'Unacceptable predicament': Information commissioner faces $700K budget shortfall due to government errors
Body: OTTAWA - Canada's access to information watchdog says she is facing a $700,000 budget shortfall that will 
hamstring her ability to hold the government to account and is calling on the Liberals to fix the ""unacceptable 
predicament.""
""This reduction in my budget will spell longer delays for complainants who are seeking information from government 
institutions,"" information commissioner Caroline Maynard bluntly told MPs on the ethics committee Thursday.
""Now is not the time for bureaucratic penny-pinching.""
Maynard said that Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC) was the victim of an overly rigid formula used by 
the Treasury Board Secretariat (TBS) to calculate salary increases for employees in her office, which combined with 
other errors by the same department that leave her with a combined shortfall of $700,000.
She says that's equivalent to five per cent of her office's annual budget.
""This will represent a significant portion of my overall IT budget, or money to cover the cost of defending my orders 
in court, or funding for a full team of investigators,"" she told the committee. She said she is currently fighting the 
government in court for access to documents in 11 cases.
The budget shortfall comes as Maynard is increasingly critical of the government's handling of the federal access-
to-information system, which she says is ""overwhelmed"" and cannot sustain the status quo.
When asked by Conservative MP Michael Barrett if Prime Minister Justin Trudeau had respected its promise that 
his government would be ""open by default,"" she replied that ""a lot more can be done with respect to transparency.""
""I don't see it (access to information) as a priority"" for the Liberals, she said.

Page 2 of 3
'Unacceptable predicament': Information commissioner faces $700K budget shortfall due to government errors
In a letter to the acting head of TBS( https://www.oic-ci.gc.ca/en/resources/reports-publications/letter-acting-
secretary-treasury-board-concerns-regarding ) sent on Tuesday, Maynard was no less pessimistic about her office's 
budgetary situation. She wrote that a $700,000 shortfall means she will have to eliminate up to eight of the 128 
current full-time-equivalent positions in her office.
""I cannot overstate the seriousness of the situation I am currently faced with,"" she wrote.
""For a small organization like the OIC, where every employee plays a critical role in achieving our objectives and 
fulfilling our mandate, even a small reduction in personnel will significantly strain our operational capacity at a time 
when the Access to Information system is under pressure like never before.""
In both her letter and her testimony Thursday, Maynard called on the government to change how it funds her office 
to a more ""agile"" and ""flexible"" funding model.
""This cycle of calculations based on rigid formulas, which adversely affects small organizations like mine in a 
disproportionate way, needs to be broken,"" she wrote to acting TBS head Dominique Blanchard.
""My CFO and DCFO have already met with several of your officials in an attempt to come up with solutions, but to 
no avail, which is why I now appeal to you directly.""
In a statement, TBS spokesperson Martin Potvin confirmed the department applied the standard formula to 
calculate the OIC's new operational budget after new collective-bargaining agreements were signed across the 
public service.
""This approach has been in place for many years and applies to 90 organizations across government,"" Potvin 
wrote. ""We will continue to discuss with the Information Commissioner and her office the concerns that she has 
raised in her letter.""
Maynard was invited to testify at the committee on the Liberal government's initial refusal to disclose over 600 
pages of documents related to the sudden removal and eventual firing of two scientists from Canada's most secure 
microbiology lab in 2021.
Then, in late February, the government suddenly released the documents behind the firing of Xiangguo Qiu and her 
husband Keding Cheng after a long fight by the Liberals to keep the information secret, a fight that went as far as 
taking the then Speaker of the House to court.
The documents revealed that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service determined Qiu worked closely and 
covertly with Chinese government labs and collaborated with ""institutions whose goals have potentially lethal 
military applications.""
The spy agency also assessed that Qiu's husband, Cheng, had likely lied to CSIS during an interview and must 
have been aware of his wife's scheme.
But Thursday's committee meeting never got into the topic after it was abruptly adjourned at the request of Liberal 
MP Darren Fisher, who echoed his Liberal and NDP colleagues' criticism that the hearing should not have been 
called during a parliamentary break week.
NDP MP Matthew Green went as far as accusing the Conservative committee chair John Brassard of an 
""authoritarian"" and ""highly problematic"" use of his powers when he let the meeting happen during the break week 
and swapped certain agreed-upon witnesses for others at his discretion.
Liberal members and Green voted to adjourn, whereas the Conservatives and Bloc Québécois voted against it. 
Immediately, Conservative MPs accused the Liberals of attempting a ""cover up.""

Title: Arbiter says MPP staffer was fired without cause; Mantha was removed from NDP caucus after allegations he
Body: A constituency assistant fired by the Ontario NDP after being sexually harassed by MPP Michael Mantha was not 
terminated for just cause, an arbitration decision has found.
Mantha was suspended from caucus in April 2023 and then permanently removed last August, after a workplace 
investigator found he pressured the woman to ""engage in non-consensual sexual interactions with him,"" required 
her to regularly hug him, asked her to send sexually explicit photos of herself and to share sexual dreams about 
him, and pressured her to work from the office so he could be near her and ""continue his practice of sexually 
touching her."" 
Mantha did not seek to participate in the arbitration proceedings, despite being notified by the NDP, arbitrator Jasbir 
Parmar said in the decision released Thursday.
Reached by phone Friday afternoon, Mantha told the Star he had not yet seen the arbitration decision, but added 
""there are many things that I didn't agree with"" regarding the workplace investigation findings. He said he did not 
participate in the arbitration proceedings following advice from lawyers, and that he would review the decision with 
them before commenting. 
At Queen's Park, NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Mantha, who now sits as an Independent MPP, should resign from 
the legislature.
""As leader, I take my responsibility to our staff and their safety very seriously. It's why I took swift action to remove 
MPP Mantha from my caucus when allegations against him were substantiated by an independent, third-party 
investigation,"" Stiles said Friday. 
""In light of the arbitration decision being made public, I want to reaffirm the Ontario NDP's commitment to zero 
tolerance for sexual violence and harassment. Elected officials at all levels must be held to a higher standard. 
Those who take advantage of the trust and power they have been given are unfit to remain in office. They must be 
held accountable for their actions.""
According to Parmar's decision, the woman first started working for the Algoma-Manitoulin MPP in his Elliot Lake 
office in 2015. She went on a paid leave of absence after raising concerns to the NDP in August 2022 about an 
Page 2 of 2
Arbiter says MPP staffer was fired without cause; Mantha was removed from NDP caucus after allegations he 
sexually harassed now-sacked worker
""unsafe work environment,"" with the Canadian Office and Professional Employees union filing a grievance on her 
behalf later that year. The NDP hired an external workplace investigator in January 2023 to look into the situation. 
In January 2024, just over four months after Mantha was permanently removed from caucus due to the workplace 
investigation findings, the woman received a letter from the NDP caucus indicating that ""given the fact that MPP 
Mantha no longer held an elected seat within the ONDP Caucus,"" her employment no longer fell under the 
collective agreement and had been terminated as of April 1, 2023, Parmar wrote in the arbitration decision.
The union then filed another grievance in January 2024 saying the woman had been unjustly terminated. 
Because NDP political aides at Queen's Park and in constituency offices are unionized, Mantha's staff all lost their 
positions in the union's bargaining unit when he was removed from caucus last year. Sources say the woman in 
question remained on the NDP payroll months after her unionized job was eliminated.

Title: Associate testifies about texts to 'Randy'; 'Auto-Correct'; Says texts were not addressing federal minister
Body: A former business associate of Employment Minister Randy Boissonnault said that the other ""Randy"" he was 
texting in September 2022 was an ""unfortunate auto-correct"" but was unable to explain why he kept referring to a 
person named ""Randy"" multiple times in subsequent messages.
Stephen Anderson, who co-founded Global Health Imports with Boissonnault at the start of the pandemic in 2020, 
told the members of the House of Commons ethics committee Wednesday that he would be happy to share the true 
identity of the other ""Randy"" with them but only in-camera, as he said the individual's personal situation could be 
negatively affected by media exposure.
At issue is whether Boissonnault remained an active participant in the medical supply business he co-owned after 
he was appointed to cabinet, which would have violated ethics rules.
Anderson repeated several times that he never discussed business with Boissonnault after his re-election as an MP 
in 2021.
Conservative ethics critic Michael Barrett referenced nine separate text messages, which the National Post has not 
yet seen, from Anderson referencing an individual named ""Randy.""
""I don't think I want to get into asking you what you think an auto-correct is, but I can tell you that this isn't that,"" said 
Barrett.
""Are you saying that... every one of those nine (text messages) is an auto-correct?"" Anderson answered with a 
defiant ""yes.""
""I don't believe you,"" said Barrett.

Committees usually do not meet during the summer, but Conservatives and the NDP said that Boissonnault's prior

""We've been looking to find out information that, frankly ... Boissonnault has refused to provide, and he has

Boissonnault came into politics as an Edmonton MP in 2015, claiming to be a successful entrepreneur and a 
journalist and political commentator.
But in recent months, investigative reporting by Global News uncovered some ethical concerns over Boissonnault's 
business links to Anderson and Poon, while Quebec-based newspaper Le Devoir recently cast doubts on 
Boissonnault's claim that he worked as a journalist.

equipment company for a wire transfer of $500,000 to secure a shipment.
The exchange was dated Sept. 8, 2022, which is almost a year after Boissonnault was first sworn into cabinet as

Boissonnault has denied that he is the ""Randy"" mentioned in the text message, and Anderson has never unveiled

Title: Bethlenfalvy calls PCs 'an open book' Finance minister says RCMP investigators have not yet reached out to
Body: As RCMP detectives interview current and former Progressive Conservatives staffers about the Greenbelt 
scandal, Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy insists the government is ""an open book.""
Speaking to reporters at Queen's Park on Tuesday, Bethlenfalvy said he has not been contacted by the Royal 
Canadian Mounted Police and, as far as he knows, neither have any of his past aides.
Asked if he were prepared to sit down with investigators, the treasurer nodded.
""We're an open book - as the premier said, 'Nothing to hide.' They've got to do their job,"" Bethlenfalvy said as he 
announced first quarterly growth in Ontario was 0.7 per cent and the deficit of $9.8 billion remains unchanged from 
his March budget.
After the Star revealed Friday that Tory aides are being questioned as potential witnesses in the $8.28-billion 
Greenbelt land swap scandal, Premier Doug Ford signalled to the police, ""Come in and do whatever you have to 
do.""
""But I want full co-operation - they know that - because there's nothing to hide there. Let's get on with it,"" he said in 
Thunder Bay.
""We have nothing to hide.""
Ford has not been interviewed by police. The RCMP would only ""confirm that the investigation is ongoing"" into the 
premier's controversial 2022 decision to open up 7,400 acres of the two-million-acre Greenbelt to housing 
development.
While Ford cancelled his Greenbelt land-swap scheme in September, RCMP launched a criminal probe 19 days 
later.
Their investigation came in the wake of separate reports into the debacle by the auditor general and the integrity 
commissioner last August.
Page 2 of 3
Bethlenfalvy calls PCs 'an open book' Finance minister says RCMP investigators have not yet reached out to 
him or his past aides
Then-auditor general Bonnie Lysyk found developers connected to Ford's Tories had been ""favoured"" in the push to 
allow houses to be built on land deemed as environmentally sensitive.
Lysyk said the rezoning inflated the value of the 15 properties in the GTHA to $8.28 billion.
Her report - and a subsequent review by integrity commissioner J. David Wake - are apparently serving as the basis 
for the RCMP investigation.
Some of the 62 witnesses named by Wake in his report are in the process of being questioned, sources say.
Detectives from the RCMP are quietly conducting interviews with past and present PC staffers this month at the 
force's GTA detachment.
Sources, speaking confidentially in order to discuss sensitive matters, emphasized the officers are meeting with 
aides and bureaucrats viewed as potential witnesses.
Revelations about the escalation of the RCMP investigation comes as the Tories, who lead in public opinion polls, 
are gearing up for an early election call next year instead of waiting for the scheduled June 2026 vote.
Bethlenfalvy was asked Tuesday if the governing party was reconsidering a gamble on a snap vote.
""We're very focused on executing on our transparent plan for the people of Ontario,"" he said, noting the Tories ran 
and won on their 2022 budget in the last provincial election.

Title: Border agency reducing use of outside consultants; President cites ArriveCan scandal
Body: OTTAWA The president of the Canada Border Services Agency said her agency has reduced the number of 
outside consultants it employs after the disastrous ArriveCan app.
Erin O'Gorman told a Parliamentary committee on Tuesday that the agency is trying to keep more information 
technology work inhouse.
""We've reduced our consulting footprint at the start of the fiscal year, we had 25 fewer consultants than at the same 
time last year, and today we have 68 fewer consultants working in the CBSA,"" she said.
After initially not being able to provide specific numbers, O'Gorman told committee members at the end of the 
meeting that the border agency had reduced the number of outside IT consultants to 175, down from 243 a year at 
the same time in 2023.
After months of media reporting on the ArriveCan scandal, the auditor general found earlier this year that the app 
was so poorly managed that it was difficult to pin down exactly how much it cost, but it was likely around $60 
million.
The app was required for people who crossed into Canada either at land or air borders during the pandemic. In 
addition to the cost overruns, the app sent thousands of people mistakenly into quarantine. The app was contracted 
to GC strategies, a two-person IT staffing firm that subcontracted the work to other IT companies. There is now an 
ongoing RCMP investigation.
O'Gorman said the border agency has strengthened conflict-of-interest rules for contractors and employees to 
ensure no one working on a contract is also working for the government.
""We will also be requiring vendors with active IT service contracts to certify that none of the resources they provide 
to CBSA is actively employed as public servants,"" she said.
She said while the government has reduced the number of IT contracts, she said the border agency will always 
needs some outside help, but they're trying to ensure that consultants also provide information to CBSA staff.

Title: Brown says he'll clear leadership bid debt Records show Brampton mayor owes more than $420,000 to 15
Body: Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown remains in significant debt from his failed 2022 bid to become leader of the federal 
Conservative party, but the status of the investigations into why he was kicked out of the contest ultimately won by 
Pierre Poilievre remain unknown.
Records that Brown filed with Elections Canada 18 months after the race's end and recently made public indicate 
he owed $428,869.32 to 15 suppliers, including some core members of his former campaign staff.
Brown told the Star he feels confident he'll have his debt paid off by year's end, despite some roadblocks along the 
way. ""I don't anticipate any challenges paying it off,"" he said.
Brown was disqualified from the Conservative leadership contest two months before it ended following allegations 
that his campaign may have broken election law while selling party memberships and by having a third party pay for 
a member of his campaign staff. 
Following his disqualification, the party said it would no longer issue tax receipts for donations to Brown's campaign, 
which former campaign manager John Mykytyshyn said makes it hard to solicit funds.
Further muddling the issue is the party's own failure to post a public notice that Brown was holding a fundraiser last 
year, a violation of election law. That led to Brown's campaign having to return all of the donations it received - 
around $300,000, Mykytyshyn said. 
""Our fundraising efforts have been complicated,"" he said.
Brown has always denied his campaign broke any laws. He returned the money to the third party who had paid one 
of his campaign staff, saying his understanding had always been she was working for his campaign on her own 
time. Elections records have revealed that third party was a luxury real estate development firm in Oakville.
The Star also first revealed that Poilievre's campaign ultimately paid the legal fees for the worker who blew the 
whistle on that arrangement. She remains heavily involved in Conservative politics and is frequently seen at 
Poilievre events.
Page 2 of 2
Brown says he'll clear leadership bid debt Records show Brampton mayor owes more than $420,000 to 15 
suppliers
The status of the various complaints lodged with commissioner of Canada Elections over Brown's actions is 
unknown.
The commissioner's office notifies individuals in writing if they are under investigation ""as soon as feasible,"" 
unless if has formed the opinion that doing so would hinder or compromise a probe. The Brown campaign told the 
Star it has never been notified that an investigation is underway.
The commissioner's office has consistently cited privacy requirements in the Elections Act in its refusal to answer 
the Star's inquiries on the status of the complaints.
The law, however, does allow for the commissioner to disclose the status of an investigation if they deem the matter 
is in the public interest.
Brown is not the only candidate from the 2022 leadership race whose campaign had debts long after the contest 
ended. Eighteen months later, former Quebec premier Jean Charest still owed $185,137.56 to his suppliers. He 
last had a publicly listed fundraiser in February. Failure to pay can have legal repercussions, including a prohibition 
on being allowed to run for Parliament or to sit as an MP.

Title: Chestermere elects Dean, shuns previous regime; New mayor gets 56% of the vote, more than 3 times of any
Body: Shannon Dean has been elected the next mayor of Chestermere and will head a largely fresh-faced council, with 
voters in Monday's byelection choosing to close a political chapter rife with controversy.
""My first thought is the same thing I told everybody whenever they told me, 'You have my support' or 'I'm giving you 
my vote' - and that is that I'm humbled,"" the mayor-elect told Postmedia on Tuesday.
""As an elected official, the residents of Chestermere are my boss, and my plan is to work every day to earn the trust 
of residents of Chestermere, whether they voted for me or not.""
Dean, a former teacher, principal and longtime community volunteer, earned 3,559 votes - 56 per cent of the total 
and more than three times that of any of his competitors.
He takes the helm after more than two years of turmoil in the 25,000-person city, during which he served as a city 
councillor under JeffColvin, the former mayor who was removed from office by the Alberta government last 
December.
Colvin ran again but failed to reclaim his seat, as did the three councillors fired alongside him - Mel Foat, Blaine 
Funk and Stephen Hanley.
""Our residents were looking for elected officials - mayor and council - who are going to be focused on doing what's 
right for Chestermere and not being involved in the drama that we've witnessed over the last couple of years,"" Dean 
said.
Dean was among the councillors spared from Municipal Affairs Minister Ric McIver's dismissals - alongside Ritesh 
Narayan and Sandy Johal-Watt, the latter of whom has since resigned and taken a job in city administration.
Joining Dean on the city's next council are Narayan and five firstterm councillors: Murray Grant, Kiran Randhawa, 
Janelle Sandboe, Robert Schindler and Rob Wawrzynowski.

Title: Chestermere residents head to polls for Monday byelection
Body: Chestermere residents will head to the polls on Monday, tasked with choosing their next mayor and five councillors 
from a slate of more than two dozen candidates - including the ex-mayor and councillors who were fired by the 
province last year.
The much-anticipated vote was triggered by the Alberta government's rare decision to boot the city's then-mayor 
Jeff Colvin, councillors Mel Foat, Blaine Funk and Stephen Hanley, and three top city officials last December. 
Municipal Affairs Minister Ric McIver said at the time council had failed to quell dysfunction identified by a 
municipal inspection and didn't adhere to a province-installed supervisor or the binding directives it was handed as 
a result of that investigation.
All four men are now running to reclaim their respective positions.
""This is just a bit of a bizarre series of events,"" said Mount Royal University political scientist Lori Williams. ""And it's 
got to be frustrating for the people of Chestermere with all these questions swirling around and so many barriers to 
effective governance in their municipality.""
Three councillors, Sandy Johal-Watt, Shannon Dean and Ritesh Narayan, were spared by McIver's dismissal order, 
though Narayan is the only member of the last council with a confirmed spot on the new one. Johal-Watt resigned 
and took a job in city administration, while Dean stepped down to run for mayor.
Colvin and Dean are joined on the mayoral ballot by Marshall Chalmers, another ex-Chestermere mayor, and 
former city councillor Christopher Steeves. Twenty-three candidates are running for the five open councillor 
seats.
NEW COUNCIL TO ADDRESS FINANCIAL INQUIRY FINDINGS
Williams said while Monday's vote could mark the end of turbulence within Chestermere's government, it ""isn't 
going to settle the issue."" The four ousted politicians are still pursuing legal action against the province's dismissal 
order and making numerous claims about bias, corruption and conspiracy being behind their dismissals.
""We are not going to hear the end of this; this is going to be an ongoing controversy for some time to come,"" said 
Williams.
Page 2 of 3
Chestermere residents head to polls for Monday byelection
""Both publicly and legally, I think this is going to continue - the allegations and the objections are going to continue. 
But, again, I think for the people of Chestermere, their primary concern is whether (candidates) will be able to 
govern effectively for the interests of their municipality."" As directed by the province, one of the new mayor and 
council's first orders of business will be to formulate plans to address the 94 recommendations of a recent financial 
probe of the city. The Deloitte-led investigation - ordered by the province after the dismissals - found a laundry list of 
issues, including multiple expenditures made without proper council approval.
Last week, the city sued Colvin, Foat, Funk and Hanley for more than $650,000 - based partly on Deloitte's findings. 
The city claims the four improperly spent taxpayer dollars on lawyers to fight their dismissals, booze, and equipment 
to surveil city staff, among other costs.
The four have denied all of the allegations, and Colvin has said the lawsuit amounts to interference in the byelection 
by city officials.
The city's claims have not been tested in court.
ELECTION STAFF PREPFOR HAND-COUNT
Among the myriad changes enacted by the province's recently ratified Bill 20 is one that bans electronic vote 
counters, meaning Monday night's tally will be done by hand, delaying unofficial results.
Returning officer Noshy Karbani said the count would likely end hours after polls close at 8 p.m. in the early hours 
of Tuesday, with a preliminary tally to be unveiled soon after. Each candidate will be allowed one person in the 
room - a person or scrutineer of their choosing or themselves.
""It would be ideal if we could have everything done by 1 a.m., 1:30 a.m. But that is if everything goes according to 
plan,"" Karbani told Postmedia last week.
Karbani said with Chestermere's population swelling to more than 25,000, voter turnout could be higher than the 
4,700 ballots cast in the 2021 election.
Almost 2,800 people voted in advance polls between June 15 and June 17.
Residents will vote throughout the day at the Chestermere Recreation Centre.

Title: Chestermere sues fired mayor, councillors to recover $650K in unapproved spending
Body: The City of Chestermere is suing its fired mayor and councillors for more than $650,000 in public funds that the 
municipality says were spent without approval - including personal legal fees, cameras to surveil city staff, booze 
and travel expenses for a councillor's wife.
The City of Chestermere filed a statement of claim against ex-mayor Jeff Colvin and former councillors Mel Foat, 
Blaine Funk and Stephen Hanley in the Court of King's Bench in Calgary on Monday. Postmedia obtained a copy of 
the lawsuit, which claims the ousted officials caused the city to expend taxpayer dollars without proper budgeting or 
authorization on several occasions.
The city alleges the four beleaguered politicians are jointly responsible for more than $430,000 of unauthorized city 
spending between 2022 and 2023 and that Colvin alone is liable for an additional $223,000 - all of which the city is 
attempting to recover. Under the Municipal Government Act, elected officials are liable to municipalities for cash 
spent without necessary approval.
The city's claims have not yet been tested in court.
Municipal Affairs Minister Ric McIver booted Colvin, the three councillors and three top city officials from office in 
December last year following two years of head-butting over a municipal inspection that found the city was 
mismanaged. The dismissals were rooted in council's failure to adhere to binding provincial directives resulting from 
that probe.
In the wake of the firings, McIver ordered a second municipal inspection, a financial probe conducted by 
professional services firm Deloitte that focused on the municipality's time under Colvin's leadership.
The financial inquiry's laundry list of findings( https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/province-to-release-
findings-of-chestermere-financial-probe ) formed the basis for many of the city's claims outlined in the lawsuit, 
coupled with additional information the city provided to its lawyers after the Deloitte report was released last month.
Legal spending to 'advance their personal interests'
Unsanctioned legal fees represent the majority of the alleged unauthorized funds, accounting for more than 
$415,000. The lawsuit says the four retained two firms for purposes of failed injunction applications against McIver - 
Page 2 of 4
Chestermere sues fired mayor, councillors to recover $650K in unapproved spending
at costs of $140,000 and $240,000 - noting one of them as a bid ""to advance their personal interests in remaining 
on council.""
Colvin and his supporting councillors are accused of retaining another law firm for more than $35,000 to ""undertake 
unauthorized investigations,"" according to the claim.
""This included an investigation into the background of another member of council for the purpose of publicly 
discrediting him. In fact, the private investigator's report disclosed no basis to discredit that member of council,"" it 
reads.
Former Chestermere mayor Jeff Colvin arrives at Camp Chestermere, in Chestermere, east of Calgary on 
Wednesday, April 3, 2024.
The lawsuit says the city purchased ""mini cameras and a hidden device detector"" for more than $200 to ""covertly 
surveil staff or others at the city's staff offices."" The city bought the devices through a company owned by one of the 
city's top officials, Kim Wallace, and her husband.
To prove those cameras didn't exist, the city paid $15,000 to have a company conduct a ""sweep"" for electronic 
listening devices after officials learned of an RCMP criminal investigation( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/ousted-chestermere-mayor-councillors-claim-government-rcmp-collusion ) 
into Colvin and Wallace for the alleged surveillance.
A document Colvin provided to Postmedia in December states the sweep found no evidence of any such devices. 
At the time, he called the accusations and the criminal investigation ""completely false, made-up claims.""
Alcohol, personal items purchased on public dime
The lawsuit again points to issues with Colvin's use of his city credit card, alleging the ex-mayor spent almost 
$6,500 on booze on the taxpayer's dime.
The Deloitte report noted the mayor spent more than $50,000 on his city credit card over the course of his two 
years in office, the majority of it on food and booze, though the meal expenses don't appear to be included in the 
city's lawsuit.
The most sizable item the city's going after the mayor for is $160,000 in funds related to a clean-up at the site of a 
long-defunct waterslide park in the city - including a $4,000 environmental fine( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/chestermere-legal-action-recover-misspent-funds ) related to that work. 
Colvin directed multiple city departments to conduct work on the privately owned property after multiple attempts to 
give the owner a more than $100,000 tax refund( https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/chestermere-tax-
refund-100k ) were snubbed by a province-installed supervisor, states the lawsuit.
""At or about the same time, Mr. Colvin instructed city staff, and retained private contractors, to conduct cleanup 
work at the waterslide park. Mr. Colvin caused the city to expend significant sums of public money to conduct 
cleanup work on these private lands without any authorization by the city,"" it reads.
Additionally, Colvin is accused of improperly spending $46,000 on a summer carnival in the city last year without 
the approval of council.
""The city's event department was entirely unaware that the Summer Carnival was being organized by Mr. Colvin 
until after it was publicly announced by Mr. Colvin,"" reads the claim.
The lawsuit claims Colvin is also responsible for $5,600 in unauthorized spending to hire Dan Buryn - a former 
councillor in Thorhild County in northern Alberta who was fired by the province( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/court-rules-in-favour-of-three-councillors-dismissed-in-thorhild-county ) in a 
similar fashion in 2017 - for ""consulting services"" in December 2022.

Some other unauthorized funds tied to Colvin that the city is looking to recover are as follows:
A $94.72 spend on Colvin's city credit card for a ""digital family crest"" and ""personal seal"";
A $375 expenditure to have Colvin's personal piano moved to city hall;
A $3,100 purchase of a painting at an RCMP fundraising event, at Colvin's direction;
More than $4,200 spent on memberships for ""various individuals"" in the Chestermere Regional Community 
Association, which manages the local recreation centre.
Additionally, the city is pursuing under $700 in improper expenses by Foat, comprising $230 for headphones and 
close to $450 for undefined travel expenses for his wife.

Jeff Moroz, the lawyer for the four, told Postmedia he has not yet seen the statement of claim.

Colvin's team has long cited investigations he ordered of past corruption and financial wrongdoings at the city as

He's alleged McIver, Deloitte, opposing councillors and past city staff, among others, have conspired against him to

Title: Conflict of interest commissioner says he is not investigating ArriveCan scandal
Body: OTTAWA - Canada's conflict of interest commissioner said he is not investigating the ArriveCan scandal 
because it is not under his jurisdiction.
Conflict of interest commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein told MPs at the public accounts committee on 
Thursday that no one who has been named in the scandal so far is under his supervision.
""I understand there are ongoing investigations by other organizations. To our knowledge, no person subject to the 
act or the code were involved in this matter, and we have no jurisdiction,"" he told MPs.
Von Finckenstein's office oversees the conflict of interest act, which covers public office holders, including cabinet 
ministers, their staff, people appointed to federal boards and deputy ministers.
Deputy ministers are the highest ranking bureaucrats in government departments and appointed by cabinet, but 
other bureaucrats are not subject to the act. von Finckenstein said everything that has come up so far about the 
scandal has involved contractors or lower-level bureaucrats.
""None of the people involved in this so far, that have been mentioned, either in the AG's report or in the public 
proceedings before you, qualify as reporting public office holders so I have no jurisdiction to look into it.""
The auditor general found the ArriveCan app, which returning travellers were forced to use to report their 
vaccination status and quarantine plans during the pandemic, cost at least $60 million.
The auditor's report said the documentation of the apps rollout was so poorly done that she couldn't even be certain 
about the final price tag.
Conservative MP Larry Brock suggested that the Liberals had wanted to waste time by bringing in von Finckenstein.
""You have no mandate, yet the Liberals wasted this committee time and wasted your time sir, from doing the good 
work that you are obviously doing,"" he said.
Brock was corrected by the committee's chair Conservative MP John Williamson, who said that the commissioner 
was there at the invitation of all members.
Page 2 of 3
Conflict of interest commissioner says he is not investigating ArriveCan scandal
""The witness is here at the invitation of the full committee. So, you're welcome to raise his relevance, but he's a 
committee witness.""
On Wednesday, the committee heard testimony from Diane Daly, a civil servant who was involved in the 
procurement of the app. Kristian Firth, co-owner of contractor GC strategies, who received the largest portion of 
money spent on the app, named Daly as someone he had worked with in developing contracts his firm later won.
Daly denied Firth's claims and said she had no technical knowledge and simply processed the procurement. She 
testified to MPs that she was suspended after an interview where she believes more senior bureaucrats wanted her 
to blame two other civil servants Antonio Utano and Cameron MacDonald for the scandal.
The government suspended Utano and MacDonald over concerns about their work on the app.
Daly was specifically asked about whether the procurement minister Jean-Yves Duclos, who is a public office 
holder, was involved and she said no.
""I believe he has tried to do the right thing, but he wouldn't have known what was going on until at least the fall of 
2023.""

Title: Conservatives stymied over summer committee meetings; Liberals, Bloc, NDP all opposed to practice
Body: As the House of Commons winds down for the summer break, the Conservatives are spending the last days trying 
to get most parliamentary committees to sit for five meetings from July to September to shine a light on the Liberals' 
failings.
Their efforts have been in vain, with the Liberals, the Bloc Québécois and the NDP voting down the official 
opposition's attempts to sit during the summer.
This week, the House of Commons will rise for the summer until Sept. 16. During that time, MPs are typically busy 
meeting constituents and stakeholders and participating in events in their ridings - often, with busier schedules than 
during their time in Ottawa.
But Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer said it is ""urgent"" for committees to continue meeting during the 
summer to address pressing issues facing Canadians.
""There's a cost-of-living crisis that Justin Trudeau has caused with his inflationary deficits and wasteful spending. 
As a result, interest rates are still way higher than when Canadians locked into mortgages almost five ago,"" he said 
in an interview.
""Most Canadians are struggling just to be able to live, let alone take a lavish vacation, so that's why we've 
proposed a reasonable work plan for the summer, so that we can tackle the issues that are facing Canadians, 
propose solutions to fix what Trudeau has broken,"" he said.
Conservative MPs have presented the same scheduling motion, whether it be in the veterans'affairs committee to 
talk about how the high cost of living has affected the men and women in the Armed Forces, or the human 
resources committee to talk about the housing crisis.
In other cases, Conservatives insisted that committees keep sitting in the summer to continue investigating ethical 
concerns concerning the Liberal government. ""Part of the summer work plan will absolutely be to highlight the 
corruption and wasteful spending and potentially illegal spending that Justin Trudeau has engaged in over the past 
few years,"" said Scheer.
Page 2 of 3
Conservatives stymied over summer committee meetings; Liberals, Bloc, NDP all opposed to practice
For instance, he said, it was through committee work that MPs discovered the extent of the mess around the 
ArriveCan application and the pressure put on the Liberals at committee forced the federal government to release 
its economic costing of the carbon tax.
But NDP MP Matthew Green has been countering the Conservatives'efforts by proposing a motion of his own in at 
least two committees to ""not meet during Parliament's summer recess,"" unless there is consensus among members 
to hold an emergency meeting.
Those motions did not pass because Conservatives made sure to run out the clock, delivering lengthy speeches to 
prevent a vote on Green's motion.
An NDP source, speaking on background, said that committees chaired by Conservatives have been unilaterally 
calling emergency meetings during constituency weeks, and that the party does not want to set a precedent by 
allowing meetings over the summer.
The source added that MPs do important work during the summer - and are a lot busier than when they are in 
session in Ottawa.
""It's very frustrating to see the NDP constantly refer to themselves as the 'worker bees.'But then every chance they 
get, they buzz off and cover for Justin Trudeau,"" said Scheer.
Scheer also said it is ""incredibly frustrating"" to see Green try to ""pre-emptively prevent a committee from even 
meeting"" and said it will ultimately be up to the NDP and the Bloc to explain to their voters why they don't believe 
that it is necessary to meet over the summer.
""If the other parties don't want to do the work that they're supposed to do as an opposition party, we're going to 
keep pushing. It's our responsibility,"" he said.
At least one parliamentary committee will still exceptionally meet during the summer break despite the partisan 
squabbles between Conservatives and the NDP.
On Tuesday, members of the ethics committee agreed to invite two former business associates of Employment 
Minister Randy Boissonnault during the week of July 15 in hopes of finding out the identity of ""the other Randy"" 
who managed private business dealings in 2022.
The motion calls for Stephen Anderson, co-founder of Global Health Imports with Boissonnault, and Kirsten Poon, a 
lobbyist with business ties to the minister, to appear before the committee for an hour. They both indicated they 
were available in July.
The Conservatives have been pounding the issue because they suspect that the mysterious ""Randy"" in text 
messages sent to Anderson about a late wire transfer payment was in fact Boissonnault, but the minister has firmly 
denied it was him.
The NDP agreed to hold this meeting even though it is during the summer.
""Members around the table are very well aware of my feelings about arbitrary meetings in non-sitting times. I would 
caveat it that this is not arbitrary,"" Green told MPs.

Title: Coun. Matt Luloff faces impaired driving charges, with a broad range of potential outcomes
Body: Orléans East-Cumberland Coun. Matt Luloff was charged with impaired driving earlier in July. How will the legal 
process unfold and what does it mean for Luloff's future as a city councillor?
Luloff, a second-term councillor, also serves as Ottawa Public Library Board chair and was the Conservative Party 
of Canada candidate for Orléans riding in the next federal election until he stepped down from that candidacy on 
July 10, citing personal reasons.
According to the charges filed in court, Luloff, 40, was arrested and charged on Saturday, July 6.
He was charged with two counts related to impaired driving, the filing shows. The first charge alleges Luloff was 
operating a motor vehicle while impaired. The second charge alleges that Luloff, ""within two hours after ceasing to 
operate a (vehicle) had a blood-alcohol concentration that was equal to or exceeded 80 mg of alcohol in 100 mL of 
blood.""
The allegations have not been tested in court.
Luloff's defence lawyer, Lawrence Greenspon, signed an ""enhanced designation of counsel"" on July 9. That means 
a defence lawyer can appear in court on Luloff's behalf.
Here's a look at some of the factors at play.
Q: Is impaired driving a criminal matter in Canada?
A: Yes. The Criminal Code of Canada prohibits driving while impaired to any degree by drugs, alcohol or a 
combination of both. Penalties range from a mandatory minimum fine to life imprisonment, depending on the 
severity of the offence. Reforms were passed by Parliament and given Royal Assent on June 21, 2018, creating 
new authorities, increasing deterrence, making it easier to detect impaired drivers and simplify investigations and 
proof of impaired driving offences, according to Justice Canada.
Q: What could happen to someone charged with impaired driving for the first time?
A: A range of possibilities exist.
""You should not expect much leniency when it comes to drunk driving in Ontario,"" Ottawa criminal lawyer Fady 
Mansour says in his blog.
Page 2 of 4
Coun. Matt Luloff faces impaired driving charges, with a broad range of potential outcomes
""While some latitude is granted to first offenders and you can avoid the worst consequences with strong legal 
representation, do not underestimate the trouble you're in if you're pulled over and charged with impaired driving,"" 
Mansour writes.
Driving with a blood alcohol content of more than 80 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood is also a separate offence, 
commonly known as ""driving over 80."" A first conviction can result in a fine of at least $1,000 for blood alcohol 
concentrations of 80 to 110 mg, at least $1,500 for readings of 120 to 150 mg and at least $2,000 for readings of 
160 mg or more.
According to the Criminal Code of Canada, even a first-time offender can face a prison sentence of up to 10 years 
for an indictable offence.
""More commonly, cases proceed as a summary offence, with a maximum prison sentence of two years. Unlike 
subsequent offences, there is no mandatory minimum sentence for a first offence,"" Mansour says.
Every courthouse in Ontario operates differently, but in most cases it is unlikely the prosecution would seek a two- 
or 10-year sentence unless aggravating factors were present, such as an injury or death caused by the driver's 
actions, Mansour says.
""A 30-, 60- or 90-day jail sentence would be more typical.""
Conviction for a first offence of impaired driving also leads to suspension of a driver's licence, likely for a year, 
although that could be reduced if the driver agreed to outfit the vehicle with an ignition interlock device. Those 
convicted of impaired driving must also attend education programs.
Q: Could a conviction limit the role of a city councillor under the code of conduct?
A: Under the Ontario Municipal Act, municipalities are required to include certain areas in their codes of conduct for 
members of council and local boards. The provincial legislation specifies these areas to include gifts, benefits and 
hospitality, respectful conduct, including conduct toward officers and employees, confidential information and use of 
property of the municipality or of the local board.
Q: What about the City of Ottawa's Code of Conduct for city councillors?
A: The city's code of conduct is broader, including matters such as issues of general integrity, misuse or improper 
release of confidential information, inappropriate conduct at council or committee meetings, matters related to 
discrimination or harassment, improper use of influence and inappropriate use of municipal property or resources, 
including for campaign purposes, inappropriate conduct respecting lobbying or lobbyists and improper receipt of 
gifts, benefits or hospitality.
The city also has policies around expenses, election-related resources and community, fundraising and special 
events.
Anyone who identifies or witnesses behaviour or an activity by a sitting member of council that they believe is in 
contravention of the code of conduct may file a formal complaint to the city's integrity commissioner setting out 
""reasonable and probable grounds for the allegation.""
City council and the transit commission may also file a complaint or file a request for an investigation of any of its 
membership through a motion.
Q: Does the code of conduct address complaints outside the jurisdiction of the integrity commissioner?
A: If the complaint is not, on its face, a complaint about non-compliance with the City of Ottawa's code of conduct, 
or if the complaint is covered by any other legislation, including a criminal matter, the integrity commissioner 
advises the complainant of next steps. In the case of allegations of a criminal matter, that would be to notify police.
Page 3 of 4
Coun. Matt Luloff faces impaired driving charges, with a broad range of potential outcomes
""If the complaint on its face is an allegation of a criminal nature consistent with the Criminal Code of Canada, the 
complaint shall be advised that is the complainant wishes to pursue any such allegation, the complainant must 
pursue it with the appropriate police service,"" the code of conduct says.
Q: Does Ontario municipal law ban those facing criminal charges or who have been convicted from running for or 
holding municipal office?
A: Under the Ontario Municipal Act 2001, having a criminal record does not make a person ineligible to run for or 
hold office. Anyone who is entitled to be an elector in a municipality - meaning able to vote - is qualified.
However, the Ontario Elections Act addresses this in a roundabout way. Section 17 stipulates that some people 
are prohibited from voting in a municipal election, including ""a person who is serving a sentence of imprisonment on 
penal or correctional institution.""
In other words, if a person can't vote in an election because they are serving time, they can't be on a municipal 
council.
Q: Does an impaired driving conviction affect a politician's chances of getting re-elected?
A: That was not the case for Rob Ford in his 2010 run for Toronto mayor. After a driving under the influence 
arrest in Miami in 1999 became public, Ford's share of the vote increased 10 per cent, according to journalist 
Robyn Doolittle 's 2014 biography titled Crazy Town: the Rob Ford Story.
In November 2013, Toronto city council voted to remove Ford's authority during emergency situations and stripped 
his power to hire and fire the deputy mayor and appoint members of his executive committee, limiting his powers as 
mayor.
Q: When will Luloff next appear in court?
A: His first court appearance is scheduled for Aug. 8. The criminal matter will then be adjourned to Oct. 31, 
according to the court file.
Q: What has Luloff's lawyer said about the charges?
A: Lawrence Greenspon said Monday that he intended to defend his client.
""There was no accident involved. We will be defending Mr. Luloff, and he is to be presumed innocent,"" Greenspon 
said.
Q: Have City of Ottawa legal officials commented?
""Given the range of potential outcomes, it is not appropriate to speculate on any one outcome that may or may not 
ultimately occur. As the matter currently rests before the courts, the City of Ottawa cannot provide further 
information at this time,"" city solicitor Stuart Huxley said in a statement.

Title: Critics slam Hurley over lack of full sewage plant audit
Body: Critics slammed Burnaby Mayor Mike Hurley's first comments as chair of Metro Vancouver after he stuck with plans 
for a review, rather than a full-fledged audit, into how the North Vancouver sewage plant ended up billions of dollars 
over-budget.
""This needs to be an independent, external review,"" he told the Metro board meeting on Friday, his first after been 
named chair of the regional district, but insisted his approach to the review would be different than that of his 
predecessor.
Hurley said Metro would hire an external lawyer - not one involved in the duelling lawsuits over the plant - to help 
the board and Metro staff set the terms of reference for the review.
The terms of reference should include examining Metro's governance and organizational structure, he said.
And then, he said, Metro would hire an ""independent individual, a very independent individual"" to actually conduct 
the review.
Construction on the partly built North Shore plant began in 2018 with a budget of about $700 million. Its 
construction is now stalled, much delayed and costs have skyrocketed to $3.86 billion.
New Westminster Coun. Daniel Fontaine said Hurley merely repeated the stand of the previous board chair, Delta 
Mayor George Harvie, that Metro will conduct a review rather than a full-scale audit.
""This is Mayor Harvie 2.0,"" said Fontaine. ""You can ask any accountant.
There is a very big difference between hiring a consultant versus using an external auditor.
""What I had hoped Hurley would have said was, 'Based on public feedback, my first phone call will be to B.C.'s 
auditor general to provide the board with a few paths to consider.'"" It would have been a signal of a different 
approach, he said.
In mid-June, Premier David Eby suggested an audit should be conducted.
But Harvie had only said there would be a review of the sewage plant project, not an audit.
Page 2 of 2
Critics slam Hurley over lack of full sewage plant audit
Fontaine brushed aside Hurley's comments about an ""independent review"" using ""external lawyers,"" arguing that 
these professionals would still be on the payroll of the district.
Community, residents and homeowners on the North Shore also reacted with dismay to Hurley's first comments on 
probing the financial missteps at the wastewater plant.
""The concern right now is what appears to be a conflict of interest,"" said Daniel Anderson, a spokesman for the 
newly established North Shore Neighbourhoods Alliance, which includes seven associations.
""You have a bunch of politicians on a payroll asking bureaucrats as to how (the cost overruns) happened. It's a 
recipe for less clarity, rather than what everyone is demanding.""
Anderson said the public needs to be able to pose questions and for answers not to be potentially buried in legal 
arrangements.
In 2021, Metro terminated the construction contract with Acciona Wastewater Solutions LP and filed suit for $250 
million in damages, citing delays and escalating costs. Acciona sued Metro, alleging the regional district had 
provided unsuitable site information and other incorrect info that led to changes. Metro sued Acciona, alleging that a 
confidential report, which contained legal advice about Metro cancelling the Acciona contract, had been leaked to 
the company.
Anderson said there is concern that Metro and Acciona could settle the lawsuits with non-disclosure agreements 
that would mask to the public what errors were made by whom leading to the cost overruns. jlee-

Title: Ethics commissioner flags conflict at Sustainable Development and Technology Canada
Body: OTTAWA - The former chair of a foundation responsible for doling out hundreds of millions of dollars in federal 
funds for green technology projects failed to recuse herself from decisions that benefited organizations to which she 
had ties, the ethics commissioner said Wednesday.
Sustainable Development Technology Canada was abolished last month in response to an auditor general report 
that cited lapses in the green fund's handling of public money.
The organization received $2.1 billion in federal funding since its inception in 2001. The most recent agreement with 
the federal government, signed in 2021, outlined $722.5 million in funding, through to 2028. 
Annette Verschuren became chair of the board for Sustainable Development and Technology Canada in 2019, and 
remained chair, CEO, and majority shareholder of NRStor Inc. — a company she founded.
During the COVID-19 pandemic she voted to give emergency relief payments to all companies that had previously 
been approved for funding, including her own, ethics commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein revealed in a report 
Wednesday.
Von Finckenstein determined Verschuren ""participated in those decisions knowing that NRStor would benefit from 
the funding. They furthered her private interests, and she should have recused herself.""
She also continued to serve on the boards of the Verschuren Centre for Sustainability in Energy and the 
Environment and the MaRS Discovery District.
She failed to recuse herself from decisions that benefited the two organizations with which she was affiliated, 
though she did often abstain from voting, the ethics commissioner said.
Because of her role on the various boards, Verschuren ""improperly furthered the interests of the beneficiaries of 
SDTC funding to companies associated with those accelerators,"" the report said. 
Verschuren’s practice of abstaining from the vote instead of recusing herself ""regrettably deviated"" from the 
organization’s conflict of interest policy and ""fell short"" of the requirements in the Conflict of Interest Act, it said.

Page 2 of 3
Ethics commissioner flags conflict at Sustainable Development and Technology Canada
Verschuren resigned from her position as chair in November 2023. 
Conservative ethics critic Michael Barrett first brought the allegations to the ethics commissioner, and took aim at 
the Liberal government over the findings released Wednesday.
He said the report determined the then-industry minister ""was warned of Verschuren’s glaring conflict of interest, 
but proceeded to appoint her and leave her in the position until she was forced to resign.""
He said she ""only did this after being exposed for wasting an enormous amount of Canadian taxpayers’ dollars on 
projects that benefited her financially."" 
Barrett called for the Liberals to recoup ""all taxpayer money that was funnelled inappropriately to Liberal insiders.""
Earlier this year, the auditor general looked at 58 Sustainable Development Technology Canada projects. That 
report found 10 were ineligible but received a total of $59 million in funding anyway. 
Innovation Minister François-Philippe Champagne said at the time the organization’s activities would be moved to 
the National Research Council, where they would be subject to the Treasury Board’s rules on the management of 
public funds.
A statement from the green fund in response to the ethics commissioner’s report said it has strengthened 
governance of its board to make sure conflict of interest rules are followed. 
""A new board of directors has been appointed, with a mandate to transfer SDTC programming to the National 
Research Council.""
The House of Commons industry committee has also been investigating the organization. The committee held 
seven meetings, most recently hearing from former industry minister Navdeep Bains in June. 
This report by The Canadian Press was first published July 24, 2024.
