Title: Fall session shrouded in scandal; Deaths of children in care, triple-deleted emails dog government
Body: B.C. MLAs adjourned for Christmas break Tuesday, after a fall session in which minor housekeeping legislation was 
overshadowed by growing scandals in the children's ministry and over freedom of information records.
The Liberal government passed 12 bills, including protection for franchisees, new riding boundaries for the 2017 
provincial election and changes to workers' compensation spurred by coroners' inquests into fatalities at sawmills in 
Prince George and Burns Lake.
But the governing party was also roundly mocked for wasting time debating a special annual day to fight red tape, 
which critics say was an empty partisan gesture that cheapened existing days like Terry Fox Day and Holocaust 
Memorial Day.
""I acknowledge that the fall session did not include headline-grabbing controversial statutory provisions,"" said 
Liberal house leader Mike de Jong.
""That's not really the objective ... I, and the government, and the premier, do not measure success by the number 
of laws we pass.""
Instead, he said British Columbians care about growing the province's economy.
The start of the seven-week session was dominated by the deaths of children in government care, beginning with 
the case of 18-year-old Alex Gervais, who fell from a window in an Abbotsford hotel, where he had been housed 
against government policy.
The mother of 19-year-old Carly Fraser, who committed suicide 20 hours after aging out of government care, also 
came to the legislature looking for answers.
Embattled Children's Minister Stephanie Cadieux ordered several reviews, including an
independent probe into a sex abuse case in which social workers ignored a judge's order and returned a child to an 
abusive father.
Page 2 of 2
Fall session shrouded in scandal; Deaths of children in care, triple-deleted emails dog government
A scathing report by B.C.'s privacy commissioner kept the Liberals on the defensive, as it detailed how senior 
officials in the premier's office and ministries deliberately delete emails to avoid the Freedom of Information law.
The Opposition NDP argued government's inability to find any records related to major projects like the $3-billion 
George Massey bridge project, or the scandal involving the 2012 firing of health researchers, shows it's hiding 
records from FOI.

Title: Five things learned Wednesday from Duffy's second day of witness testimony Day two of Duffy testimony: Five
Body: OTTAWA - Five things to take away from Wednesday's second day of testimony from Sen. Mike Duffy at his fraud, 
breach of trust and bribery trial:
1. Right after his appointment to the Senate, Duffy says he was told to file housing allowance claims and per diems 
while staying at his home in Ottawa, indicating it was his secondary residence. He says senior Conservative Sen. 
David Tkachuk suggested this would insulate him from criticism that he didn't live in Prince Edward Island and 
didn't qualify to represent it.
2. Duffy spent $98,500 upgrading his cottage in Cavendish, P.E.I., to make it a year-round residence, including 
pouring a deep foundation and installing a drainage system on the property. That amounted to nearly $20,000 more 
than the Senate funds he claimed against the residence in Ottawa.
3. Former prime minister Stephen Harper would make comments on important documents using removable sticky 
notes in order to avoid leaving ""fingerprints"" later, Duffy testified. He said Harper's principal secretary Ray Novak 
was Harper's ""shadow,"" and would act as a conduit for messages to and from his boss.
4. Duffy and his wife received a total of $162,595 in inheritances from family members between 2011 and 2013, all 
of which was non-taxable. The details were emphasized in court to discredit the Crown theory that Duffy was living 
beyond his means, giving him a motive for fraud.
5. Duffy's former Conservative colleague John Wallace wrote a prescient letter to key Conservatives at the height of 
the spending scandal in 2013, arguing that Duffy and Pamela Wallin were only following the rules as they were 
written when they filed their claims. Wallace, who recently left the Conservative caucus, believed the Conservative 
Senate leadership should have stood by the senators, while acknowledging the rules needed fixing. ""I think this will 
be the only way to diffuse the obvious blowback and media hysteria that will flow from Duffy's repayment,"" he said.

Title: Five Things to know about the mike duffy trial
Body: 1 THE END IS NEAR The end may be in sight for Sen. Mike Duffy's long-running legal and political saga. Judge 
Charles Vaillancourt agreed Friday that closing arguments in the Duffy trial will be heard Feb. 22 to March 4.
2 MANY MONTHS OF LEGAL DRAMA Duffy, 69, has pleaded not guilty to 31 charges of fraud, breach of trust 
and bribery in relation to his Senate expense accounts, a scandal that reached directly into the office of former 
prime minister Stephen Harper. The trial at Ottawa's downtown courthouse a few blocks from Parliament Hill 
opened last April 7 amid a media circus; it resumed with explosive testimony in August in the opening days of the 
long federal election campaign; and testimony wrapped up this week with Duffy himself on the stand during a 
curiously abbreviated Crown cross examination.
3 I DIDN'T KNOW IT WAS AGAINST THE RULES In all, the court heard 61 days of testimony. Duffy testified he 
was coerced by the Prime Minister's Office for reasons of partisan political optics into repaying housing expense 
claims he felt he did not owe. His defence is that Senate rules were lax, vague or confusing and that Duffy followed 
the same expense practices as other senators.
4 FEBRUARY FINALE ON THE HORIZON The judge, in a threeminute scheduling hearing Friday morning, 
suggested he's heard enough. The judge asked to see written submissions from the Crown and the defence in 
advance of February's fortnight finale.
5 IT MIGHT NOT TAKE TWO WEEKS ""I'm also hopeful that will focus the oral submissions and we won't require 
two weeks,"" the judge noted before adjourning. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights

Title: Following the thread of the Duffy trial: What have we learned? Following the thread of the Duffy trial
Body: OTTAWA - With three categories of charges being tried, a diverse array of witnesses and a mountain of documents 
entered into evidence, it can be hard to follow the thread of Sen. Mike Duffy's trial.
Here are some of the key things learned since his fraud, breach of trust and bribery case opened in February in 
Ontario Provincial Court. The trial resumes Thursday.
The Herculean efforts to make a scandal go away:
When the media began digging into Mike Duffy's living expenses in late 2012 and early 2013, figures inside then-
prime minister Stephen Harper's office and his Senate leadership began looking for ways to put a lid on the 
controversy. There were drawn-out talks among Duffy and key operatives on how he would make the public believe 
he was going to repay his expenses, while Harper's chief of staff Nigel Wright would secretly cover the $90,000 bill. 
The Crown wants to prove that Duffy was either the instigator or an equal partner in the plan, while the defence 
says he was coerced into going along with the scheme.
The Conservative caucus kept Duffy busy:
Duffy is facing several charges related to travel expenses he claimed while zipping around the country to a variety 
of events which he said were Senate business. Many of those events were organized by Conservative MPs, some 
of whom told the court that the former broadcaster was a popular draw for fundraisers. Often the cost of the travel 
was many times higher than the funds raised. Duffy's lawyer has argued the Senate lists partisan activities as 
""inherent and essential,"" while the Crown is trying to prove the senator defrauded the public by dressing up 
personal or political events as legitimate Senate work.
The strange business of Senate contracts:
Duffy awarded his friend Gerald Donohue $65,000 worth of contracts for research and consulting, which the Crown 
has framed as a slush fund. Some of that money was later paid out through Donohue's family business to other 
Duffy service providers, including a personal trainer, an intern and a makeup artist. The defence says the payments 
might have been unorthodox, but they did not constitute fraud - no kickbacks or favours were ever requested in 
return.

Page 2 of 2
Following the thread of the Duffy trial: What have we learned? Following the thread of the Duffy trial
Those darned Senate rules:
The dullest part of the trial for observers, but perhaps the most important for Duffy, are the details around the 
Senate's expense rules. The court has heard that there was no clear definition of what constituted residency when 
Duffy was appointed to the chamber. Senators had broad discretion to award contracts with little oversight after the 
fact to determine if the services were delivered. The rules around what constituted Senate business for travel were 
also vague. Prosecutors have tried to make the case that some of the issues are just matters of common sense, 
such as where a person actually has their primary residence.

""This prosecution was effectively trying to put a square peg in a round hole,"" McCann said Tuesday as he and 
Carson left the courthouse. ""Basically, what the judge found is, it just doesn't fit. This was business with First 
Nations, not business with the government."" Carson was a senior adviser to former prime minister Harper from the 
time the Conservatives took office in 2006, until he left the post in 2008.
Page 2 of 3
Former Harper aide not guilty of improper lobbying effort
After leaving the Prime Minister's Office, Carson was named director of the Alberta-based Canada School of 
Energy and Environment (CSEE), where he maintained ties with several high-ranking government officials, 
including cabinet ministers and Harper.
In February 2010, Carson met McPherson while he was in Ottawa and the two became romantically involved, court 
was told.
Without a high school diploma and no experience in marketing, McPherson was hired later that year as H2O's 
exclusive agent for sales of the company's point-ofuse water systems to First Nations communities.
The group Democracy Watch is urging the Crown to appeal.
Carson still faces charges under the Lobbying Act in connection with his work for the Energy Policy Institute of 
Canada, where one of his colleagues once dubbed him the ""secret sauce"" in the organization's ability to sell its pro-
business agenda to the Harper Conservatives. The case, expected to go to court in January, also revolves around 
Carson's role at CSEE. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: Former Senate finance clerk returns to stand at Mike Duffy's trial Former finance clerk returns to Duffy trial
Body: OTTAWA - Senate officials never asked detailed questions about who or what services they were cutting cheques 
for, relying largely on senators themselves to explain how contracts supported their parliamentary functions, Sen. 
Mike Duffy's criminal trial heard Friday.
Former Senate finance clerk Nicole Proulx returned to the stand and was grilled by Duffy's defence lawyer on 
whether she asked any questions about contracts Duffy and the Senate signed, or if she was concerned about the 
practice of contract dates being amended if they were submitted after the work was complete.
There was a policy that contracts couldn't be backdated, Donald Bayne noted, yet evidence submitted in court 
shows there was what amounted to an ""administrative work-around"" in place that just saw the date of work being 
changed so the contracts would conform.
Proulx said the way contracting services were handled was one of many risks Senate officials highlighted previously 
and several memos were issued to remind senators that contract work could not be done before a contract was 
signed.
She said she never personally sought to verify what services were actually being provided nor who was providing 
them, but court later heard that her colleague in the human resources department had raised questions about 
duties outlined in at least one of Duffy's contracts.
The system for handling Senate office expenses and contracting was reviewed by independent auditors in 2009-
2010 and cautions were raised about existing policies being ""outdated, inadequate or non-existent"" court heard.
Those audits took place at the same time Duffy was signing the contracts that are now at the heart of his criminal 
trial on 31 charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery.
He has pleaded not guilty to all charges. A key line of his defence is that he did nothing criminal in his handling of 
expenses and contracts and was playing by admittedly unclear rules.
The audits recommended that polices on expense claims and contracting be clarified to senators and their staff 
and Bayne pressed Proulx on why she thought that might be.

Page 2 of 2
Former Senate finance clerk returns to stand at Mike Duffy's trial Former finance clerk returns to Duffy trial
""They should know the policy. They are the ones using the resources,"" she said.
But Bayne suggested another answer. 
""It's because it is obvious from this, that given the lack of clear guidance and criteria on what activities constitute 
parliamentary functions, as they were linked to the eligibility of expenses, it's a benefit to senators and their staff to 
have clear rules, to know, not to find out after years later, sitting in the prisoners' position, in the accused position, in 
a criminal trial what senate officials years later say 'this is what we meant by that',"" he said.
The trial resumes Monday with more testimony expected from Gerald Donohue, Duffy's longtime friend who, over 
the span of three years, took in roughly $65,000 in taxpayer money for a variety of contracts, directing the money 
through a firm owned by his wife and son.
He also signed several cheques on behalf of the firm to other individuals and companies that Duffy wanted paid for 
Senate work, including an intern, a makeup artist and speechwriters.

Title: Former top aides face data charges
Body: Six years after two controversial gas plants were set for construction in the Greater Toronto Area, charges have 
been laid against two top aides to former Ontario premier Dalton Mc-Guinty.
David Livingston and Laura Miller - who served as chief of staffand deputy chief of staffto McGuinty, respectively - 
face three counts under the Criminal Code for ""wrongdoing involving the handling of computer data,"" the Ontario 
Provincial Police announced Thursday.
It's been a long road to the courthouse: Thousands of documents were examined in a committee probe of the 
billion-dollar decision to shutter the two gas plants in Oakville and Mississauga, where the plants were first slated 
for construction in 2009.
Oakville was cancelled in 2010, a year out from the 2011 provincial election. During the last few weeks of that 
election campaign, the Mississauga plant was also cancelled, after which the Liberals formed a minority 
government at Queen's Park.
The cancellations prompted a legislative committee investigation of the decision, which later prompted the 
provincial Tories to call in the OPP when they thought key documents and emails were being withheld or had been 
destroyed.
While McGuinty himself was never subject of police investigation, Livingston and Miller were top staffin his 
administration in the days before he resigned in October, 2012, and leading up to the transition to Premier Kathleen 
Wynne in early 2013.
It's in those last few weeks in power that Miller and Livingston are alleged to have breached the public trust by 
interfering with the retention of government data. Specifically, they are said to have paid Peter Faist - Miller's 
longtime partner - $10,000 out of party funds to wipe hard drives in the premier's office.
The charges announced Thursday are breach of trust, mischief in relation to data, and misuse of a computer 
system to commit the offence of mischief.
All of the charges were laid under the Criminal Code in consultation with federal prosecutors brought in to avoid any 
conflict of interest with the provincial attorney general's office.
Page 2 of 3
Former top aides face data charges
Because the OPP investigation was already underway in June 2013, some observers have questioned the length of 
time it has taken for charges to be laid.
However, ""I realize that although properly completed investigation may seem lengthy to the general public, we do 
believe it is absolutely necessary to invest the time to thoroughly analyze the information gathered so the true 
nature of the allegations and the actions of the involved individuals are to be revealed,"" said Det. Dave Truax.
""It is not unusual for such a complex investigation to take multiple years to complete.""
In a statement released through his lawyer, McGuinty said the charges laid Thursday clear him of any wrongdoing.
Both Miller and Livingston plan to fight the charges in court.
A statement by Livingston's lawyer, Fredrick Schumann, said his client ""did nothing wrong and certainly did not 
break the law as alleged.""
""He was consistently open about his actions in the Premier's Office,"" Schumann said of his 63-year-old client, who 
lives in Toronto.
""He always believed that those actions were proper and in accordance with normal practices. And he has co-
operated with the police investigation. We are confident that he will be vindicated.""
Miller, 36, who until Thursday was executive director of the B.C. Liberals, stepped down after she was informed of 
the charges. In a statement, the Vancouver resident said she plans to ""vigorously defend against these charges.""
Miller also suggested she is being charged by the OPP because of a formal complaint she filed over one 
investigator's appearance before a legislative committee. She has retained high-profile Toronto lawyer Clayton 
Ruby in the matter and said the charges have shaken her faith in the police.
""I have always had trust and confidence in the police,"" her statement said. ""Today, that is not so."" In a statement, 
Wynne said the allegations stem from actions that predate her term in office and it would not be prudent for her to 
comment on a situation currently before the courts.
Both Livingston and Miller will appear at the Ontario Court of Justice in Toronto on Jan. 27. Neither was arrested 
but instead issued a court summons for that date. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights 
reserved.

Title: Harper ordered repayment, Duffy says
Body: Sen. Mike Duffy only repaid the housing expenses that led to his suspension from the Senate because Stephen 
Harper personally ordered him to and because he'd been threatened with the loss of his seat, he testified at his 
criminal trial Tuesday.
""Why would I want to put a stain on my name, my wife, my kids and grandchildren, who are going to hear, 'Oh, 
that's your granddad, the cheat?' I'm not a cheat,"" Duffy said, testifying in his defence to charges of fraud, breach 
of trust and bribery. ""I don't break the rules. And I was not going to embrace this kind of process and I was 
pleading with them to show some decency. All these born-again Christians are throwing me to the lions.""
Duffy's voice broke at the memory.
""No honest person would ever agree to what they were demanding,"" he told the court. But every day, he'd get up at 
3 a.m. and await the arrival of the Ottawa Citizen at his home to find out what the latest allegation was against him.
It never occurred to him that accepting more than $90,000 to cover the housing repayment - money he believed 
was coming from the Conservative party, he testified, though it was actually from Harper's chief of staff, Nigel 
Wright - could be illegal. In any event, he said, the money wasn't for him.
""I didn't accept anything for me. And anything I did in this political manoeuvre was done for the prime minister's 
benefit, not mine,"" Duffy testified under questioning from his own lawyer, Donald Bayne.
He's on trial on 31 charges, including some relating to his claims for housing expenses at the Kanata house he'd 
owned for years before Harper named him a senator to represent Prince Edward Island. In the Crown 
prosecutors' account, the $90,000
payment was a bribe Duffy demanded; in his, it was forced on him as part of a scheme to make him take the fall for 
a problem he hadn't created.
He'd claimed housing expenses because he needed to prove he was really an Islander. At the very beginning of 
Duffy's senatorial career, a University of P.E.I. professor named David Bulger had challenged his eligibility to sit as 
a Prince Edward Island senator. Senior Tories, including Sen. David Tkachuk, told him he absolutely had to claim 
that his Kanata house was a secondary residence to bolster his claim to be an Islander, he said.
Page 2 of 3
Harper ordered repayment, Duffy says
""They're the ones who insisted I claim from the beginning, the very first claim before I was sworn in, to shut down 
Professor Bulger. This is on them,"" Duffy said. ""It's politics at its most despicable. And after all I've been through, 
why would anyone want to get involved with these kinds of people?"" He didn't even need the $90,000, Duffy 
testified, but he'd pleaded poverty, playing a ""last card"" by saying he couldn't repay the expenses even if he'd 
wanted to. Wright said it would all be taken care of, Duffy testified.
Duffy said he begged Wright, Harper's personal aide, Ray Novak, and even Harper himself after a Conservative 
caucus meeting (in a moment captured by Harper's photographer), not to be made to apologize for anything.
""It's going to besmirch my reputation and, (Harper said), 'No, no, no, no. I know it's unfair, Duff. I know it seems 
unfair. I know you didn't break the rules. But the rules are inexplicable to our base, and therefore you're going to 
have to pay the money back. Nigel will make the arrangements.' And with that, he kind of dismissed me the same 
way Nigel did,"" Duffy testified.
""What was your reaction to that?"" Bayne asked him.
""I was in shock. I went down the hall to the Senate reading room and I just couldn't believe it. How could someone 
be so disloyal to someone who's been so loyal to him?"" Although Duffy insists he'd never broken any rules, and if 
anything was amiss it was because he'd followed the directions of top Tories in the first place, he conceded on the 
witness stand that he'd sent Wright an email implicitly offering to repay the housing money.
It was a set of bullet points from his then-lawyer, Janice Payne, who was advising Duffy on his predicament. 
Although nothing had been settled, that email included four options for putting the scandal to rest, all of which 
involved Duffy repaying various amounts of his claims. It wasn't written for anybody but Duffy, but he sent the whole 
thing on to Wright.
""If I'd been less stressed, I'd have cut out that bottom part,"" Duffy testified. ""I was simply trying to tell him that my 
lawyer, who'd looked into this as much as she could given the material they'd give her, had confirmed that I was 
within the rules.""
None of them involve Wright's covering the repayment costs, as eventually happened, but one of them does involve 
the Senate's covering Duffy's legal bills, which is how the idea that Duffy might get some money back in the 
arrangement appears to have entered the discussions.
What finally convinced him to go along with a plan he believed was dishonest from the start, he said, was when 
multiple senior Conservatives (including fellow senator and former Ottawa police chief Vern White, whom he called 
""a thug"" three separate times) phoned him at a hotel where he was staying alone in Charlottetown, warning him the 
Torycontrolled Senate could conclude that he'd never really been a Prince Edward Island resident at all, and he'd 
be thrown out of the red chamber.
""I realized then that - everything that had been done to me, through the Senate and the media, that this seemed like 
a very live option. That they wouldn't hesitate to do this. So I thought in my mind that night, 'This is it. I'm cooked.""
He was ill (weight up, blood sugar going wild, heart surgery on the horizon, every bone in his body hurting) and 
desperate and contemplating his ruin, he said.
""You're unemployed, you've got a mortgage, you've got all these obligations that you've rearranged so I could go 
into the Senate and gave up a better-paying job in TV, and why? So I could do something for my country.""
Ultimately, Duffy went on television in Prince Edward Island to say he would pay back the housing expenses. He 
compared himself to a North Korean prisoner, forced in front of cameras to recite scripted lines.
Even afterward, he said, he kept looking for opportunities to plead his case, but was stymied by Tkachuk and other 
top Tories who, above all, wanted him to stay quiet.

Title: Hudson in expensive fight with ex-director
Body: Hudson town council officially dug in its heels in its ongoing dispute with former director general Catherine Haulard.
On Monday, council unanimously voted on two resolutions calling for legal recourse against Haulard. Although two 
councillors were absent from the meeting, Natalie Best, whom Mayor Ed Prévost publicly noted was offsick, and 
Robert Spencer, who later told the Montreal Gazette he could not attend due to his work schedule.
This past February, Haulard was suspended for 10 days for allegedly refusing to work with a consultant, Judy 
Sheehan, tasked to work on a collective agreement with the town's unionized workers. Haulard never returned to 
work at town hall and has since launched a lawsuit against the municipality seeking damages.
As well, Sheehan is also suing the municipality over unpaid invoices totalling about $26,000.
The mayor had told the Montreal Gazette the town held back Sheehan's payments due to outstanding issues of 
legality regarding the contract which had been awarded to her. Haulard, as the DG, had initially recommended 
council hire Sheehan in early 2014.
Council has mandated legal measures against Haulard for the retrieval of a town computer and files they claim she 
kept in her possession after she stopped working at town hall. The resolution notes a civic employee, under terms 
of Quebec Cities and Towns Act, must return any assets or objects belonging to the town with a month of their 
departure.
As a recourse in warranty, council is also seeking to have Haulard included in the damages claim filed against the 
town by Sheehan.
Prévost said a demand letter has been sent to Haulard, but the town has not yet received a response.
After the meeting, Prévost said the laptop computer in question has confidential town files on its hard drive. He said 
the town didn't take legal action until now because Haulard was initially suspended for 10 days in February, after 
she left town hall, she was then asked through lawyers to return the computer but that never happened. ""It's what it 
contains and the principle of it,"" the mayor said.
The town is justified in targeting Haulard with these legal actions, Prévost said.
""We want to get it resolved,"" he said, adding while the town is seeking a reasonable settlement for both parties, the 
dispute is far from being resolved.
Page 2 of 3
Hudson in expensive fight with ex-director
Prévost said the town's lawyers advised him that Haulard, who was Hudson's director general for about 18 months, 
was seeking a ""preposterous"" severance package.
""I could be in court the next three years and still (not reach that amount),"" he said, adding the director general has 
an annual salary in the vicinity of $100,000.
At the time of Haulard's suspension, Spencer, who opposed the disciplinary action, told the Montreal Gazette that 
there was friction regarding the contract awarded to
Sheehan to be the chief negotiator for the collective agreement. Spencer stated that himself, councillor Ron 
Goldenberg, Haulard, town clerk Vincent Maranda and the town lawyer's deemed Sheehan's contract to be illegal.
Meanwhile, councillor Goldenberg noted when presenting the town's expenditures for November that about 
$95,400 was solely for legal fees paid to the town's firm, Dunton Rainville. Of that amount, two invoices totalling 
$67,463 regarded the dispute over Haulard's suspension/resignation. The legal bills for last month involved files of 
people who were once associated with the town. Aside from Haulard and Sheehan, the list references Louise 
Léger-Villandré, the former director general who faces criminal charges for fraud; former mayor Michael Elliot; the 
town's former accounting firm Boyer Bourassa, which is also suing the town for damages; former treasurer Sylvain 
Bernard who resigned in 2014 about a year after being the first to report alleged mismanagement and improper 
payroll deductions at town hall; and Trail Grubert, a former public works manager who is in a dispute with the town 
over overtime payments. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: Justice officials face questions on contract
Body: Justice department officials will be summoned before a legislature committee next year to explain how the contract 
for Alberta's $10-billion lawsuit against Big Tobacco was awarded.
MLAs on the all-party public accounts committee voted Tuesday in favour of calling senior civil servants from 
Alberta Justice to respond to questions about how the contract was awarded in 2010.
""This file looks like it merits the full scrutiny of the auditor general and the public accounts committee. We need to 
understand how this happened so it will never happen again,"" said Wildrose justice critic Scott Cyr.
Former premier Alison Redford, while justice minister, gave the contract to the International Tobacco Recovery 
Lawyers consortium.
The move sparked accusations of conflict of interest because Redford's ex-husband, Robert Hawkes, is a partner 
at one of the firms in the consortium.
CBC Edmonton reported last week that internal government documents show the International Tobacco Recovery 
Lawyers consortium was awarded the lawsuit contract despite being ranked third among three possible firms.
Redford was investigated and cleared in 2013 by former ethics commissioner Neil Wilkinson, but the Alberta 
government this week appointed former Supreme Court of Canada justice Frank Iacobucci to review that 
investigation.
Justice Minister Kathleen Ganley said this week a review was necessary because Wilkinson may not have had all 
the information necessary for his inquiry.

Title: Key players in Ontario 's gas plants scandal
Body: Ontario Provincial Police have laid criminal charges over the deletion of government documents regarding the 
cancellation of two gas plants near Toronto. Here are the key players in the long-running controversy:
DALTON MCGUINTY
McGuinty, who was first elected as Ontario's premier in 2003, was re-elected with a minority Liberal government in 
October 2011.
In that election, his party saved all their seats in the Mississauga-Oakville area where two controversial gas plants 
were cancelled after local opposition.
In October 2012, after increasing criticism over the costly decision to cancel the plants, McGuinty abruptly 
announced a plan to resign as premier. He also prorogued the legislature until February to allow for a coolingoff 
period after a bitter contempt of parliament debate erupted in the legislature over his energy minister's refusal to 
produce all documents related to the plants.
In May 2013, McGuinty told a justice committee looking into the gas plants that he was the one who made the 
decision to scrap the controversial projects ahead of the 2011 election, and that he did so without knowing how 
much the actions would ultimately cost.
McGuinty was interviewed by police in April 2014 as part of an investigation into the deletion of emails related to the 
cancellation of the plants. He told investigators his office was ""verbal in nature"" and kept few records. He also told 
police he was unfamiliar with records management policies and didn't recall talking about the issue with David 
Livingston, his former chief of staff.
DAVID LIVINGSTON
Livingston was McGuinty's chief of staffas the gas plants scandal reached its boiling point.
In 2013, police said he was under investigation for breach of trust in relation to the deletion of records related to 
the plants' cancellation, but he denied breaking any laws.
Ontario Provincial Police alleged in a court document that it was Livingston who brought in an outside tech expert - 
who was the partner of another senior McGuinty staffer - to wipe clean dozens of computer hard drives in the 
outgoing premier's office before it transitioned to premierdesignate Kathleen Wynne. Police managed to recover 
Page 2 of 3
Key players in Ontario 's gas plants scandal
some emails from the deleted hard drives they seized in a search warrant carried out on government offices, 
including one where Livingston instructs staffin the premier's office to wipe emails and keep as few records as 
possible.
Livingston was charged by police on Dec. 17 with breach of trust, mischief in relation to data and misuse of a 
computer system to commit the offence of mischief. His lawyer has denied his client did anything wrong.
LAURA MILLER
Miller, McGuinty's deputy chief, came under scrutiny when police began probing the deletion of records related to 
the cancelled gas plants.
Opposition parties alleged she was among senior officials in McGuinty's offices who conspired to pressure the 
Speaker of the legislature to change a preliminary ruling that found the Liberal government in contempt of 
parliament over the release of records on the gas plants.
Miller defended herself, saying her emails on the matter - which the opposition parties pointed to as proof of 
pressure tactics - were misinterpreted and that she had done nothing wrong.
Miller was then named in unsealed court documents that were part of the police investigation into deleted emails 
about the plants' cancellation.
Police alleged that Miller's partner, Peter Faist, was paid to wipe the hard drives of 24 computers in McGuinty's 
office after he resigned as premier in October 2012.
After leaving McGuinty's office in February 2013, Miller served on the B.C. Liberals' campaign team, and went on to 
become the party's executive director.
Miller was charged Thursday with breach of trust, mischief in relation to data and misuse of a computer system to 
commit the offence of mischief. She stepped down from her role with the B.C. Liberals and accused the OPP of 
having a bias against her because of a complaint she filed with the Ontario Independent Police Review Director.
PETER FAIST Faist, the partner of McGuinty's deputy chief of staff, was allegedly brought in to clear out the hard 
drives in McGuinty's office after he resigned amid controversy over the two cancelled gas plants.
Provincial police alleged in unsealed court documents that during the transition period to Wynne's administration, 
Faist, who wasn't a government employee, was believed to have accessed 24 computers.
The documents also allege Faist was never officially hired by the government and did not undergo security 
screening.
Police later alleged in court documents that the Ontario Liberal caucus paid Faist $10,000 to wipe the hard drives 
in the premier's office.
Police said Faist was under the impression that the Cabinet Office was aware of his presence and the work 
requested of him.
The Liberals said Faist's services with the party were terminated in March 2014, after Wynne became premier.

Title: Letters spell out alleged misdeeds
Body: The Charbonneau commission's bark was worse than its bite.
The corruption inquiry sent out hundreds of ""notices of blame"" to individuals and companies, warning they might 
be singled out in its final report. In the end, however, no one was singled out and the warning letters were never 
made public. But after the commission issued its report, it published lawyers' response letters from some of those 
who received the notices. Some spell out the alleged misdeeds for which those people and companies thought they 
might be reproached. Here is a look at some of what we learned about four people and one company.
GÉRALD TREMBLAY, FORMER MONTREAL MAYOR Ignored links between Notice: political donations and 
Montreal municipal contracts, and had heard that his Union Montreal party's lead fundraiser, Bernard Trépanier, 
was collecting three per cent of the value of contracts to bankroll the party. Tremblay denies any Response: 
wrongdoing. His lawyer suggests he is a ""collateral victim"" of the commission, at which he was unjustly tarnished. In 
a 6,500-word response, Tremblay rebuts the 13 points in the commission's notice. On being reproached for not 
doing anything about contract kickbacks going to his party, for example, Tremblay said he was never informed of 
the practice. The former mayor says he heard ""vague"" rumours about the practice in 2008 or 2009. The rumours 
were published by newspapers at the time. Despite that, ""not only Mr. Tremblay but nobody, including the police, 
was able to intervene if such a practice was taking place. It would be more accurate to say that in view of the 
rumours, absolutely nobody was able to act."" ""No
Quote from the response: one has questioned the honesty of Mr. Tremblay."" Tremblay Commission report: ""took 
few initiatives"" to require that city employees and senior officials meet the highest integrity standards. ""He only took 
actions when scandals broke, or when he feared they might explode.""
PAULINE MAROIS, FORMER QUEBEC PREMIER As leader of the Parti Notice: Québécois, she permitted the use 
of ""sectorial fundraising"" (targeting construction and engineering companies for donations to the party), and she did 
not monitor party fundraisers who allowed ""a certain proximity between political financing and the granting and 
management of public construction contracts."" Marois denies any Response: wrongdoing. As party leader, she 
played no ""surveillance"" role when it came to fundraising. She says the party did not target certain industries for 
fundraising, noting that the PQ relies heavily on donations by party members. If individual PQ members took part in 
illegal activities, they were isolated cases without Marois' knowledge. Marois pressed the Liberal government to 
hold an inquiry into corruption and to now blame her would be ""paradoxical, counter-productive and unjust."" ""She 
Quote from the response: served Quebec for many years with integrity and irreproachable honesty. ... It is simply 
inconceivable that the commission intends to draw negative conclusions against her."" The commission

Commission report: found that some of the PQ's fundraising activities contravened the spirit of Quebec's election 
law.
MARC BIBEAU, FUNDRAISER, LIBERAL PARTY OF QUEBEC Used his position at the Notice: Liberal Party of 
Quebec to influence the doling out of contracts in exchange for political donations, among other things.
Response: Bibeau denied all of the commission's conclusions regarding his activities. He complained that he was 
never given a chance to testify publicly and the commission ignored testimony Bibeau gave to the commission 
under oath, behind closed doors. ""The Quote from the response: extremely serious unfavourable conclusions being 
contemplated against Mr. Bibeau would seriously damage his reputation and leave a major stigma. ... We 
respectfully submit that the commission did not fulfill its duty of procedural fairness to Mr. Bibeau."" Bibeau
Commission report: played a leading role in Liberal fundraising that targeted construction and engineering 
companies in activities that contravened the spirit of Quebec's election law.
NATHALIE NORMANDEAU, FORMER QUEBEC DEPUTY-PREMIER No details revealed, but Notice: suggests 
she was involved in misconduct.
Response: Normandeau denied any wrongdoing. In her testimony at the commission, she was ""frank, accurate and 
complete."" Normandeau ""respected all laws and regulations (and) at all times an impermeable wall was erected to 
appropriately separate her roles of minister"" and Liberal party member. ""There Quote from the response: is no 
evidence casting a shadow on her testimony. There is no evidence to cast doubt on her credibility and reliability."" 
Normandeau's Commission report: testimony illustrated Liberal party ""double talk"" about fundraising activities 
involving construction and engineering firms. ""When it comes to attracting contributors to party activities, Liberal 
fundraisers did not hesitate to promise direct access to decision-makers (the premier and ministers). However, 
when questioned about this process, the ministers argue that donors did not derive any benefit.""
SNC-LAVALIN, ENGINEERING COMPANY Thirteen unfavourable Notice: conclusions, including being involved in 
collusion with other engineering companies, financing former mayor Gérald Tremblay's party in return for municipal 
contracts, giving gifts to Montreal and Transport Quebec officials in exchange for contract favours and breaking 
political financing rules. Denies wrongdoing.
Response: Complains that the commission's work has been characterized by ""a lack of consistency (and) perhaps 
rigour."" In response to one of the conclusions, the company suggests that it wasn't part of a secret pact to deceive 
the city under former mayor Tremblay. Instead, the ""system set up by the city of Montreal together with the political 
party in power looks much more like a form of blackmail by which they cashed in on political power via the awarding 
of municipal contracts."" ""The Quote from the response: potential unfavourable conclusions contained in the notice 
are incorrect. They are not based on any conclusive evidence whatsoever, and in some cases are not even 
supported by any evidence presented at the hearings."" The company's Commission report: employees contributed 
far more than any other engineering firm to provincial political parties between 1998 and 2011. They donated more 
than $2.5 million, with more than half going to the Liberals. The three companies whose employees contributed the 
most generously (SNC-Lavalin, Dessau and CIMA +) received the most Transport Quebec contracts.

Title: Liberal strategist fined $396K for tax evasion
Body: Prominent Ottawa lobbyist and senior federal Liberal strategist Herb Metcalfe has been sentenced to house arrest 
and fined $396,259 for tax evasion, the Canada Revenue Agency says.
Metcalfe was given a conditional sentence of two years less a day, including 12 months of house arrest, plus the 
fine, which was equal to the taxes evaded.
Metcalfe headed former deputy prime minister John Manley's failed campaign for the Liberal leadership in 2003, 
and Stéphane Dion's successful campaign for the same job in 2006.
He was also a senior adviser to Dion during the disastrous 2008 federal election, which saw the Liberals reduced to 
thirdparty status.
In the 1970s and 1980s, Metcalfe worked in the offices of several Liberal cabinet ministers before turning to 
lobbying.
Metcalfe's wife, Isabel, also a lobbyist, consultant and longtime Liberal, was an adviser to then-heritage minister 
Sheila Copps in the 2003 leadership race and has run federally for the party.
Metcalfe co-founded the lobbying firm Capital Hill Group. The firm said he has left the company.
""Herb is no longer involved with the Capital Hill Group or its operations,"" account manager Joanna Carey said in an 
email. ""We continue to move ahead with business as usual.""
Metcalfe's biography page had been wiped from the firm's website Monday.
Metcalfe pleaded guilty in the Ontario Court of Justice to a single count of tax evasion after a revenue agency 
investigation.
The court was told that Metcalfe received payments and benefits from 2002 to 2006 totalling $1,366,411, which he 
did not report on his personal income tax returns.
The revenue agency said that Metcalfe prepared his returns each year by hand, and knew - or was wilfully blind to 
the fact - that the income he received was taxable and was required to be reported on his returns.
""The Canada Revenue Agency pursues tax evaders to maintain public confidence in the integrity of the tax 
system,"" Vince Pranjivan, assistant commissioner of the Ontario region, said in a news release.

""Canadians have to trust that our self-assessment system is working and that it is fair.""

Title: Longtime friend of Duffy denies getting paid As trial resumes, former CTV colleague says senator asked for
Body: Gerald Donohue, a retired local CTV employee and longtime friend of ex-broadcaster Mike Duffy's, says the 
senator asked him to ""help with some projects"" and maybe he could ""get me some money"" to pay others who did 
some of the work, a court heard Thursday.
But Donohue denied he ever got paid personally for his work brainstorming ideas with Duffy, or for signing cheques 
to make payments for Duffy for other services that were issued on a Donohue family company. He said it would 
have put him at a ""disadvantage with Revenue Canada."" Donohue was at the time receiving disability benefits and 
not entitled to earn other income.
After a three-month hiatus and a federal election, the fraud trial of the Conservative-appointed senator, resumed 
with an anti-climatic stutter.
Two minor witnesses were first called to bolster the Crown's case that Duffy deliberately tried to skirt rules on filing 
travel expenses and cellphone plans; and the day's star witness, Donohue, couldn't complete his testimony due to 
an Ottawa storm that frazzled the video link to his home in a nearby suburb.
Donohue's testimony, first expected in April and postponed repeatedly due to his ill health, was long overdue. 
Duffy's lawyer Don Bayne had suggested at one point Donohue might not ever make it.
Yet when he finally testified via an oft-garbled link Donohue did not seem as enfeebled as court had been led to 
believe. He spoke clearly and told a tale of an odd friendship between one of the network's biggest stars and a 
former broadcast technician with a Grade 10 education who moved up to become a local CTV human resources 
director.
Donohue said even after he took disability leave due to ill health, he and Duffy talked for hours about whatever 
came to Duffy's mind, everything from whether to lease a car to his wife's pension to causes that he might take up 
as a senator.
""He'd call me up and ask me what I thought of this idea or that idea,"" testified Donohue.
Page 2 of 3
Longtime friend of Duffy denies getting paid As trial resumes, former CTV colleague says senator asked for 
'help with projects'
""Mike asked me if I could help him with projects he could undertake, he said maybe he could get me some money,"" 
Donohue told Justice Charles Vaillancourt, when asked whose idea it was to channel Senate money to Donohue's 
wife's company, Maple Ridge Media, later renamed Ottawa ICF.
The trial has already heard that Duffy issued about $65,000 in contracts to the company that the Crown alleges was 
used as a kind of slush fund for Duffy to pay for services including fitness training, makeup, photo framing and cell 
data plans that either weren't reimbursable by the Senate or for which Duffy had already exceeded his office 
budget's capacity.
Donohue said he wasn't an officer of the company, did not have signing authority, and didn't receive a salary, but he 
helped Duffy find contractors to do the work, went ""hunting on the Internet"" for information needed, and signed off 
on cheques issued from the Donohue-owned company to help his friend, paying little attention to some of the 
details. ""I simply signed what was sent out.""
In response to Crown attorney Mark Holmes' questions, Donohue had shaky recall of details he claimed to 
remember well, saying he always wrote Sen. Duffy's name in the left-hand corner of cheques issued to cover 
Duffy's makeup, photo framing, or for a volunteer in Duffy's office, for example, when in fact he frequently didn't.
Earlier, Gillian Rokosh, executive assistant to two other senators, testified to deny she trained Duffy's office staff or 
suggested to them it was acceptable to have senators pre-sign blank travel expense forms, as a previous witness 
suggested. She said she never worked that way, and no executive assistants trained others in how to run the 
offices. She said training was available from the Senate's administrative offices, and if there were questions that 
was where they were to turn.
James Cooke, head of telecom and IT services at the Senate, said the rules allowed senators to be covered for 
only seven data or voice plans on mobile devices, but that Duffy's office asked to set up an additional device for a 
staffer, saying he would pay for it personally, as was required by Senate policy.
Bayne sought to shred the witnesses' memories or relevance of their evidence to the core of the case. On the one 
hand, Bayne attacked their ability to recall events six or seven years ago when Duffy joined the Senate. On the 
other hand, he attacked the Senate rules and policies as vague, or as simply allowing Duffy to do things like charge 
Senate funds for extra cellphones.
Bayne argued that office staff needed proper equipment to do their work, and that there was room under the rules 
for it to come out of the senator's research budget.

Title: McGuinty top aides charged in gas-plant scandal; 'Computer Data'
Body: Six years after two controversial gas plants were set for construction in the Greater Toronto Area, charges have 
been laid against two top aides to former Ontario premier Dalton McGuinty.
David Livingston and Laura Miller - who served as chief of staff and deputy chief of staff to McGuinty respectively - 
face three counts under the Criminal Code for ""wrongdoing involving the handling of computer data,"" the Ontario 
Provincial Police announced Thursday.
It's been a long road to the courthouse: Thousands of documents were examined in a committee probe of the 
billion-dollar decision to shutter the two proposed gas plants in Oakville and Mississauga, where the plants were 
first slated for construction in 2009.
Oakville was cancelled in 2010, a year out from the 2011 provincial election. During the last few weeks of that 
election campaign, the Mississauga plant was also cancelled, after which the Liberals formed a minority 
government at Queen's Park.
The cancellations prompted a legislative committee investigation of the decision, which later prompted the 
provincial Tories to call in the OPP when they thought key documents and emails were being withheld or had been 
destroyed.
While McGuinty himself was never subject of police investigation, Livingston and Miller were top staff in his 
administration in the days before he resigned in October, 2012, and leading up to the transition to Premier Kathleen 
Wynne in early 2013.
It's in those last few weeks in power that Miller and Livingston are alleged to have breached the public trust by 
interfering with the retention of government data. Specifically, they are said to have paid Peter Faist - Miller's long-
time partner - $10,000 out of party funds to wipe hard drives in the premier's office.
The charges announced Thursday are breach of trust, mischief in relation to data, and misuse of a computer 
system to commit the offence of mischief.
Edward Prutschi, a lawyer with Adler Bytensky Prutschi Shikhman, says the nature of the mischief charges, which 
relate to the handling of government - and therefore public - data, suggest the allegations are a direct result of the 
possible deletion of emails related to the scandal.
Page 2 of 3
McGuinty top aides charged in gas-plant scandal; 'Computer Data'
""The suggestion seems to be (they) made use of government computers, government technology, for the purpose 
of erasing and destroying that evidence,"" he said.
All the charges were laid under the Criminal Code in consultation with federal prosecutors brought in to avoid any 
conflict of interest with the provincial attorney general's office.
Because the OPP investigation was already underway in June, 2013, some observers have questioned the length 
of time it has taken for charges to be laid.
However, ""I realize that although properly completed investigation may seem lengthy to the general public, we do 
believe it is absolutely necessary to invest the time to thoroughly analyze the information gathered so the true 
nature of the allegations and the actions of the involved individuals are to be revealed,"" said Det. Dave Truax.
""It is not unusual for such a complex investigation to take multiple years to complete.""
Another example is the investigation into the province's Ornge air ambulance scandal - a probe that started in 
February, 2013, and is now almost three years old.
In a statement released through his lawyer, McGuinty said the charges laid Thursday clear him of any wrongdoing. 
Both Miller and Livingston plan to fight the charges in court.
Although breach of trust carries a maximum five-year jail sentence and each count of mischief a possible total of 
10 years, legal experts say the maximums are rarely handed down.
Livingston, 63, currently lives in Toronto. A statement by his lawyer, Fredrick Schumann, said his client ""did nothing 
wrong and certainly did not break the law as alleged.""
""He was consistently open about his actions in the Premier's Office,"" Schumann said. ""He always believed that 
those actions were proper and in accordance with normal practices. And he has co-operated with the police 
investigation. We are confident that he will be vindicated.""
Miller, 36, who until Thursday was executive director of the B.C. Liberals, stepped down after she was informed of 
the charges. In a statement, the Vancouver resident said she plans to ""vigorously defend against these charges."" 
Miller also suggested she is being charged by the OPP because of a formal complaint she filed over one 
investigator's appearance before a legislative committee. She has retained high-profile Toronto lawyer Clayton 
Ruby in the matter and said the charges have shaken her faith in the police. ""I have always had trust and 
confidence in the police,"" her statement said. ""Today, that is not so.""
In a statement, Wynne said the allegations stem from actions that predate her term in office and it would not be 
prudent for her to comment on a situation currently before the courts.
New Democrat Peter Tabuns noted however that Wynne was at the cabinet table when the decision to cancel the 
plants was made. Tory energy critic Vic Fedeli - who along with former MPP Rob Leone first contacted the OPP to 
launch the probe - said the police took so long in order to get things straight.
""We've seen this as systemic to the Liberal party,"" he said, adding that in addition to the Ornge investigation, 
criminal charges have been laid in the Sudbury byelection scandal and a separate provincial investigation is 
ongoing.
Both Livingston and Miller will appear at the Ontario Court of Justice in Toronto on Jan. 27. Neither was arrested 
but instead issued a court summons for that date. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights

Title: Mike Duffy says his Senate appointment was meant to boost Harper Senators appointed to help party image:
Body: OTTAWA - Sen. Mike Duffy says former prime minister Stephen Harper appointed him and other previously non-
partisan people to the Senate to help the Conservative party's image and attract voters.
""What they were trying to do was put people in the Senate who would, in effect, provide third-party validation of 
Stephen Harper as someone Canadians can trust,"" Duffy told Ontario Justice Charles Vaillancourt, noting that in 
2008, many voters were still unsure about Harper.
It was the first time Duffy has spoken publicly since he stood briefly to plead ""not guilty"" to the 31 charges of fraud, 
breach of trust and bribery back when the trial started in April.
The 69-year-old is much thinner now and so is the crowd in the courtroom, much of the excitement around the affair 
having evaporated with the October electoral defeat of the Conservative government.
Duffy has long waited to tell his side of the story on his contested living and office expenses and the clandestine 
$90,000 he received from Harper's chief of staff Nigel Wright to repay some of those claims.
Duffy has maintained that he was railroaded by Harper's staff into repaying the claims, when he never thought he 
had done anything wrong.
""Nothing in my life ... has been simple or straightforward,"" Duffy told his defence lawyer, Donald Bayne, at one 
point.
That Harper saw Duffy as a political tool is central to one aspect of the defence's case. A large portion of the 
charges relate to travel expenses that involved political fundraisers and other partisan activities and the defence 
argues Duffy was expected by the prime minister to do that work.
Earlier in the trial, a photo was entered into evidence with Harper's inscription: ""One of my best, hardest-working 
appointments ever.""

Page 2 of 3
Mike Duffy says his Senate appointment was meant to boost Harper Senators appointed to help party image: 
Duffy
Other senators appointed at the same time as Duffy included fellow broadcaster Pamela Wallin and Patrick 
Brazeau, former national chief of the Congress of Aboriginal Peoples.
Duffy recounted a meeting with Harper in December 2008, when the prime minister asked him if he would sit in 
the Senate for Prince Edward Island.
Duffy suggested he represent Ontario instead, because that's where he lived most of the time.
""I said, going in for P.E.I. would not be popular,"" said Duffy. I'm from P.E.I., but many people will complain I'm not of 
P.E.I.""
But Duffy said Harper ""was bound and determined it was going to be P.E.I.,"" and was satisfied that the cottage the 
TV host owned in the province made him qualified to represent the island in the Senate.
When an academic began suggesting in the media that Duffy was not qualified because he wasn't actually 
""resident"" in the province, Duffy said the PMO and the Senate leadership assured him he had nothing to worry 
about.
That constitutional qualification is not being challenged at the trial, but Duffy has hinted that he was told he might 
lose his seat if he didn't go along with the PMO's face-saving plan to have Wright repay his expenses.
In other words, he was not bribing anyone to pay back his expenses, as the Crown suggests, but the operatives 
were threatening him.
The defence strategy on the first day of testimony was to build a portrait of a man with: solid ties to Prince Edward 
Island; a long, successful journalism career with no experience running an office; chronic health problems that 
made him vulnerable to pressure.
Bayne began by taking his client painstakingly through his family ties to The Island. Duffy's grandfather Charles 
Gavan Duffy, for example, was the Speaker of the provincial legislature. His parents spent their lives there and his 
siblings are still there.
Duffy outlined how he parlayed a TV gig as a teenager into a newspaper job at age 17. He then moved into radio 
and wangled his way to Ottawa and eventually a job with the CBC.
Along the way, he became captivated by politics, calling it: ""A fascination and what I committed my life to.""
By 1978, he was working as a national CBC reporter and travelling the world.
That's when his first marriage began to fall apart, which he blamed on overwork. He lost his children. He slept 
poorly, started to drink too much, piled on pounds.
""I was pretty depressed,"" Duffy said in response to a question about his mental health.
Still, Duffy's career continued upward. He was eventually hired away from the CBC to host a CTV show called 
""Sunday Edition."" He met his current wife Heather while working there.
He spent 20 years with the network before receiving the invitation from Harper to sit in the Senate in late 2008.
Duffy is expected to testify for at least the next few days.

Title: Mysterious friend lifts curtain on services provided to Duffy; 'Essentially Anything'
Body: There he was at last, the shadowy figure prosecutors say ran a slush fund filled with taxpayers' money for Sen. 
Mike Duffy.
Gerald Donohue shuffled into view Thursday on a screen in Courtroom 33, wearing a green-checked button-down 
shirt under a zip-up grey fleece. Then he sat down to testify over a choppy video link from his home in Carp, Ont., a 
round man with thin hair, squinting at his own screen through heavy glasses. At rest, his mouth hung open and his 
head nodded with a tremor.
Like Duffy, Donohue suffers from a heart condition and other undisclosed ailments that have kept him from 
speaking to his old friend's fraud and breach-of-trust trial. He can answer questions only for a couple of hours at a 
time, every other day.
The trial, in fits and starts since it began last April, has heard from Senate employees who arranged research and 
writing contracts for Donohue at Duffy's behest. It has heard from people who received cheques from Donohue for 
assorted services - some of them research and writing, others, such as photo finishing and makeup work and 
personal training, distinctly not.
""We spent a considerable amount of time, primarily on the telephone, talking back and forth about numerous 
issues,"" Donohue said. They'd done it for years, as friends do.
""What kind of issues?"" Crown prosecutor Mark Holmes asked.
""He could call me up and ask me about leasing a vehicle, or, um, I just can't recall all the issues he would have 
called about. But anything he felt I had knowledge of, he would give me a call. I would usually have the information 
for him at the time.""
When Duffy became a senator, the chats continued, Donohue said. Only now with tens of thousands of dollars 
headed his way from Duffy's office budget.
""What service or services did you perform for Sen. Duffy?"" Holmes asked.
Page 2 of 3
Mysterious friend lifts curtain on services provided to Duffy; 'Essentially Anything'
""Essentially anything that he asked me to do. If it was to do some research on a particular project ... a whole range 
of ideas ... that he wanted to get more information on,"" Donohue said.
""Can you tell us about the whole range of ideas? Tell us about all of them if you can.""
Donohue thought for a bit. The aging of the population was one, he said.
Donohue was a television technician who became a human-resources boss, with a Grade 10 education. What 
research did he do on aging, exactly?
""Go hunting on the Internet, mainly. That was my best source of information,"" Donohue said.
For this, Donohue - or rather his family company, variously known as Maple Ridge Media and Ottawa ICF, for 
""insulated concrete forms"" when it was a construction business - was paid something on the order of $20,000. He 
eventually quit because the Senate insisted on sending him income-tax documents in spite of his repeated 
insistence that the work was actually being done by the company, for tax reasons.
Another $45,000 or so, Donohue dispensed to people Duffy's defence lawyer, Donald Bayne, has suggested were 
subcontractors, providing essentially legitimate services for Duffy's Senate work even if Duffy paid them in an 
unorthodox way.
The Crown alleges that in a few instances, Duffy committed fraud by using Donohue to pay bills he knew the 
Senate would have rejected.
""The payments that you made ...
how did you know who to pay, Mr. Donohue?"" Holmes asked.
""I would be instructed by Sen. Duffy,"" he said. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

Title: NDP wants to reopen robocalls investigation
Body: The federal New Democrats are calling on Commissioner of Canada Elections Yves Côté to reopen the 
investigation into misleading phone calls to voters made during the 2011 federal election campaign.
The NDP says testimony given by Sen. Mike Duffy at his trial suggested Conservatives used robocalls dirty tricks in 
the 2008 election in the Vancouver Island riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands, where Green Party leader Elizabeth May 
was attempting to unseat Tory cabinet minister Gary Lunn.
According to Mr. Duffy, NDP deputy national director Karine Fortin writes to Côté, the Conservative Party used 
""automated calls, or robocalls, to encourage New Democrat supporters to vote for NDP candidate Julian West 
despite the fact Mr. West had already dropped out of the race.""
West had withdrawn his candidacy over a report that he had once gone skinny-dipping in front of a group of 
teenaged girls in 1996. Because he dropped out too late, his name still appeared on the ballot.
The Saanich robocalls, the NDP alleged, attempted to ""deliberately misdirect voters in an effort to split the vote"" to 
ensure Lunn's re-election.
During testimony in his fraud, bribery and breach of trust trial, Duffy described his visit to the riding in 2011 and 
meeting with Lunn. ""He'd had a close call during the previous election and it was only through the divine 
intervention of Doug Finley's black ops group at Conservative headquarters that he managed to get himself re-
elected,"" Duffy testified, referring the party's 2008 campaign manager. (Finley has since passed away.)
Duffy added, ""They used robocalls to misdirect NDP voters, to split the vote.""
After an extensive investigation of robocalls made in the 2011 election, Côté's office eventually laid a single charge 
against Michael Sona, a Conservative campaign worker who was later convicted for his role in the misleading 
""Pierre Poutine"" calls to voters in Guelph, Ont.
The judge is Sona's case said that it was probable that Sona didn't act alone, though no one else has ever been 
charged.
Côté looked into more than 1,300 complaints about 2011 election robocalls outside of Guelph but found no 
evidence of a co-ordinated effort to mislead voters.
Page 2 of 2
NDP wants to reopen robocalls investigation
Earlier this week, an advocacy group called the Council of Canadians also called on Côté to reopen the robocalls 
case. It wants the Liberal government to give Elections
Canada more powers to stop electoral fraud.
The council launched a 2012 Federal Court challenge of the election results in six closely contested ridings. The 
application was denied because the judge found not enough evidence that the telephone calls changed the 
outcomes of the elections.
But Judge Richard Mosely also said there was evidence of a widespread attempt to use automated phone calls to 
suppress votes.
""Mike Duffy has said under oath that the Conservatives effectively conducted a trial run of that kind of operation in 
2008, and that it was orchestrated by the head of the party's election campaign,"" Gary Neill, the Council's executive 
director said in a statement. gmcgregor@ottawacitizen.com !@COPYRIGHT=© 2015 Postmedia Network Inc. All 
rights reserved.

Title: Never-ending marvel that is the Duffy trial; The senator's criminal trial is pausing again until next Monday,
Body: Q What? What's going on this time?
A Crown witness George Furey's mother-in-law died over the weekend. He's a Newfoundland and Labrador 
senator on the committee that deals with senatorial discipline, including expense problems that make up a good 
chunk of the 31 charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery that Duffy faces.
At first they were going to have Furey testify by a video link to an RCMP detachment in St. John's, but then he was 
supposed to be back in Ottawa before the opening of Parliament at the end of the week and able to testify in 
person.
Now he has obligations that are keeping him home longer than expected. By the time he gets here, he'll have duties 
as a senator, including attending the speech from the throne Friday, but he expects to be ready to testify on 
Monday.
Q Do courts normally let witnesses testify at times they choose?
A Judge Charles Vaillancourt has been pretty accommodating of witnesses in Duffy's trial, many of whom have 
been MPs or Parliament Hill staffwith some unusual responsibilities. He's not treating Furey much differently.
Q Couldn't they do something else useful with this time?
A Unfortunately, Furey is the Crown's last witness. After he testifies, the focus will shift to the defence and any 
witnesses Duffy's lawyer, Donald Bayne, wants to call, but it's a pretty strict rule that the defence isn't required to 
start bringing its case (except through cross-examinations of Crown witnesses) until the Crown prosecutors have 
presented absolutely everything they've got, so the defence knows what it's dealing with.
Q When was this thing supposed to be over with?
A. Originally the case was supposed to be finished before last summer. But a 41-day schedule hadn't accounted for 
Bayne's detailed cross-examinations. Then Crown prosecutors Mark Holmes and Jason Neubauer added a few 
witnesses, and the two sides spent days making legal arguments over the admissibility of some evidence.
Page 2 of 3
Never-ending marvel that is the Duffy trial; The senator's criminal trial is pausing again until next Monday, 
raising the possibility it could drag on into 2016....
More court time in August still wasn't enough (it was also cut slightly short because Bayne's stepmother died), then 
they booked trial time from Nov. 18 to Dec. 17 in the expectation that would be more time than they'd need to finally 
put the case to bed.
Q Any chance they'll make it?
A Actually yes. I mean, you'd think not: Bayne has said in the past that he expects to have about two weeks' worth 
of witnesses, then each side gets to make closing arguments that'll probably take a couple of days each. If Furey 
testifies on Dec. 7 and the defence starts Dec. 8, the math doesn't work at all. (Even though they're going to start 
each day an hour early to make up what time they can.) Bayne has talked a few times about having Duffy testify in 
his own defence and a Crown cross-examination of the accused senator would take time.
But Bayne could shorten things. He could declare the Crown's case so weak it's not worth responding to and send 
everyone straight to closing arguments (maybe with a couple of days offto prepare them), or call a minimal number 
of witnesses. If Duffy had motivation to take revenge on Conservatives who abandoned him when he got in trouble, 
that's probably evaporated since they lost the federal election, and the risks in a crossexamination are potentially 
profound. Although Bayne has said Duffy will testify, that's not an enforceable promise.
Q OK, but what happens if they aren't done?
A The two sides and the judge will book more court time in the new year sometime, which will depend on the other 
cases Holmes and Neubauer have scheduled (the long break in the fall was so each of them could prosecute 
murder cases) and even the availability of the courtroom. Crown and defence also have the option of submitting 
their closing arguments in writing rather than making them live, but that's not likely in a highprofile, precedent-
setting case like this.
Q When might we expect a verdict?
A It's entirely up to Vaillancourt. But with the complexity of the numerous charges Duffy faces, other senators 
facing criminal trials on some similar ones, and yet more senators under police investigation, he'll likely take 
several months. His previous rulings on legal questions in the case have not been quick.

Title: No charges against former Alberta Tory over bribery claims
Body: Police say no charges will be laid following a bribery investigation into a former Alberta politician.
Naresh Bhardwaj was a Progressive Conservative backbencher when he was accused in March of tampering in a 
heated nomination race in his Edmonton-Ellerslie constituency.
A resident of the riding swore an affidavit alleging Bhardwaj and another man offered him $10,000 to help disqualify 
a rival for the riding nomination.
Bhardwaj denied the allegations and temporarily stepped down as associate minister for persons with disabilities. 
He later withdrew his candidacy, saying he didn't want
the matter to be a distraction for the Tories.
The NDP, which was voted into power in May, had asked Edmonton police to investigate. Bhardwaj said in a 
statement that he's happy the investigation is over.
""I have said it all along that I will continue to vigorously work to clear my name with complete and full confidence, 
and my innocence will be proven absolutely,"" he said.
""I have also repeatedly said that it is an absolute lie and the truth will always be victorious."" !@COPYRIGHT=©

Title: OPP charge two former McGuinty aides in connection with gas plants scandal OPP lay charges in gas plants
Body: TORONTO - Ontario Provincial Police laid criminal charges Thursday against two top aides to former premier 
Dalton McGuinty in a gas plants scandal that cast a cloud over his final days in power.
David Livingston, McGuinty's former chief of staff, and Laura Miller, the deputy chief who went on to work for 
British Columbia Premier Christy Clark, are each charged with breach of trust, mischief in relation to data and 
misuse of a computer system to commit the offence of mischief.
The charges stem from the destruction of thousands of government emails about the Liberals' decision to cancel 
planned gas plants in Oakville and Mississauga prior to the 2011 election. The province's auditor found the move 
will cost ratepayers up to $1.1 billion.
McGuinty's lawyer, Ronald Caza, issued a statement Thursday saying the charges against Livingston and Miller 
""confirm there was no wrongdoing on the part of the former premier.""
Miller resigned from the executive of the B.C. Liberal Party after the charges were laid.
""In British Columbia, Laura Miller is known to her colleagues as a person of integrity,"" Clark said in a statement as 
Liberal party leader. ""She has stepped down as executive director to focus on clearing her name.""
Miller issued a statement accusing the OPP of having a bias against her because of a complaint she filed with the 
Ontario Independent Police Review Director.
""Officers involved in a substantiated complaint should not have been allowed to continue investigating,"" she said, 
vowing to ""vigorously defend"" herself against the charges in court.
""Every Canadian expects and deserves impartiality and fairness in police charging decisions,"" Miller said in the 
statement. ""I do not believe that to be the case here.""
Both Livingston and Miller are scheduled to make their first court appearances in Toronto Jan. 27. Livingston's 
lawyer has also denied his client did anything wrong.

Page 2 of 3
OPP charge two former McGuinty aides in connection with gas plants scandal OPP lay charges in gas plants 
scandal
Documents released during the investigation showed Livingston and Miller compiled a list of senior Liberal staffers 
in the then-premier's office whose computers would be purged. The OPP alleged in court documents that the two 
spent $10,000 to hire Miller's partner, Peter Faist, a computer expert who was given a special password by 
Livingston to wipe clean at least 20 hard drives in the premier's office.
The OPP served search warrants at provincial government offices in Toronto during the investigation, seeking the 
electronic mailbox and its backup tapes for Miller and Livingston, between May 1, 2012 and Feb. 11, 2013 - the day 
Kathleen Wynne was officially sworn in as premier.
Police said then that Livingston was under investigation for breach of trust, but lawyers for Miller and Faist had 
said their clients were not the focus of the OPP investigation, so the charges against Miller came as a surprise to 
many.
It was the Liberals' initial refusal to hand over gas plant documents to the legislature's justice committee that 
sparked a contempt debate that eventually forced McGuinty to resign as premier under a cloud of scandal in 
October 2012.
Wynne has apologized repeatedly for the gas plants scandal, which the opposition parties called ""an expensive 
Liberal seat-saver campaign.''
The premier said Thursday that all of the events happened before she came to power, and the OPP made the 
decision to lay charges independently.
""It was a surprise in terms of the timing,"" Wynne told The Canadian Press in a year-end interview. ""The 
government co-operated fully with this investigation and will continue to do so.""
Last year, Wynne's Liberals shut down legislative committee hearings before Miller and Faist could be called to face 
questions about the wiping of the hard drives.
The premier defended the decision Thursday, saying the committee had already heard thousands of hours of 
testimony.
""It was time to write the report,"" she said. ""I think that the information that was necessary was in the public.""
The Progressive Conservatives said it was disgraceful that police had to lay charges against senior Liberals for 
destroying government documents.
""I don't know what Kathleen Wynne can do to restore credibility to the office of the premier now that the OPP has 
laid charges against top Liberal operatives,"" said PC Leader Patrick Brown.
The New Democrats said people deserve better from their governments.
""This government has grown increasingly out of touch, preferring to put its own interests ahead of those of 
Ontarians,"" said NDP Leader Andrea Horwath.
Both opposition parties pointed out a senior Liberal in Sudbury was charged with offering a job to a former 
candidate to step aside, and that Wynne's deputy chief of staff, Pat Sorbara, is also being investigated for possible 
Elections Act violations.
The OPP said it will not comment further on the charges against Livingston and Miller ""in order to protect the 
integrity of the investigation and the ensuing court process.""
